text: 33 is the sleeper candidate of Lafayette Square - people go to the area with the intention of dining/drinking at Chocolate Bar but end up at 33, either because Chocolate Bar is entirely too crowded or because a person can only drink so many chocolate martinis. That's not to say that 33 is a winner by default in any way; rather, it's the JFK of wine bars in St. Louis. Can't tell you how many times I've been here, but I always stumble out having said something I know I'll regret the next morning. Maybe it's because the wine is flowing or the loud, dark interior suggests that one can just "let it fly", but either way I've definitely had some "insert foot into mouth" kind of moments at 33 - but there's usually a lesson learned at the end of the discretion. Last night, I mistook pride for pretentiousness when one of my companions asked if they carried anything that was like Budweiser. She didn't necessarily want a Bud heavy, but something that would reminder her of it. The response from behind the bar was: "We don't carry cheap beer." And that initially rubbed me the wrong way. In all fairness, why would a nice wine bar carry cheap beer? I get it. But there was a certain smugness to the statement that I didn't care for. It was like those parents who correct you when you ask what high school their kids attend and they make it known that their children are enrolled at a "country day school" - whatever the heck that means. But just like proud parents, the folks behind the bar at 33 make it clear that they're not running some hole-in-the-wall joint with hipsters drinking PBR out of a can. I totally respect that. What I also respect is the many disclaimers on their website: http://www.33wine.com/contactus.asp - these people aren't messing around when it comes to what they stand for. And they'll defend their stance face-to-face if given the opportunity to do so. And they're not too smug to clean up the occasional mess on the sidewalk if necessary :) What did I learn last night? Don't judge a bartender by his reaction to a silly request. And don't write a quick tip on Yelp if you aren't ready to stand by your statement. Oh, and no one needs to end the night with a half bottle of champagne.
label: POS

text: Monks is a great place to go out for the night, but I can't eat there. The fries are inconsistent. some are crispy, some are soggy. The Mussels, are also inconsistent. Some of the sauces are good, like the thai red, but the butter and garlic is blah. I think the butter and garlic moules are at least the basic standard and you can't mess that up. The other Pet Peeve is the doneness of the mussels. If you order the large bucket, the top tends to be good while what's left halfway to the bottom, a good portion of the mussels, are raw or undercooked. I like raw shellfish, but not when they are slightly warm. Their bread is good. Their beer selection is good. But I can get the same beer selection and better mussles at Eulogy. Eulogy may not be as trendy, but the food is better, the bar tenders and servers are more relaxed and friendly (unless you ask for a coors light) and you have the rest of Olde City after you are done. Monks would be great, if the food is better, but my wife and I are Foodies and the quality of the food is important to us.

text: The Arts Condo building is located in the old Sylvania hotel building at 1324 Locust Street. Billed as "luxury condominium", one is easily fooled upon walking in the front door. The lobby is gorgeous - marble and hard wood, amazing modern chandeliers and leather furniture, velvet chairs, a security staffed front desk, gleaming new elevators. This is where the luxury ends. A little over a year ago my spouse and I had to move out of our apartment unexpectedly because our landlady decided to sell without telling us. (Yes, we sued. Yes, we won.) Not wanting to relocate out of our own neighborhood we rented a studio apartment at The Arts Condos. The studios run for between $800-1100 depending on how well refurbed they have been inside, but make no mistakes - these are studios at the truest sense of the word. They are extremely small, the size of a large master bedroom. They have tiny kitchenettes with one cabinet and a mini fridge. There is no oven, no counter space. The bathroom is equally small, room for one and one only. The building tries to explain away the high cost of these tiny apartments by including all utilities including digital cable access, but it just isn't worth it. Granted I haven't seen the one or two bedroom units that are available, but the majority of the condos are studios. One of the worst parts of the building is the central air and central heat which you cannot control in your unit. Sure, you're SUPPOSED to be able to do so, but you can't. I managed to live in not one, not two, but THREE different units over a year and two months in the building. I left the first unit after two months, demanding that the landlord let me out of my lease. I did this because the knob that was supposed to allow me to control my central air did not work, and it was the dead of summer. I stayed in the second unit for 10 months, but it was an ongoing struggle to get anything done. Right after moving in the central air stopped working for my entire floor, and it stayed non-working for 3 1/2 weeks. We got a notice from the management company saying that they were not responsible for helping us with the problem. Fortunately our landlord allowed us to buy a window unit and deduct it from the rent. However the problems continued - plumbing being a major issue in the entire building. Another big issue is that the property management office - which by the way is ONE employee ONLY - is only open from 8-5 on Monday-Friday, so if you have an after-hours or weekend problem, there is no one to go to for immediate assistance. This means that if you put your laundry and detergent into a washing machine in the laundry room and then it won't work, you're screwed. And yes...that happened. In the winter the heat wasn't working properly, and when I reported it to the property manager I was told that she thought the problem had been fixed...LAST YEAR. It was always something, and it was clear that the property management company didn't give a crap about residents. Only about property OWNERS. Another thing they try to use to "sell you" on living or buying in the building is an "office center" in the lobby which ostensibly provides you access to the things one might need for office purposes. What this amounts to is two PC computers in little cubby areas and one printer. The computers are internet enabled but useless for anything practical as practically every feature has been disabled. And the printer is good for copying ONLY, because it is not attached to the computers for actual printing! Eventually our landlord stopped responding to our complaints, which admittedly isn't the management company's fault, but I think he was just fed up of the constant complaints and mad that the management company wouldn't help. We ended up suing him to get out of our lease. Unfortunately we wound up stuck in a THIRD apartment on a month-to-month lease for 2 months because the arrangements we'd made to live elsewhere fell through. Those two months were our best in the building thanks in part to a hugely attentive landlord but also because we stopped taking the crap of the staff and began standing up for ourselves. One of the other things the building doesn't do anything about is disturbance by neighbors. The building is FILLED with college students; every day it seemed there was some 19 year old taking a tour with his/her parents. Consequently there is a ton of drinking and pot smoking, and partying. In the first and third apartments we had problems with neighbors being too noisy, and in the third it was a big problem. I filed complaint after complaint about the late night noise and the smell of weed coming through the walls, and nothing was done. We finally left after 14 months, one lawsuit and a lot of nonsense. Just as we were finally leaving they managed to put together a condo association. I'm glad we won't be there to see that. The Arts Condos is a MUST AVOID property in Philadelphia.
label: NEG

text: I work in the Cool Springs area and mostly eat lunch at Whole Foods but today I decided to mix it up a bit. I was finally able to visit this eatery today. The decor was typical of a chain restaurant, stuff hanging everywhere, but it was Mexican themed. It was neat looking actually with the tree limb lined ceiling, gorgeous tile work on a few walls. The patio area looked fun. The idea of the hand-rolled tortillas was nice. Everyone was friendly. I ordered the Combination #6 for lunch, which included a beef taco, cheese enchilda, and a chicken chalupa with mexican rice and refried beans. I was expecting at least middle of the road Mexican food but oh no. The tortilla chips, which were not seasoned but were the perfect thickness) and the taco were the best things in my meal and the only things that I can eat besides the salsa. The salsa tasted fresh but there was something missing that I just couldn't put my finger on. The enchilada itself was extremely bland and the texture of it was horrible, it was sort of gummy almost. The chicken on the Chalupa had no flavor. The Mexican rice was also bland as was the refried beans. It is possible that I caught the kitchen on a bad day. I may go back to have a cerveza and some queso but this was the beginning and the end of my culinary adventures at Chuy's.

text: Ever hear the saying, " You can lead a horse to water, but you can't make them drink"? Not one person in our neighborhood has gas! We depend on oil to heat our homes. Now we all know what the price of oil is and has been in the past few years, better off to have gas, it's much cheaper to have the refined product believe it or not. I still mutter at the pumps when filling my car, but I mutter so much more when I get my oil bill. For years we have used Meenan Oil and we agreed year after year on their platinum agreement for servicing our grandfather oil burner, until we decided to put grandad to rest three years ago and buy a brand new furnace. For all those years we locked into separate oil agreements for oil pricing and another for servicing. This can be done two ways, either lock in at a fixed price for a year or lock into a ceiling priced agreement which fluctuates and of course is a gamble. I always fixed myself before but in recent years I fluctuate. Since we stopped using the platinum agreement to service our brand new furnace I wanted to shop around for my oil deliveries and Meenan just could not get that through their head! Recently Meenan delivered at the tune of $3.399 per gallon when I had called other oil companies that would deliver it for $2.899 per gallon. I was livid! I've asked them for three years to stop delivering oil to my home and to allow me to shop around. Each year they give me a huge discount when I call in all upset, like "how could you?" Each year I cave in to those then offered discounts after getting myself all wound up. What deep down gets to me every time is the fact that they are there 24/7 and if I ever needed service they will be right here to keep me warm. Plus they'll spend all the time I want to discount my bill and make me happy! But why oh why should I have to go through this? I just want to go back to the good old days with Meenan, when I did not cringe after seeing that oil bill in my mailbox. Stop over charging good loyal customers and putting them in a tiz when you know you will soften those blows eventually.
label: NEG

text: For the money I'm not sure you'll find a better Indian Buffet in the St Pete area. I am Indian-American and know what good Indian food is. They serve the buffet 7 days a week (11am-3pm), and it is only 8.95 on the weekends - which is a steal. Curriez (located right nearby) charges 11.95 for a sub-quality (compared to this) buffet. They have all the 'standards' on the buffet (Vegetable Korma, Butter Chicken, Tandoori Chicken, Beef Curry, Veggie pakora, Saag Paneer, and some others). Nothing is spiced too hot - normal for a buffet (I bring my own crushed red pepper for this purpose). They also have a great Tamarind Chutney, as well as a thick Kheer (rice pudding) and a superb Gulab Jamun (sweet dough balls in rose-sugar sauce). The Naan is served NON STOP "all you care to eat" during the meal, fresh and hot. Need more, just ask...but I doubt you'll need to ask - they keep it flowing. I have not had their menu items ala carte, this review is only for the buffet. This is a smallish, nice little place with a good atmosphere and quality, TASTY food at extremely good prices. You will NOT be dissapointed whatsoever. This is my "go to" Indian buffet when I just need to get crippled on a few plates of good food! EDIT: I have since had the chance to dine off the menu several times. My review is now up to 5 stars from 4 stars for this reason. Special recommendations are the Korma (I have had both the lamb and chicken - both spiced HOT perfectly according to my request), the Samosa Chaat (samosas placed in a dish and covered in a garbanzo sauce, tamarind chutney and other goodies - kindof a "deluxe samosa". Once you have it, you'll never go back to plain Samosas!). I have eaten at Indian places all over town (there's hardly any in the Pinellas area compared to other metro areas I have lived) and Taste of Punjab is absolutely and without reservation the best I have had in the St Pete area. Edit: some other reviews fault the place for less than complex flavors. I recommend some of the tamarind chutney to zest things up a bit and add more depth. This is "homestyle" Indian food (like what I had growing up) and you should enhance it to your taste using the available chutneys, sauces etc which are there for you to use to do just that!

text: I had a wedding this past weekend outside Philly. On Saturday night we wound up inside the Sofitel lobby for drinks. There was the plan to get cheesesteaks later that evening.with Jim's being the crowd favorite. However someone got hungry early and went in search of food. Said person, my friend Montu, returned ranting and raving about the best cheesesteak he had ever had, and the place closed at 9. Now my friend is no stranger to food or cheesesteaks, so this was an impressive statement. So we all went over to what turned out to be Tony Luke Jr's. Let's talk about the sandwich. The steak is hand cut rib-eye in larger chunks that some other places. It had whizz and onions, which is really the only way to get a true Philly steak. However the bread was special. Not soft, but crunchier which made it somehow better. At around $7 a steak, it was a good amount for the price. Maria, who worked there was terrific and quite gracious considering we arrived 5 minutes before they closed and ordered around 8 sandwiches. It is true that the worst cheesesteak in Philly is better than the best cheesesteak anywhere else. If you're looking for a great sandwich and you're in the Rittenhouse Square area, this is your spot. text: The story of Cabana is a sad one for me. We were like college sweethearts who grew apart but denied it for a few awkward, painful months. My girlfriends and I used to take advantage of Wednesday martini specials for a dressy girls' evening out. The white bean hummus was (and is) spectacular. The waitresses were friendly and knowledgeable. The service and clientele changed drastically though and I no longer feel the same level of comfort. The music was the first change. I was told by one of the cocktail waitresses they stopped playing rap and other similar genres because they wanted a change in clientele. I gave them the benefit of the doubt by assuming they meant a change to the older, sleeker set which began filing in soon after. The drink prices went up slightly. The whole fee began to slowly change. I was still willing to forgive and adapt until one fateful day when the bartender yelled at us over my friend's $10 tab. My friend had put the money on the counter on top of his receipt. It had disappeared. Mysterious and disappointing sure, but we were treated as though we were trying to scam her even though the other three of us had already paid our more expensive tabs. "You can't just place cash on the bar," she said. Really? Because you can at every other bar ever. When the senior bartender approached we assumed it would be to calm her and remind her that customers, especially regulars, should be treated with respect. He did not. By then it had become a bit of a scene and other customers around us were making the "Are they serious?" eye contact with us. By the time a third employee joined and still refused to listen to reason we left. It's just one story, but to me it explains the impersonal effects of their attempt to re-market their restaurant. Frankly, even if we had been trying to stiff them, is it worth losing four customers over $10?

text: Can't say enough fabulous things about Vincente's. They used to be located in Wilmington, in Independence Mall, but he moved to Glen Mills for a little while, and now he's down on Kirkwood Highway. Yay! The restaurant is owned by Vincente, who is this adorable old Italian guy who has been running this restaurant for almost 50 years, I bet. He is AWESOME. I go to this restaurant just to see him, he is simply that cool. The dude is a freakin' institution. Anyway, when you first walk in, you'll be asked if you want a paper menu or "the walking menu." For the love of God and all that is holy, get the walking menu! The walking menu is simply this: Vincente himself comes to your table and asks you what you're in the mood for. Steak? Pasta? Seafood? Chicken? (I picked steak.) Then he asks what kind of steak you like. Prime rib? Filet? Something spicy? (I picked something spicy.) He asked me if I liked bleu cheese, and I said, "Amen, brother." So he said, "One steak au poivre!" and the waitress next to him jotted it down. The guy has this schtick down to a science. It is a script he's been reciting for 50 years. Listen to this man, he is a pro. He asks if you want some soup. He tells you the soups. We go for the minestrone, and we are very very happy. Then he asks if you're in the mood for salad. You are an idiot if you say no. You must get the Caesar salad, even if you hate Caesar salad. Trust me. I normally don't care about a Caesar salad either way, but dude, you will lick the plate and beg for more. What makes this Caesar salad special is the fact that he makes it tableside, in a wooden bowl he's been using for 50 years. Yes, he uses raw eggs; just suck it up and live on the edge, fer cryin' out loud! Then... he takes a little bowl of grated parmesan cheese and picks out a cheese wad that invariably forms... and then he flicks the cheese wad into the wooden bowl with a teeny spoon. Yeah, OK, no big deal. Then he takes 10 steps back and flings again. He shoots! He scores! Then he walks *clear across the room* and this 75-year-old guy whips a cheese wad right into the bowl. It is amazing. And if he misses you don't even care, because he is just so awesome and warm and terrific. And yes, the salad is absolutely, unspeakably delicious. Fresh, crisp, amazing. The steak au poivre arrives and it is melt-in-your-mouth perfection. That is all you need to know about that. One friend gets gnocchi and is sent to heaven. My boyfriend gets a chicken thing and he is doing the happy-food-dance. To finish off the night (because you haven't eaten quite enough yet), they'll present you with a dessert menu. We opted against dessert (we were full); however, we chose the "Cafe Diavolo: Coffee of the Devil!" Which is basically a ton of booze set on fire with a splash of coffee in it. Again, he makes this elaborate concoction table-side, and it is a delight to watch, as this schtick too is well-practiced over 50 years. It tastes great, and it will get you snockered. So be sure to linger a bit so you're OK to drive home. I guarantee you'll be saying "Cafe Diavolo: Coffee of the Devil!" for a month after you leave this place. Please go there before Vincente is no longer there. I'm telling you, you will not regret it. It is .0001% cheesy, and it is .00002% campy. Go with it. Feel the love. Bask in the history and greatness of this man. He will flirt with the ladies in that grandpa way, and you will LOVE it. If you've got any Italian in your lineage, you will be convinced you're related to him. When you're there, you're family. Please be aware that it ain't cheap, but then again, you are spending a good chunk of time there (think 2.5 - 3 hours). For two people, it was just over $115, I think. But it is worth every penny. This is my mom talking: Don't be a slob when you go there. Look nice, be respectful, and remember your manners.

text: Wow, let me start off by saying how surprised I am that most of these reviews are from tourists who visited SB once for a weekend. Granted, it says that I live in Seattle, but I lived in Santa Barbara 6 times longer than I've lived in Seattle. So let me give you all some context and a history lesson, and hopefully it should clear some things up. First, Mexico is a big country. So "Mexican" food does not just mean burritos, rice, and beans. De acuerdo? This food is the most authentic Mexican food you are going to get. Second, tourists hang out on State Street. What do you find on State Street? Bad restaurants, tourists, and stores that sell tourist shit. If you want to see the real Santa Barbara, cruise down Milpas. If you want to eat where the locals eat, go to La Superrica. Or if you want your rice and beans and your big Sunday brunch, then stay on State St and go to El Paseo. Why is there a line out the door? 1) Because the window to order is right inside the door. It's a small place. So you stand on the street. But it's not like it's cold, or hot, or rainy, or windy. So enjoy the sunshine and get your vitamin D while you wait. 2) There is also a line out the door because it's freaking good food. Why does the line move so slowly? They make the food when you order it. I know, novel idea, huh? Now for the history lesson- the owner of La Superrica was originally a grad student at UCSB. At some point he decided grad school was not for him and so he went back to Mexico, learned how to cook, then came back up to Santa Barbara and opened La Superrica. And I would say he's a lot more successful than other students who ended up getting PhDs. Because no one's writing about them on Yelp. Viva La Superrica!

text: Upon verification that the chorizo stuffed chicken wings were still on the menu, It was a return to Mosaic for us tonight. Drinks: Despite the snow, it was a summer drink fest for us. Caipirinha (I swear, I have no idea how to pronounce this) for me, the Mango Love for the beautiful wife. The Caipirinha did indeed come with cane rum (cachaça I presume?) No Bacardi here. Per the wife, the Mango Love was tasty, except for the last round, where (per the waiter) the bartender got busy. And made what clearly tasted like a Greyhound instead. Oh well. Still tasty. The plates: The aforementioned chorizo stuffed chicken wings, two favorites (lobster salad and plato curado) and the short rib sliders (technically listed as mini-burgers, but you know, this isn't White Castle). Would it be cheating to copy and paste from my wife's previous review? Maybe not cheating, but lazy. And you know what? I'm feeling lazy. Let's just do bullet points: Lobster salad -- butter lobster, guacamole, Valencia oranges, and chive sour cream (no longer "creme" apparently). Freakin' delicious. Oh, it has these crunchy garlic toast crunchy things. Anyway, it works. Plato curado: Italian speck, andouille, manchego wrapped with proscuitto, and dried chorizo. And olives. Strangely enough, the speck which was so great the first time, didn't shine as bright this time. Maybe it was the wrong side of the pig. Who knows? But the dried chorizo tasted more lively and the andouille resulted in a fork fight (three pieces for two people. Truly a Missouri Compromise was reached. Minus the ugliness of slavery. OK, bad example). Anyway, short rib mini-burgers came out next, along with a set of Rocky Mountain Oysters on a skewer. Oh wait, those were potato croquettes. My inner juvenile thought "fried balls on a stick!" But I digress. The burgers are wonderful -- you can really taste the difference in meat. And the potato croquettes are a class above similar fare at other places (see Morgan Street Brewery). The potatoes have a whipped creamy consistency -- nothing heavy here. Finally, the pièce de résistance, the chorizo stuffed chicken wings. Two hefty drumsticks cooked to perfection. Served with whipped gorgonzola and a "guajillo chile and agave nectar BBQ" sauce. One major problem - not nearly enough sauce was provided. The ketchup packets at McDonald's packs more than what they provide. Not that one should drown their food (http://www.retrojunk.com/details_commercial/149/ for those over a certain age), but at the same time, this is tasty stuff. I felt slighted. Just a little. Service was great (outside of the last round of drinks taking a wee bit longer than expected as noted above). Nothing felt rushed, despite us being one of three tables in the main dining area.

text: I, too, will never, ever use Budget again. In fact, I'm going to make it a point to actively bad mouth Budget from here on in. Everywhere. All the standard big brands are available, but in the deli and bakery sections are better service for fresh meat, fish, cheese and salads. I seem to recall back when this store first opened that there was a wood fired oven for gourmet pizzas. But I didn't see that this time, so either I wasn't looking hard enough, or I imagined the pizza ovens from back then. Whatever. The produce section wasn't any better than other places, but the staff there was very nice and obliged my odd request to collect loose onion skins (that's another story). It was also a very blustery morning, and I walked into the store cold and windswept. The big rotisserie in the deli section was very warm and comforting just at the moment I needed it. text: One enters El Rey under an illuminated theatre marque which proclaims (in Spanish) that "El Rey will change your life". These words are a bit of an overstatement, perhaps, but El Rey will certainly change your evening. Like all of Steven Starr's "venues", restaurant aesthetics is as important to the dining experience as the food. This place gets 5 stars on both counts. The design aesthetic of El Rey, however, is a major departure from the big budget refined productions we are accustomed to with Starr. The space was formerly occupied by the Midtown Diner - a mid-century nondescript grease-pit of sorts. The Midtown Diner was subtly retrofitted and redeployed by Starr to create El Rey. El Rey is reminiscent of dingy border town diner one might expect to see in a Quentin Tarantino flick, with a soundtrack to match (from the speakers blare an inconsistent variety of genres, ranging from old school country and soul, to Mexican, funk, and surf music). The mishmash of tunes are delightful. As are the obscure vintage Mexican wrestling flick posters plastered to the walls, and the framed original prison art. Very dark and eerie. Very Tarantino. The surreal mood is set. Servers sport mostly flannel and denim. They are uber-friendly, hip, and helpful. The (intentional) dinginess of the place contrasts superbly with the wonderful food and drink - alive with flavor. Lubricate the evening with fresh-fruit-filled sangria - rojo or blanco. Or try one of the several varieties of margaritas. I enjoy the sour/bitter tamarind version. Start your feast with one of the fresh fish and lime ceviches (having recently returned from a week on Costa Rica's Pacific Coast, I can attest that the El Rey incarnations are very reminiscent of the roadside offerings ). The corn on the cob, with its coating of spices and cheese, is a must try. Then work your way up to flavorful tacos or enchiladas (the short rib variation is my preference). I also highly recommend the stuffed peppers. The dishes are Mexican with a twist - but just the right twist (not too much that they loose all of their authenticity). Clearly this is not authentic Mexican (as other reviewers have pointed out). But I don't believe it pretends to be. What it is is a variation on a theme that is interesting and flavorful, and served in a quite unique context. If there can be such thing a "subtly over-the-top", El Rey fits the bill. For the experience, the cost is modest. One can get reasonably stuffed for plus-or-minus $15. And at about $7 for a margarita, you can get reasonably buzzed without breaking the bank.
label: POS

It was an outdoor feeling "European Market." Tables were spacious, menus were cute and the perfect amount of candle light. Our server couldn't be more charming. A good mix of terrified and helpful. She was always there to get water, bread etc. Finally, the bathroom was clean which is a big plus in my book. Ok, so the bad... the FOOD! It was pretty terrible, god bless their souls. My entree was "Chickpea Ragout with parmesan breadcrumb crust." I've had similar dishes at other restaurants. It was literally chickpeas in pasta sauce with a sprinkle of parmesan cheese. My partner likened it to being stuck home in snow storm and all you have is a jar of pasta sauce, can of chickpeas and kraft cheese in the fridge. You mix it up and think, "Well, that'll last until I can trek to wawa tomorrow." My partner's food was equally unpleasant, she got the chicken. The vegetables! I'm a big veggie person, but the only veggie they had was squash, which with the same seasoning was the appetizer AND the entree. In other news, the banana chocolate cake we had for dessert was delicious! Other people would probably be annoyed, but I was amused by the young-ness of the student servers. Some were seen sword fighting with giant spoons, the other doing a dance with a "fish face." We happened to be seated where they all "hang out" in between being wait staff. So, if professionalism is your thing steer clear. If you remember sweet youth enjoy the show.

text: I am a self admitted history dork, seeing as it was one of my undergraduate majors. So this place seemed like a necessary stop. I personally like the section that showed the sacrifice that the people left in the states had to make in order to support the troops. Almost the complete opposite of what we see today. The section concerning American and Japanese propaganda also just goes to show how people have to dehumanize the other side in order to carry out the horrible acts that constitute a war. On that note, I might want to ad that the section concerning the war in the Pacific did have some graphic and disturbing imagery. There were some parents with some young kids which I thought was a little out of place seeing as there were some definitely R rated photos. The museum goes far to convey the insanity and cunning it took to liberate Europe, as well. Having been to Normandy I think that gave a great picture of D-Day. A great place to take a half day and break from the food and drink of New Orleans and get your history groove on.

text: We arrived to a not full restaurant but were seated in the front bar area where the tables/chairs feel like you are sitting in an elementary art class. Bit disappointed. Perhaps if I would have worn a dress with cowboy boots, we would have been seated in the dining room? Drinks were great - hats off to the bartenders. I tried an Amazonas (some berry combo cocktail on the menu) - not overly sweet and very good. My friend had a perfectly made Kettle 1 dirty martini. Per the waitress' recommendation we tried the Stuffed Peppadews (small peppers stuffed with goat cheese, skewered and grilled) and Fried Artichoke (panko battered artichoke served over hummus and panesco, a roasted red pepper pesto type dip/spread). Peppadews were tiny, bland and not something I would recommend to guests. The artichokes were fine, the bland spreads added nothing to the artichoke - could have provided some naan chips to eat the spreads for $12. We also ordered a trio of Satay - chicken, beef and tofu. The sauces were great and the chicken and tofu were fine, but the beef was overcooked, very chewy/tough and tasteless. They obviously used an extremely cheap cut of beef and didn't cook it properly - ugh. Starting to think this could be our 1st and only visit to Rumba, we orded 2 more items to give them another shot - the Peppadew/Pepperoni pizza and the Barros Luca (a steak sandwich). The pizza tasted like it was a frozen pizza - horrible processed sauce and dry/bland crust , completely overpowered by the sweetness of the Peppadew. The Barros Luca had the same cheap tough/chewy steak that was used on the satay - inedible. The only highlight of the Barros was the tempura green beans which our waitress said we could substitute for fries - definitely get these! They are lightly seasoned with soy and remind me of tempura vegs from good Japanese restaurants. Since we were still hungry from not eating most of the food served, we wanted to try the Tres Leche dessert. Luckily, our waitress didn't bother to ask us if we wanted dessert as she set the bill down on the table and walked away. After reading on the website that drinks are "half-price on Tuesdays", I was a bit irritated when the bill arrived. Apparently, the half-price drinks are well liquor and domestic beers - would have been nice if our waitress mentioned this. My fault for assuming the advertising was honest. Won't willingly go back to Rumba, but would have a cocktail there if forced by friends in the future.

text: Awful. Really awful. I've had a lot of "Meh..." Thai food, but I had never had any that I would have considered outright "bad" until I went to this place. And the food being bad can often be made up by excellent service or atmosphere, but my whole experience with this place was negative. In my years in Tucson, I've been to the majority of the Thai restaurants in town and have never found any that I liked (I know everyone loves Char, but I've been there twice and don't like it), but I was never really disgusted by any of them. If I want good Thai, I usually wait for a California trip. Even Phoenix has better Thai food than we do here, and my time in Houston yielded some pretty decent stuff (especially when an all-vegan place was still open there). But, in spite of always living in the central area while in Tucson, I had never been to Bangkok Cafe. It was a party of six on a Saturday night. The place was about half full, so, although I had been worried about our lack of reservations prior to arriving, that proved to be a non-issue. We were seated toward the back at a table that had been set up for six, but had two of us set up between two tables, on a crack. Placed the drink orders and looked over the menu. Fairly standard Thai fare but with more soups than I had seen on others and some unattractive specialty dishes. I had initially ordered a Coke and water but, when the drinks arrived, I sent the Coke back because it was just a can ($1.50 for a can of Coke? no thanks), and the server forgot one of our party's beers. My companion and I ordered the Ka-Ree curry and a fried rice dish with barbecue pork and sausage to split. After ordering, the one missing the beer flagged down another server and tried again. After a couple of minutes, it arrived. Waiting, waiting, waiting... After about 45 minutes, I started watching what the kitchen was doing, and noticed that virtually nothing was coming out, even though there were others waiting. Our dishes were not that complex, and I don't think that, especially when the place isn't full, that six dishes should ever take that long. While that was going on, the staff started moving tables around, in preparation of a large group. There was a couple seated in the corner, who were also waiting for their food, and I noticed that the staff actually asked them to move so that they could build the big table. Wow... The food finally arrived, about 75 minutes after the order was placed, and, damn, it was awful. The curry was flavorless except for a bit of spice, and the fried rice was just awful. Really no other words to describe that rice. Everything was also excessively oily. Wait service was generally crappy throughout the meal, although they were always smiley: water refills had to be asked for, there was the beer thing that I mentioned, then they also ended up double-charging for that beer. And that comes to the prices, which weren't crazy but, for the quality of the food, were definitely high. Dishes were generally $10+ I felt a little compelled to complain, just because a lot of people likely tell them how great they are and the others, who dislike them, probably just never come here again. I didn't do this, and I'll just remain in the latter category. So, if you really, absolutely must have Thai while in Tucson, then you can do a hell of a lot better, but I would just avoid the cuisine in general here.

text: I've only been in a few actual English pubs, which were either overrun with American tourists, who are twice as irritating abroad as at home, or the English, who drink like blackouts are a religious obligation. The Crown and Anchor is more like the English pubs of my imagination: dark wood, dim coziness and a congenial atmosphere. It's covered in fascinating bric-a-brac, mostly mugs and old British advertising. The little touches are homey and endearing, avoiding the belligerent, fantastical contrivance of other bars and restaurants that try to create ambience by sticking farm implements on the walls. Here, it just works. The beer is good. They serve a fairly small selection, and are often out of the couple of popular and rare specialty brews they serve. I really like the Tetley's, but the supply chain is apparently one old man in a rowboat, who is further delayed by a fox, a bag of grain and a duck. You do get a full 20oz Imperial pint. As for cocktails, they're not bowler-hatted, sniffing Williamsburg mixologists, out to ruin everyone's fun by turning the cocktail into a play-acting fetish. Ask politely and be considerate, and you'll probably get a good cocktail. I would not recommend demanding a shiso-infused grappa appletini; it will enrage your friendly bartender, taste like lip gloss dissolved in nail polish remover, and make you look a right twit. The service is casual but generally effective, particularly if you are mindful of your basic civilities. The bartenders may not look it, but all are grizzled veterans and know your tricks and shenanigans. The crowd seems fairly local and fairly regular, and is more friendly than, say, the Old Point Bar. Food is limited to convenience snacks with a British pub theme (Walker's Crisps and Scampi Fries). They have darts, but playing on a crowded night would be inadvisable because of space limitations. There's also well-attended pub quiz on Thursdays Executive summary? It's a great little local bar, worth a visit even for non-locals. It's got character, or maybe is a character. Either is shockingly rare in New Orleans, which is so often a city contrived for tourists, or contrived to be unfriendly to anyone who went to the wrong high school (I swear, they treat high school like a secret handshake). And whoever stole the poster from the gents', you're a horrible jerk and the prime reason why we can't have nice things.

text: The short review: I'd heard such good things about this place before I went there - it's a shame my experience was so awful, mostly due to service. The experience might've been salvaged if the food was amazing, but it wasn't ... it was normal diner food. Overpriced diner food. If you're looking for an enjoyable, relaxing breakfast where you don't get yelled at for asking for anything, DON'T go here. It might be different on a Wednesday at 10:30 am, but us poor work-a-day folks on a weekend brunch schedule deserve a decent breakfast experience too. The amazingly bad details: 1) You'd think that a veteran breakfast joint would know to have a lot of food available on a Sunday morning. We tried to order FOUR different items off the specials list, and the server crossed off each one as we ordered it. He then checked, told me there was one order of X available, and ten minutes later, came back to tell me he was wrong, and that was sold out as well. How does a diner run out of food?? C'mon. It's ALL YOU DO, people. If you're a diner, you might want to, I don't know, have more food available. So we ended up with overpriced, normal eggs, pancakes, bacon. Fine if we're going to the Melrose. NOT fine when we pay $30 for breakfast for two. 2) My companion asked if they could add bacon to the frittata - the server snapped "No special orders today!" Um, okay. Fine. No need to be snippy. 3) Any server worth their salt will be able to deal with a busy Sunday brunch with minimal problems. This particularly cranky server forgot to bring the hot chocolate (after I reminded him twice), forgot ketchup, forgot the pancake syrup (twice), and totally forgot our order of grits. Then gave me a dirty look when I asked for these things again. I'd normally give some slack because it's busy, but when a server makes ME feel bad for asking for something a few times... well, that's pretty inexcusable. Again, it's what you do. Don't be bad at it and expect a good review. Or tip. 5) When we got the not-small check and noticed grits were still on the bill, we asked about it POLITELY. The belligerent server then snapped that he already took it off, and then said to the host (still within earshot to us) "I hate that f***ing table." Seriously? For politely asking one question after you've overcharged us, don't have anything on the menu, and forgotten everything we DID order? Bullocks to that. You couldn't pay me to go back to the Morning Glory, and if a friend asked me for a choice between this place and another, I'm pretty sure I'd always choose the other. Shame.

text: Beautiful, spacious, clean yoga location. Classes are held in large rooms with high ceilings, exposed brick walls, and large window views out onto Broad (or Walnut). I went for a Vinyasa Beginner/Intermediate class with Katy. The class did a good job of covering the basics, while also introducing the second-level poses for the more intermediate folks. She also called the breaths (handy in beginning vinyasa), and in a way that didn't upset the flow of the practice. I liked that the spiritual aspect of yoga was present, but not overemphasized. The staff was friendly. While there was the expected nudge to have me sign up for a package, I liked that it wasn't over-sold. The woman at the front desk was also very friendly. On all the non-price aspects, I give this place 5 stars. It drops to 4 stars because of the pricing... $18 for a drop-in normal non-morning/lunch class. That drops to $16 if you buy 10 and so on. I know there are studios elsewhere in Philly where I can go for $10 (went this weekend somewhere else for 1hr30mins for $7 versus YS's rough equivalent which is 1hr for $15). I'm having a hard time justifying the price, despite how much I love the place. If the pricing is a non-issue for you (or if downtown convenience outweigh cost), then I highly recommend this place. text: A few years ago my girlfriend asked if I wanted to join her for an authentic Italian meal. I thought we were heading to a restaurant but she brought me to the local Italian community hall. I recall surprisingly well what we ate: salad, meat and cheese, fresh pasta, veal parmesan, chicken, prime rib, deep fried frittata stuffed with spinach, mushroom and cheese and puffed pastries filled with fresh cream. We hobbled out of there, patting our bellies. The food was fantastic, but one of my favourite parts of the brunch was that we dined with people we didn't know. Gino and his wife shared our table, and it was such a lovely way to connect with a community that has such a strong pulse - and penchant for divine cooking. Forget Sorrentino's or Italian Pasta Kitchen - this is the best home-cooked Italian food in the city. Everyone needs a friend named Gino whose mama makes a mean plate of pasta!

They've got a large arcade area featuring many different games that cover all your bases. From DDR to shooting games to racing games, there's something for everyone. It doesn't stop there, however, Strike and Spare has bumper cars, a roller skating rink and even laser tag! Whether you have kids or just like acting like one, it's a great place to spend hours running around being ridiculous. I can't forget about their bowling though. They offer the largest number of lanes in town and it is practically impossible to come and not find a free lane. Their pricing is great you can pay per game or by the hour and they've got specials and deals pretty much every day of the week. They of course serve beer but for some reason not pitchers and their food is of the expected greasy quality (although their menu is a little more extensive than some bowling alleys). Because of its diverse selection of activities it is a popular place for birthday parties and get-togethers for all ages. The place is bright, cheery and clean which are typically things you don't associate with a bowling alley. text: There's not much pleasurable about traveling by Greyhound. Sadly, the Philadelphia Greyhound terminal doesn't make it any easier on you. If you a novice traveler, the Philly station can be quite daunting. Luckily (does this really make me lucky???), I'm so desensitized to the whole Greyhound experience from years of use that I know just what to expect. Expect to be provided with little information (in regards to times and terminal gates) unless you specifically wait in line and ask a teller. Expect to be treated by the teller at this terminal with the same lethargic pace and met with the same apathy whether or not you are the only person in line... or there is a line of twenty. Expect to try to be scammed by the hustlers at the front door on Filbert Street, if you look lost or confused. Expect long lines for each bus, especially if you traveling to or making a connection at NYC Port Authority. So show up early enough. Do not expect the bathrooms to always be open, in particular in the overnight hours. Do not expect to sleep in the station overnight without a ticket. You will be continually woken up by security/maintenance to see if you're a traveler or a bum. That being stated, I've been in worse Greyhound stations. TIP #1: Get there early. The staff does not care if you make your bus or your connection. As distasteful as it may seem to wait around in the station, Greyhound overbooks their buses routinely. If you're at the end of the line and the bus is full, you're shit out of luck. You will have to wait for the next bus (whether that's in an hour... or twelve hours). A Greyhound ticket guarantees you a seat on a bus, but not necessarily the time you purchased your ticket for. TIP #2: Try to purchase your ticket in advance online at the abysmally designed Greyhound.com website. This benefits you in two ways -- you don't have to deal with a teller; you can often find cheaper web fares.

Everything is great and obviously put together with great care and understanding of balance (textures, flavors) and presentation. People rave about the poblano queso but I thought it was just ok. The tapanade was great, though - really, really great. So was the flatbread it was served with. Elegant touch: Individual carafes of chilled water for each table, without ice cubes in them. THANK YOU! I need cool water to drink with my beer, and I hate places that tip the pitchers on their side so your glass gets filled with ice and about two sips of water. And thank you for letting me serve myself, so I don't have to wait, thirsty. (Not that waiting for service really happens here; even at its most crowded, the servers have been attentive but not hovering.) Beer & Wine: Don't be afraid to tell the bartender what you like and ask for suggestions. I'm a picky drinker and they've been right on the money every time for me. That's the great thing about a place like this, where everyone obviously knows their stuff: You can order your old faithful favorite, or you can expand your horizons. text: This is another unique mom-and-pop ethno-pizza combination along the lines of Brownsburg's Adriatic Pizza, but close by on West 38th street, just west of Georgetown Rd. His business model is similar to Eduardo's "Charlie Biggs Chicken with Filipino-on-the-side," i.e., cater to American tastes to pay the bills, but also share your own speciality on the side. In short: Indian/Pakistani Halal-Zabihah* Pizza ! The owner, from either Pakistan or India, wants the restaurant to be known as _American_ cuisine, specifically California style pizza. Their signature pizza crust is crispy on the bottom, and soft and delicate on the top. I loved the crust on the pizza I had, it was not heavy and chewy "industrial dough" like most of the big chains. The menu includes standard American pizza shop fare, cheese sticks, wings, potato wedges, curley fries, onion rings, garlic bread, green salad, Philly steak sub, New York steak sandwich, cheeseburgers, California style cheese pizzas with your selection of the standard toppings (but NO PORK products), oven baked chicken, and fried chicken pieces. However, the attraction for us ethnic food lovers are the Pakistani items, and the Indian style pizza with ginger. They offer chicken burgers, chappli burgers and chappli kabab, based on Pakistani recipes. Chappli is minced beef with spices. They also have a "Chicken Tikka Pizza," and an Indian style vegetarian pizza with _ginger_. I tried it, and YUM! Their other speciality pizza is a Chicken or Beef combo, with Halal-Zabihah* meat of course. (All meat served in the restaurant is Halal-Zabihah.) The Chicken or Beef combo Pizza comes with either a Red Pizza Sauce, or a Creamy Garlic Sauce. I also had the Indian style vegetarian pizza with ginger. They ask you what level of ginger spice you want. I requested "medium", but that was still enough for the ginger to have a noticeable after-bite, and lingering after-taste. But that's what I like about ginger. The toppings (mushrooms, olives, green peppers, onions, tomatoes) were cut in small pieces, but were generously applied. I'm going back to try the chicken burger and the chappli kabab. But even as a "pizza only" place, it's worth going there just for the pizza. They don't deliver at present, but do have carry out. The dining area is very large, with a large screen TV. They invite you to hold your party there, with free room rental when you order the food from them. Hours are 11am to 10pm. The dining area was clean and orderly, but without decorations. The men's room was cleaner than I expected. ----------------- * "Halal" means "permitted/allowed" [meat] (sort of "kosher") to a Muslim, and "zabihah" means it was slaughtered according to Islamic regulations.

text: I've been coming to Rose's for years, and it's one of the most underrated and under-appreciated places in Reno. I guess part of that is due to its location; it's on Center street in an area that's mostly residential, and it's in a cute old brick house that doesn't look at all like a restaurant. Driving past it without knowing any better, I would easily pass over it. Rose's specialty is sandwiches, and they make a wonderful sandwich. Their menu has a surprising amount of variety for how little it looks. I've always been pleasantly surprised at the freshness of the ingredients and the quickness of the kitchen. Rose's serves most of their sandwiches with grilled/pressed bread, which is unique. The sandwiches aren't pressed like a panini, and the entire sandwich isn't hot. The meat/fillings are cold or room temperature. It's just the bread that's warm and toasty, and it's a wonderful combination of temperatures, textures, and flavors that sets Rose's apart from the myriad of other sandwich places in Reno. My favorite things about Rose's are the bread, the bacon, and the salad dressing. They have one of the best dutch crunch rolls I've ever had. They toast/press their sandwiches, but they aren't paninis. They're just warmed and slightly toasted. The bread is soft, crisp, and buttery. Their bacon is always crisp and tasty, without being too fatty or salty, and they use a homemade poppy seed dressing on their salads which is wonderful. They're also one of the only sandwich places I've ever been to which serve their tomatoes thinly sliced and at room temperature. Chilling a tomato kills the texture and flavor, and on a sandwich, turns it into a lump of dense, fibrous "blech." Room temperature tomatoes have the bite they're supposed to have, and I never pick them off at Rose's. My favorite sandwich there is the Monet - turkey, avocado, bacon, tomato, and mayo. I always get it on dutch crunch and I always get the salad. They also give you a little brownie with your sandwich, and it's touches like that, that really set this place apart. Prices are good, especially considering the food you get. $9 or less for the sandwiches, which come with salad or chips. They don't have a soda fountain, so you get cans that are individually priced. Soda drinkers might not appreciate that. I usually stick with water, or I get a milkshake. Their milkshakes are fantastic and rival the Gold & Silver's. They're made the old fashioned way with ice cream and milk in the tin, and they're big. Definitely one of the best sandwich places to go in Reno, especially if you're looking for something a little different.

I've tried several of the low calorie muffins which are a bit styrofoamish, but not bad. The cakes look lovely, but I haven't tried them. I would definitely give this place 5 stars if it weren't for the short hours (they stop serving food at about 3 PM, which drives me nuts), the sky high prices (my salad typically runs more than $10), and the policy to disrupt wi-fi access at peak hours. I understand, because the place is often crowded and without available seating...but as someone who often goes to coffeehouses to work, I end up bypassing this one for other places for that reason.

text: This is part one of my review, since Yelp limits reviews to 5001 characters. Who needs Michelin stars anyway? Who cares that one of the former executive chefs went on to become the one of the worst Food network personalites (in a league with such intolerables as Bobby Flay and Robert Irvine). Who cares that this place used to be a brothel, or that it's one of the ubiquitous Brennan establishments. This place, despite all that it seems to have going against it, is a godsend in a day and age where molecular gastronomy is considered "hip and with it." There are no bullshit foams, sous-vides, or liquid nitrogen encapsulations. No. This place is "inventive classic" which is exactly what New Orleans stands for. If you want boring and uninventive classic, then try Galatoire's, which is a great place and all, but if you want to be wowed, go and eat at Commander's Palace. I really hate doling out 5-star reviews, because I tend to find imperfections in most all restaurants I go to, and am never really satisfied. Well, I've gotta say I was completely floored upon eating here. I was really expecting it to be all hype, but without a doubt this is probably my favorite restaurant (in the world?). First thing's first. This place is not in any way "palace-like". It is not over-indulgent, decadent, or opulent. Though some may find this to their detriment, I thought that it was perfect because while I love fine dining, I do not like overtly stuffy places, and this is in no way stuffy. The space was refined and inviting. You got the feeling that you were dining in a nice restaurant, but you didn't feel like "oh my God how much is this going to cost me?" sort of deal. The service is amazing, and typically you'll have a head waiter attend to your table. We had a guy named Todd who was nice and all, but his biggest accolade was how much he knew about the place. I was shocked to discover he'd only been working there a year (I figured New Orleans waiters were typically long-term type of people). Though it took a little while to get started, once we did, Todd was very helpful. He knew a lot about the dishes, as well as the history of the place. I didn't know if Chef Torrie McPhail was still there at Commanders, so I asked Todd. He said, "yep, he's back in the kitchen. Would you like to go see him?" This definitely was not something I expected to be offered. While I politefully declined, I did ask for a tour after our meal, since we finished up right after closing time. He politefully obliged, and showed us the kitchen, the courtyard, and even over for a peek at the Brennan residence (from the outside). This guy gets six stars if it were possible. Before I get into the food, let me say that we had a group of six. For bigger groups, I would recommend booking two weeks out if you can. I called a week before, and they were all full. They did tell me to call a few days before in case there's any cancellations, and luckily a table had opened up. Even still, to be on the safe side if you know you'll be eating here, then I recommend booking early. I think it's easier to book for two or four, but do know that reservations are harder to come by. Nothing ridiculous, just a week or two out and you should be good. So into the food (this is what you're dying to read anyway if you haven't already skipped the rest of this review). There were several options on the menu ranging from a la carte dishes to a seven-course tasting menu for two that was $130. There was a three-course reveillon (Christmas) prix-fixe option that was $40, which included a soup of your choice, a choice of hand-selected entrees, and any dessert. $40 may sound like a lot, but for a restaurant like Commander's, I expected it to cost more. $40 seemed like a value to me. So to start the meal, they bring you garlic bread (I know, it sounds de classé), but the garlic bread was amazing. Light and airy french bread perfectly buttered and toasted in a refined manner. We started with three appetizers to split between six of us. There were two oyster dishes: Oysters Remy, and the Oyster Dome. The Oysters Remy were decently sized gulf oysters fried, atop a bed of local greens with an extremely delicious sauce. This was an excellent dish. The Oyster Dome was not as exciting but still extremely good. It was a baked concotion of oysters, heavy cream, and lord knows what else (artichoke hearts maybe?) The star of the appetizer course was seared Foie Gras. I'm still relatively new to Foie, but compared to the other two times I'd had it, Commander's takes the cake. The foie had a nice char to it, but just instantly melted the second it enters your mouth. It even came with a cafe au lait shooter that paired extremely well with the Foie. The flavors going on in that plate are beyond explainable and are probably one of the dishes I would have served at my final meal.

text: Tried the $49 Seafood Buffet, only available on Thursday nights! It wasn't very hard to find seating here if you intended to sit indoors. The shrimp was good. I didn't have a problem with that. The crab legs varied in taste. Sometimes it was good and tasted normal. Other times it was crunchy (still partially frozen). And other times it just tasted funky, but that was rare. The lobster was a bit disappointing. If you go to a place like Red Lobster, the meat usually comes out in one piece and is pretty tender. But the lobster meat here was stuck to the tail and was pretty difficult to get out. And in the end, there wasn't much flavor to it either, so I thought it was more trouble than it was worth and didn't eat much of it afterward. On the plus side, they bring out the lobster tails pretty quickly (as opposed to other restaurants which may bring them out every hour). The sashimi here was good, too. I can't tell if it was fresh or not. I think it was? There were also some California Rolls to fill me up. The servers here are nice, too. They're always around to clear your plates. They don't just stand behind the table and slice you fish but will look around for things to do to help and will answer your questions if you have any. Overall, 3 stars for the food (kind of pricey and the bulk of the price, which is probably the lobster, wasn't all that great), and an additional star for the atmosphere. I guess if you're planning on coming here, try making reservations for a table outside.

Shiner on tap is only $2.50 and the pool is pay by the hour not the game so you won't break the bank coming here. The tables are kept in great condition as evidenced by the bar's popularity with weekly league matches. Cue's is right above Pizza Perfect, next to Lone Wolf tattoo, and it's open every night. Come on by and make some new friends, admire the imposing row of trophies, and laugh at the pictures of regulars that line the walls. Next pint is on me if you can find the photo of the N*Sync member who stopped by one night!

text: There aren't a lot of non-franchise, quality BBQ places in the area so it's great to have one in your own backyard. Prices are very reasonable. text: Sheesh. Don't forget to bring your twenties... This little food market doesn't play around. It's a nice, much cleaner alternative with slightly better food options than the rest of the Suburban Station trench warfare fried chicken/Mickey D's/pizza hut selections. With a second DiBrunos', La Scala, Mexican Post, and a Termini Brothers outposts - along with a Jake & Max salad/soup/sandwich deli, Sookhee's produce/juice bar, Frank's Philly's sandwiches,Tokyo Sushi, Under the C seafood/prepared foods - you'd think you'd be able to eat to your heart's content. If you're ready to drop about 15 buckaroos for a ho-hum lunch (that includes a beverage), I guess you can. Jake and Max and The Mexican Post are the most affordable of the bunch - but their offerings aren't very appetizing. The DiBruno's, is just a replica of the one on 18th with a smaller selection. Tokyo and Under the C are pretty pricey and they too, offer pretty average stuff. La Scala seems to be the better of the bunch, but only if you're prepared to spend a little more for their gourmet pizza entrées and salads. Sook Hee's produce is fresh and the juice bar is pretty good. They've got a nice orange juicer and I like to treat myself every once in a while to a small one at $2.99. I'd still prefer to get my produce at Sue's (definitely cheaper) on 18th, though - even with the walk. If the weather is shite and you're stranded in Suburban with nowhere to go, the Market is a good option - it gets pretty crowded during mid-day lunch rush (go before noon or after 1:30), but there are always tables available. Despite all the glitz though, I don't find it to be any better than what they offer at Liberty Place only two blocks down.
label: NEG

text: Recently, I wrote about the disappointing search for good pad Thai in my area. I promptly placed my order and was told it would be ready in 20 minutes. A half hour later, I pulled a huge container of steaming hot goodness from the brown paper bag. The noodles did not appear oily at all, which meant the dish was created by Thailand standards as opposed to most Americanized versions which are made with oil (yeah, I looked it up- Wikipedia rocks!). My request to 86 the tofu was honored. Not only was the serving size large enough for two lunches, it was also light, flavorful and just all-around awesome. Pad Thai victory!!!

text: So ... I'm a New Yorker, recently visited Nashville, taken by old friend to Virago when we settled on wanting sushi. It's not the worst sushi I've ever had by far, & also not the best. I would give this place 3 or even 4 stars except for the fact that this was perhaps the very worst service I have received at any restaurant in my entire lifetime. And I am not exaggerating. The waitress (who looks somewhat like a young Meryl Streep) must be either new or just coming out of a coma. She suggested we get appetizers because we'd not ordered nearly enough for our main course. Wrong. The main courses we ordered were enough for at least FOUR adults (there were only 2 of us). Then (get this), the main courses arrive BEFORE the appetizers (which, in fact, were NEVER served ... waitress said they must've gotten accidentally taken to another table, wtf????). I got a bad feeling when I arrived about 15 min ahead of my friend & was seated & promptly IGNORED the entire time before my friend arrived ... no "can I get you something to drink?", nothing. Literally, I had to get up, go to the hostess & ask her to please send somebody to take my drink order ... and STILL it was several minutes of waiting. Then, as my friend & I are wrapping up our dinner, we glance over & see our waitress sitting at a nearby booth, patiently wrapping knives & forks in napkins even before we've finished our meal!! Um, check please???? (Any restaurant that takes service seriously does not have waiters wrapping silverware at a booth while diners are still present, good god, who doesn't know THAT?? Maybe at a diner that's acceptable, but not a serious restaurant.) Look, I know I'm from New York, where a place like this would go under in about 5 minutes w/ this kind of horrendous service. Yes, I get that it is important to "slow down" & be patient when visiting the South, & normally I LOVE that things there operate at a more relaxed pace... that is, in fact, part of its charm. But this place takes nightmare service to a whole new level. Plus, it seems to be a bit of a "scene," lots of loud, drunken, screaming girls at every other table. I felt like I was in some dive campus bar. Hope Meryl Streep's a better actor/singer/whatever than a waitress.

text: Poor Sam...his reputation as the Sushi Nazi is hardly fair. He's merely misunderstood, and considering the fact that he owns and operates his modest little sushi shop all by his lonesome, I think his behavior is perfectly warranted. Sam's is right on the corner of Printer's Alley, one of Nashville's most unique little districts. The restaurant is very small and has only enough room for two (possibly three) parties to dine there at a time. During typical lunch hours and sometimes on weekends, Sam is extremely busy and (as the sign on his door indicates) your wait time might be pretty long. But trust me...it's worth it. Sam's rolls are extremely cheap and the portions are the biggest I've ever had. Just today, Sam told me his sushi is "the cheapest in America. Maybe not the whole world, but definitely in America." The funny part? He's probably right. My buds and I got six enormous rolls and three drinks for only $19 (see the photo). The Nashville, California, Eel and Crunchy Shrimp rolls are all delectable, and the serving sizes are each about the size of your forearm. Sam's wasabi is amazing (I'm certain it's made in-house), and you'll probably need to take about half of your food to go. Sure, Sam can be a bit eccentric at times, but the man is an artist. Allow him his eccentricities.
label: POS

text: I was going to preface this review with a defense of Starbucks, but changed my mind and decided to not get into the politics and simply stick to reviewing. (Though I will say - politics does influence where I will spend my money.) In some ways, a Starbucks is a Starbucks. At least if you are at a Company Store and not a Licensed Location (of which there are thankfully few.) However, in the world of "the same" this location stands out as wonderful. The Baristas are uniquely friendly. They also do seem to try harder to be helpful than at other locations. I have on a few occasions needed to speak to a manager, not for problems, but to get information, and the woman who seems to be the store manager is knowledgeable and responsive. She also seems to have a good rapport with the staff, which may account for the quality of service. The store, and specifically the restroom, is always clean, and when I have found it lacking in a paper product, they are quick to fix the problem. Although the lines can be long, service doesn't dawdle. On the other hand, when it isn't busy, staff is happy to chat about coffee, or movies, if you are interested and don't interfere with their work getting done. There are plenty of tables, and four areas which have power outlets, which is more than most locations, so it is truly possible to be there and get work done. It does get crowded at times, especially during exam weeks at Drexel and Penn, but I have only once, out of many visits had to leave because I couldn't find a seat. This is not the ONLY Starbucks in Philly that I like, but it is my favorite! On a Company-wide note - they now use NO High Fructose Corn Syrup in ANYTHING. Desserts are back on my menu!

text: I went to the Melting Pot for the first time today. I had heard a lot about it, but somehow had never gotten around to trying it. I was not disappointed. We ordered two big things of cheese (plain cheddar and some sort of spicy salsa type of deal). It came with various types of bread, vegetables, and apples for dipping. It was all delicious. The spicy cheese was definitely my favorite, with the bread for dipping. Then we skipped right to dessert. We got a giant vat of chocolate with peanut butter mixed into it. It came with plates full of deliciousness, in the form of brownies, pound cake, rice krispie treats, marshmallows (coated in graham cracker or oreo crumbs), strawberries, and other dippable items. This was exceptionally good and I ate so much that I almost felt sick afterwards (in a good way). The chocolate and peanut butter was excellent, and my favorite items to dip were the rice krispie squares and the brownies. I also ordered this crazy drink called a Yin & Yang, or something like that. It was basically a martini with ice cream in it, topped with chocolate shavings in a way that made it looks like (surprise) a yin-yang symbol. Needless to say, it was pretty crazy delicious. And it looked so cool that I had to take a picture. The place was nice and clean and everything, and a little more formal than I expected. Our waitress was nice and friendly and provided excellent service. She was happy to recommend things when asked. Overall, a great experience with delicious food. I'll definitely be heading back at some point.

Then there was a shallow timbale of diced beets topped with faux caviar made of seaweed. Delicious and creative. My fellow diner had a sopa de tortilla which was also very good. For the entree, I had grilled seitan with raosted red pepper relish, mashed yukon golds, grilled spinach and a creamy horseradish sauce. The dish had real potential, but they went so heavy on the grill marks that all I could taste was nasty burnt carbon. I know it's tough to flavor seitan but I'd prefer bland to burnt. The other dish at the table was the Pacific Rim tofu, which suffered from the exact same problem. Seriously, its time to clean your grill. Dessert was absolutely horrendous. We had a chocolate-covered peanut butter cake with peanut butter "ice cream." The cake was inedibly dry and very oddly spiced. The "ice cream" tasted like a big dollop of refrigerated Jif. It took me five minutes just to swallow it. My friend and I each took one bite, and I was tempted to spit mine out into my napkin. We left the dessert untouched on the table, but no one bothered to ask us if everything was ok. They just brought the check. The service was fairly friendly, but very unprofessional. They were out of the bottle of wine that I ordered, which we didn't discover until five minutes after ordering it. Not that big a deal, but it meant that I had to sit there with a wine list in my lap because the appetizer had already arrived before the wine. Then, the waiter forgot our side of grilled spinach and never came by to check on us so that I could ask him for it. Then, as I said, no one asked us why our dessert went back to the kitchen untouched. The bill for this wholly unsatisfying vegan meal was upwards of $130 before tip, which was really excessive considering the lack of exotic, or even interesting ingredients. The markup on wine was huge too. Needless to say, I will never see the inside of Horizons again.

text: Fair disclaimer: I'm definitely a fan of meat, and that has a lot to do with how I feel about Lovin' Spoonfuls. But I should also mention that I am a fan of vegetarian and vegan cooking, and given the great reviews I've heard about this place, I came to Lovin' Spoonfuls filled with eager anticipation. First, the good: the owner is just so incredibly warm, friendly, and approachable. She clearly loves what she's doing, and I think that's awesome. Also I live with a vegan, and I have a number of friends who don't eat animals to varying degrees (sometimes chicken's okay; sometimes the line is at fish; sometimes as long as it's not meat we're in the clear). These are people who have grown accustomed to opening menus at restaurants and having a very few options to choose from. Seeing their eyes light up when they look at an extensive menu from which they can order anything they want...well, it's great. So primarily for those reasons, I have almost certainly not eaten at Lovin' Spoonfuls for the last time. So what's my beef with Lovin' Spoonfuls? (Okay, I'm sorry; that's a truly awful pun. I couldn't help it!) Most significantly, this: about half of the dishes on the menu are attempts at recreating meat dishes using vegan ingredients, and the straightforwardly vegetarian dishes are relatively unimaginative. Now, I can understand why something like this would be okay or even appealing to some vegans or vegetarians for whom fake meat is a novelty. But as a meat-eater, I can't help but think: If I wanted a meat dish or an unimaginative vegetable dish, I would go to a meat restaurant. I come to a vegan restaurant to eat vegetables, and none of these dishes really showcases vegetables in a unique and exciting way. I can easily make pasta primavera, vegetable stir fry, or angel hair with tomato and basil at home. When I go to a vegan restaurant, I want to see a rich Cuban black bean stew over rice with fried plantains; I want to see an ambitious take on mapo doufo; I want to see a great ratatouille; I want to see really fresh, locally grown vegetables put on display with a defiant "I dare you to buy these at the supermarket again!" And I want Indian food! But alas, no such luck. In that respect, Lovin' Spoonfuls was a disappointment. The other gripe was simply the cost of eating there. As I would expect at a vegan restaurant, portion sizes were relatively modest. But prices were relatively high, and given the only-middling refinement of the dishes on the menu, I felt like I was getting a pretty poor deal. In Tucson, $10 for dinner is a lot. I didn't feel like this was a dining experience which warranted a splurge. The grain of salt, then: If you're a vegan or vegetarian and you want a veggie burger, an imitation meat dish, or simply the experience of getting anything on the menu at a restaurant, then don't let me stop you. This restaurant isn't bad. I'm just saying that as a lover of really good, interesting food, and as someone who can't afford to spend lots of money on just average food, I don't think this place warrants a recommendation.

text: Oh, man.. This place is awesome. I am a fan of Oriental food and this place shows off some amazingly good Thai cuisine. The outside of the business does not reflect how nice it is inside. It's one part of a strip of small businesses that all seem to be "hole in the wall" kind of places. Once you step in, though, you're immediately greeted by a very kind wait staff that ask you to sit anywhere you'd like. You'll notice how small the place is, but the style and decor makes this an authentic Thai experience; it's a very quaint and comfy place to be. *My review of the food is based solely on the lunch specials* Being a 19 year old student, working at a dead end job, taking my mother out to Thai Orchid for a nice lunch doesn't have me feeling like I just burned a hole through my wallet, once the bill comes. Seriously, the lunch specials are offered at a very reasonable low price! The kind waiter brings us water in nice stemmed glasses and comes back a bit later to take our order. My mother orders shrimp Pad Thai and I order the Pa-Nang curry and a Thai iced tea. The waiter leaves and comes back momentarily with a nice cup of chicken and rice soup and a rangoon of some sort, that is served with lunch orders, for each of us. It's a nice small serving of each that is not at all filling, but keeps you content as you wait for the main course. The Thai iced tea here is really awesome. Thai iced tea isn't anything like a regular iced tea so I'd definitely recommend giving it a try, unless you're not into sweeter things. It is some kind of tea that has a layer of sweetened condensed milk on top. After I stir that baby up, I'll empty the glass in record time. Once our food is served I stare at it, just a bit, to marvel at how much of a generous portion is given. The Pa-Nang curry doesn't disappoint. It has the right amount of spice and goes so well with the chicken, vegetables, and side of rice. My mom and I always swap plates halfway through to sample the other person's stuff. The Pad Thai rocks. Can't say much else; it just rocks. Period. By the end of our meal I'm feeling good and full. The waiter drops off our checks and thanks us for choosing their place to eat at. I take a look at the cost of this wondrous meal; $19.75. This brings a smile to my face and to my wallet. In all, this place is great to meet up with or take someone for a nice cheap lunch. What you get here is amazingly authentic Thai food with a nice comfy atmosphere and kind wait staff. Give this place a shot. *To get a look at the food we ate, take a look at the photos for this place. Looks good, eh?*
