text: I am in love with this restaurant. My mom and I dined there last night and enjoyed our fabulous food, the warm friendly atmosphere and the unparalleled service. For appetizers, we split the Trio Printanier and the Sardines Grillees. Both had lively flavors and a wonderful freshness. We had mentioned while ordering that we were going to split both of the appetizers, and without asking for it, the chef plated each appetizer on two plates. The carrots were brought out first and then the sardines. It was awesome to receive service with such stellar intuition. For the main course I ordered the Rondins de Courgette-- delicious zucchini filled with a truffle infused mushroom stuffing and accompanied by baked tomatoes. It was a surprisingly unusual vegetarian entree. I don't usually order stuffed vegetables because they are frequently hard to eat and unexciting. This however, was scrupmtious.My mom ordered the Bar aux Artichauts-- perfectly crispy black sea bass with cooked fresh artichokes in a light white wine sauce. Also delicious. What I enjoyed most about the food was that it was delicately flavored and completely satisfying without making me feel as though I had eaten an overly-indulgent and rich meal. Now, onto the service. WOW! Though I've eaten many times at restaurants that change silver wear after each course and fold napkins left on seats by people using the restroom, I am usually made slightly uncomfortable by this level of attention. Not so here. The staff was so graceful and nice that their extra attention didn't feel forced or unnecessary. I was really impressed. Finally, after a leisurely meal with a few drinks, my mom and I strolled out the door. Three blocks later, our amazing waiter caught up with us and handed us the credit card we had forgotten. A + all around.

text: Blah. text: Roberto Cafe gets the five star review, because at Roberto you get the five star treatment. The moment you walk in the door, expect VIP treatment. In my first review, I described the food as "unremarkable". The limitations were were mine not theirs. The chefs at Robertos are clever and not afraid to play with flavor combinations. The dishes that require simplicity, are simply delicious. An example of the clever, is an Italian take on the Eastern European comfort food stuffed cabbages. The owner told me he loved them, and wanted to put his own spin on them. They are a home run, with ground lamb instead of ground beef, and a ton of garlic and white wine in place of tomato sauce. An example of simple is the calamari. Grilled not fried, and just a hint of lemon. They let the flavor of the squid stand on it's own. The staff at Robertos is happy to accommodate you any way they can. They will change an aspect of the dish or if you love one of the appetisers, they will double the portion and make it your entree. The owner said any way you want it is no big deal, since we are cooking it up per your order. One of our diners was a few minutes late and the owner noticed, so he went back in the kitchen and made up two kinds of brochette, and sauteed us up some fresh peppers on the house. Robertos is flying a little below the "trendy radar" so get on board because some secrets can not last forever.

Lastly, when we asked for a late check out time, the manager/concierge/chef/cleaning lady said no, and we had to haggle her to get it to 11:30am because "people were checking in at 12:30pm." I've NEVER had that happen in any inn or hotel, and I'm pretty sure no one was checking in at 12:30pm...just an added annoyance. Be wary of the prices and probably just better to stay here during the week day if you are just passing through. First of all, they seemed to have raised their prices, second, if you book a room a few days before a weekend, the site shows rooms (but only sometimes) for $30 bucks more than if you were to book it a few weeks out. text: Bobbie's has been around since the 'fifties, when there was still a drive-in movie theater on Charlotte Pike. It has that old Nashville relic feel about it , while at the same time remaining a vibrant summer hot spot. I always know winter is fully upon us when Bobbie's closes for the season, and it's always a herald of spring when they fire up their fryers again in March. Now for the superlative awards: Bobbie's has, hands down, the best fries in Nashville. They are fresh cut, real potatoes and they taste like it, served in little white paper bags spotted with fry grease. You should also try the sweet potato fries, served with a sour cream sauce. Bobbie's has a great, but not cheap, burger, and they serve two different kinds of veggie burgers. As legendary in these parts as the fries are the milkshakes. You could give yourself a headache calculating the permutations of possible combinations of flavors. My personal favorite is banana with bananas and pineapple.

text: Gosh, I don't know where to begin. Reading that it was a "must" go in my guidebook, I decided to try it out with my family. Waiting-a-bit = 1 hour+. I believe we waited about 90 minutes to get our food. The tables were really dirty and we didn't see anyone cleaning up after people. The place is really small, and because its so packed, it gets a bit hectic in there. But expecting great food, we didn't mind the condition of the place. So we ordered two half chickens, and two breasts. Having to wait so long, I guess you expect that much more. Oh boy, were we disappointed. Its fried chicken. I mean, I honestly can't say if this really is good fried chicken because I'm not too crazy about fried chicken, but the meat was dry and the bread was drenched in oil. I got mild, but that wasn't spicy at all. I just didn't see how it was any different than KFC or something. Overall, we were pretty disappointed. It was nice talking to some locals during the wait, but otherwise, I would never go back to this establishment again. Not trying to be negative here, but in my opinion, the food was not worth the time. I mean, Prince's have received some great reviews, so I'm sure its good food in context of fried chicken...its just not right for me. If you aren't crazy about fried chicken, then I suggest you go try someplace else.

text: During a recent road trip, my boyfriend and I stopped here at 11:30am on a Sunday, after some friends in NorCal told us it was not to be missed. True to all other reviews, there was a 15 minute wait - but being huge Yelp fans, we were happy to chill in line since the reviews were so positive. Boy were we disappointed. After all the hype, the food was just so-so. My bf's tri-tip taco was pretty bland, and my pork suizo had an unexpected sweetness to it, and lacked much flavor. I also ordered the alhambre pechuga, which was diced chicken with green peppers, onions, mushrooms on a corn tortilla. Again, nothing very exciting, about as plain as the menu description itself. The lone bright spots were the horchata (mexican rice milk - cold and sweet, served in paper cups with ice), fresh corn tortillas (chewy and soft), and the chorizo. That said, though, given the line and lack-luster cuisine, we won't be coming back here to get our Mexican food fix. Final note, this is my first Yelp review ever - this place was such a far cry from Yelp's usually consistent reviews, I had to speak up! Take it from a true foodie, Super-Rica Taqueria just isn't worth your time.

Sometimes the food has come out cold too and the last two times I went there, a friend ordered chicken with peanut sauce and it was as if someone had spread Peter Pan over a rubber chicken. The staff is very courteous and they will try to fix any mistake. However, I wish this place would have continued to serve quality food at good prices. You can tell they have everything made and heated instead of cooking to order, and that is never a good sign. Especially in a tiny restaurant that has the potential to become a neighborhood favorite. text: So I go to this IKEA once a week. I suppose, I am little bit of an "Ikea-a-holic". Everything in my apartment is from IKEA and a lot of it is over 5 years old and holding strong. I've been going to this IKEA for years, and my favorite things are as follows: The As-Is department- like I said I go often, so I generally know what's in their catalog at any given time so much of the stuff in their AS-IS department is in perfect working order just for cheap. Hello cheap, we love you. The foodery. you can to IKEA, you're grueling through redecorating your friends place AND you didn't eat. Well IKEA has great cheap eats ranging from simple to fancy and all their hot cafeteria style food is really actually good. The delivery section will hold your furniture for you for the day for free if theirs a really cheap as is piece you want and you didn't bring your car, or your car is too small and you need to go get a zipcar truck. no problem. The rest of the store stands for itself as it is exactly like every IKEA everywhere. You find the piece of furniture you want in it's easily laid out upstairs showroom OR categorized section, you take down the location, then you go find it. If you can't find it, you ask an employee for help, it's so simple baby chimps can handle it. I usually do most of my shopping online to find what I want and then just go to pick it up. If you you have a small car and have IKEA furniture already, definitely bring an allen wrench/ hex key that way you can disassemble your as is finds and load them easier.

text: An open love letter to Fortel's Pizza Den. Oh Fortel's how I love thee. Your divine specialty thin crust pizzas, your appetizers, your hot fresh delivery. Sure I have driven by one or more of your nine locations and thought you were just more of the same thin crust pizza with a goofy chef logo. But you are more. So much more. I remember when my sister suggested we "try" Fortel's Pizza Den in Ballwin. We had ordered pizza from all the other local pizza establishments and needed some change. I believe we ordered Lexi's Spicy Southwest Chicken Deluxe, which while not spicy, had plenty of mouth watering chicken, roasted red peppers, onions, and mozzarella cheese. Why, we even ordered a Bayley's Spicy Buffalo Chicken Deluxe with all that hot wing sauce, chicken and mozzarella. You were even so kind to offer us either some ranch or bleu cheese dressing on the side. Your love, dear Fortel's, is an addiction. We've courted you on several occasions branching out to other taste sensations like the Fred's Philly Cheese Steak Deluxe and the Brynn's Chicken Florentine Deluxe. Each time we are left stuffed and wondering why we ate the whole thing! I say one of these days I will try the make my own option and I will explore the list of sauces including, pesto, creamed pesto, southwest, bbq, white and GRAVY. But it doesn't end there with you, does it Fortel's? You have to go and offer and wide array of appetizers. I must say your mini beer battered cheese sticks are quite tasty. But offering meatballs with sauce or gravy, stuffed olives, wings, toasted ravioli and fried eggplant!?!?!? You spoil me. Let me say our relationship doesn't end here Fortel's. I still have to try your salads, sandwiches and pasta. But that is a whole other page of the menu. I'll talk to you soon my sweet!

text: I'm hoping the original location in Sparks is better. This place was awful. We went here and got a large Popeye: pesto-alfredo sauce, chicken, red onion, spinach, and fresh tomatoes. $25, so with tax and tip it was $30. That's expensive for a pizza, but we'd heard great things about this place, so we were optimistic. Eclipse Pizza and Black Rock Pizza are also expensive, but they're amazing, so I didn't mind. Wrong. The only good thing about this pizza was the crust on the rim, which I have to admit was really good. It's thick, twisted, chewy on the inside and crispy on the outside, and has really good flavor. They give you honey to dip it in, which I don't personally like but lots of people love. Honestly, you don't need to dip it in anything. It's great. So that being said, let's get to the bad parts: 1) The sauce on this pizza was neither pesto nor alfredo. It was basically greasy cheese and butter sauce, and I could get a better alfredo from Wal-Mart. Neither myself nor the other two people I split the pizza with detected a hint of basil or pesto flavor anywhere on the pizza, which was swimming in the stuff. 2) The chicken was cut in huge pieces, so much so that you really only got one piece per slice. It was thick, and fell right off the pizza as soon as we picked it up. It was also chewy and bland, like they boiled it with no seasoning at all. 3) In fact, everything was huge, thick, and fell off. The tomatoes were those flavorless fast food slices, and the onion was basically raw. Giant purple slabs of raw onion on my pizza? No thanks. If they cut all that stuff into smaller pieces, maybe it would cook all the way through and add some flavor. Instead, it just got picked off. Or fell off, rather, which brings me to... 4) The pizza was so undercooked that as soon as you peeled away a slice from the pizza and picked it up, it would fail under the weight of all the massive chunks of food on top, fold, and everything would fall off. I'm talking completely limp, almost all the way to the rim crust (which, remember, was delicious). Nothing was stuck into the cheese, which was barely melted, which didn't help the construction or stability of the pizza. This turned out to be kind of a blessing, though, because I didn't much care for anything on the pizza anyway. Our pizza box turned into a graveyard of bland tomato slices, huge chunks of raw onion, and about half a pizza that no one wanted to finish. Bummer. Maybe a less adventurous/more traditional pizza, like pepperoni with tomato sauce, would turn out better. I'll have to stop by and get the $5 pizza and soda deal. The slices are big, so if it's good, that would be cool. Based on my experience, though, I'm not expecting much. I'll stick with Eclipse and Black Rock.

text: I really don't know why I don't think of eating at Lombardo's more often. I'm sure it's because of the fairly hidden location in the Drury Inn next to Union Station, but I've been impressed every time I've gone to Lombardo's. I hadn't stopped in for a few years but based on a recommendation from a new friend, some customer's and I decided to give Lombardo's a shot. I'm glad that we did. If you're an individual who can appreciate a great toatsted ravioli then you must go to Lombardo's. The toasted rav's at Lombardo's are like no others. These giganitic pillows of perfectly crispy yet slightly soft dough stuffed with a generous amount of meat are the stuff that makes their way into my dreams at night. There is no uncertainty that these TR's are handmade and made with love. In addition, our server Mo, brought us three lobster raviolis that were topped with a cream sauce. Outstanding. Our salads were perfect as well. A St. Louis style italian sald which which tossed in a creamy italian dressing that wasn't really overly creamy in a good way. I prefer a generous amount of dressing on my salad (hence then double chin), but I dont want me salad drenched in it either. If you want to win my heart, throw an artichoke heart on top of what ever I'm eating. Yes ladies, I'm THAT easy! In the entree department, two of us went with the highly recommended Steak Angelou and the third ordered seafood linguini. Our filets were topped with, what else, provel cheese! From my recollection there was also garlic, panceta, and a few mushrooms as toppings. The new potatoes topped with garlic were fantastic. Crispy on the outside and soft on the inside (kinda like me). The potatoes made a great for a great accomplice next to the steak. Mr. Seafood Pasta did whine a bit because he has asked for cream sauce but his pasta arrived in an olive oil and garlic butter. Rather than send it back he decided to push the heart attack back a day and scarfed down his pasta with a smile. Aside from the pasta sauce foul, our server was wonderful. She played along with our relentless jokes and banter. The smile never escaped her face and was extremely attentive. Also, her co-workers all chipped in to run food and clear plates. This is a sign of a well run establishment. Lombardo's really only has a few negatives which are mainly caused by the location. The spot is basement-like on the lower level of the Drury Inn. The bathrooms require a trek up to the hotel lobby. Lombardo's does not have a bathroom inside the restaurant. Also the fact that Lombardo's also serves as the hotel bar which drew in a variety of characters. When it was all said and done, Lombardo's was an excellent choice for our business dinner. The prices were very reasonable and the food and service were both outstanding. Lombardo's also has a location at the Drury Inn at Lambert Airport. Carmine's Steakhouse in the Drury Inn by The Arch, and I believe there is a new location in Arnold as well.

text: This place was not bad but I have to say I was disappointed. I was really expecting more from a Fox restaurant. The prices were high for what you get and I really did not understand at all what they were trying to do with the theme. The decor was very modern - all plastic and Ikea looking. But then they had touches of Western here and there - like the railroad ties on the light fixtures and cactus etchings on the glass. It was very odd. We started off with the calamari. I didn't care for it since it had a tempura batter rather than the traditional breading but my husband liked it. The sauce it came with was tasty but the consistency was not conducive to dipping. For dinner we split the Kobe sliders. They were decent burgers but I thought they were too greasy. One of the reasons I like Kobe beef is that the meat is so tender than you can usually make a dish with a lower fat content and still have it taste good so I was very disappointed that these were dripping with grease. We ordered as our side the truffle fries. These were also good but tasted like ordinary fries to me - I could not taste any truffle flavor whatsoever. We even asked the waitress to make sure we got the correct fries and she said yes, that we could tell b/c the truffle fries come with shaved parmesan on top. So, burgers and fries are always good so I can't complain too much but really they just tasted like the same burgers and fries you can get anywhere - nothing at all special about them. I am glad I tried it out but I have to say it is unlikely that I would ever eat here again.

text: I think there are at least 25 hotels that I haven't reviewed, so clearly I must have my reasons for reviewing this one in particular. First, the city of Wilmington. Second, why are most rooms' windows off to the side, and only one in number? Sure the view across the street is likely that of a multi-level parking garage as is the case with most buildings in the city, but why not let the sun in? Third, with full-price rooms at $200 or more, can't the hotel afford to spend some money on upkeep? The beds are lackluster, the bathroom and amenities seem to be past their prime, and even the TVs are dated. The front desk staff members are friendly but seemingly helpless, despite my shiny Platinum status with the Marriott chain. text: Okay. I'm going to try and keep this simple: For a hotel of this size, nameplate and cost per room this hotel is a complete failure. Approaching the hotel, it looks pretty modern and nice. The lobby is pretty nice and the staff were pleasant and helpful. Like other reviewers they dropped the "remodel is coming" stuff. I got my key and headed to my room where I noticed that there were several displays with fabric and carpet swatches with renderings of said remodel. Whootpie-do! What good does that do me? Am I supposed to use my imagination and make believe when I get to my room? Which leads me to the next point... It's very easy to use your imagination when you get into your room because there is no light switch anywhere near the door so you're in complete darkness if you check in after sundown! Try and picture that earlier rendering because you're going to have to Stevie Wonder your way around the room until you stumble into the bathroom, the only place where I found a switch Bed was clean but old. Springs were hard and creaky. Hot water took about 5 minutes or more to get going (6:30 AM on a Sunday, maybe I was the first to shower). TV had all the classic hotel room channels plus the obligatory staticy channels. I've never understood why every hotel in the US has at least a couple channels with weak signal but I digress. No free wifi (hard wired internet was also at a cost). No free coffee that I was aware of. I peaked at their breakfast menu and when I saw the 8 dollar oatmeal I got my trusty (except for calls) iPhone out and yelped to the stellar Cafe Patachou. So in short, this is an awesome Motel and a lousy Hotel. Shop around.

text: I have eaten numerous times at the Jasper Avenue location of La Shish, so when I saw one had opened up in the west end I was eager to try it. My opportunity came today, and I was impressed with how large and spacious the dining area is - a major change from the half dozen or so tables on 118 street. The menu is exactly the same, featuring an array of shwarma wraps and platters, kebabs, and vegetarian items freshly prepared. I had a chicken shwarma, which was loaded with chicken, lettuce, tomato, pickles, and La Shish's famous garlic sauce. The fillings are wrapped in a pita, which is then grilled in a sandwich press. It was great. My companion had a beef schwarma and also enjoyed it, as well as the side of roasted potatoes and garlic sauce he had with his "trio:" a wrap, side of potatoes, and a can of pop for one low price. I think this was his first time trying Lebanese food. It bursts with the flavours of the Middle East. My mouth waters when I look at the menu at La Shish, because of the beautiful photographs showing all of the foods. I definitely want to come here more often and try some different meals.

text: We loved this place. The menu is enormous and everything except the fondue but including the omelet which was referred to as a quiche (either way, it's cooked in a hot pot). But we didn't get that; we stuck to our basics and then some, and had a fantastic meal. We arrived ~7PM last Friday. 2 other tables were filled, but then either a couple or small family would arrive every 20 minutes. We brought in a 6-pack from Gilligan's, and were brought a tall champagne bucket to keep the beers cold. I questioned whether I should get the crispy fried egg noodle plate, but was convinced not to (just in case it wasn't right). Until I saw it at the table behind ours. Why this was an issue? I haven't had it in 20 years. Every time I ask for crispy fried egg noodles I get that awful bag of mealworm looking things. Or they make some gelatinous mess of rice or noodles because obviously I'm insane and have no idea what I'm talking about. More on these noodles later. We started with cha gio. These were crispy, not the least bit greasy. The sauce could have been stronger, although we also could have added more fish sauce to the container (each table has fish sauce, soy sauce, hoisin sauce, chile garlic sauce, salt, pepper, and sugar). There were also only 2 pieces of lettuce for the 4 medium-long rolls; we were out of lettuce by the second piece. The filling were also a bit mild. One small order of pho tai with extra beef on the side. Mild but well flavoured. We split this bowl. Unlike a previous poster, we aren't fans of a lot of noodles. And no MSG reactions. Yeah! We were stuffed at this point. Having seen the noodles at the aforementioned table, we asked to have those noodles instead of rice with the catfish. They thought we were nuts, but decided to give us noodles, rice, and the catfish. Then an extra order of gravy. The catfish was void of bones and perfectly tender and sweet in a garlic-ginger brown sauce and cooked in a hot pot. I can't remember the last time I had such amazing fish. The sauce was perfectly seasoned--not overly salty as at many places--and the fish so good. That we made a horseshoe pie with the rice, noodles, and fish was probably completely wrong of us, but it was so good. We weren't charged for our noodles and sauce. The bill came out to $27 including tax and prior to tip. Great place.
label: POS

text: I have very mixed feelings about this place. The location of the hotel is fine. It's only about a 20-30 minute walk from the French Quarter and Bourbon Street, closer to the Garden District, and has some good restaurants nearby, including two 24-hour bars that serve good food. Also, the rooms are clean, and if you need anything, they promptly send someone to take care of it for you. Also, they serve breakfast for free in the mornings. It's not the best breakfast selection, but it's pretty decent with a wafflemaker, bagels, pastries, toast, sausages, eggs, yogurt, fruit, and cereal. Despite all of those upsides, in addition to the fact that I DO realize that although the name of the hotel is the "Maison St. Charles," it's really La Quinta Inn renamed fancy (DON'T BE DECEIVED), I was a little put off by the fact that one of the nights when I was about to go out, I came out of my room, and just jiggled the door handle to make sure that the door was locked, and it wouldn't LOCK! It just opened on me! I had a mini internal freak-out because I was imagining all of the horrible things that could have happened if I had not tested my lock and had just gone out. My laptop, clothes, etc. might have been easily stolen! And there's not a security patrol outside either! I immediately called the front desk and they brought someone over, but needless to say, I checked my lock after leaving every day from thereon. Just a little unnerving.

text: I've loved Thai food almost everywhere I've had it. Maybe my expectations were just too high, but Siam Cuisine disappointed in just about every way. Parking was a bitch, the front lot is very tight and was packed at lunchtime. Getting in and out of the back lot is one-way and inconvenient. We nearly got into an accident getting out because someone wasn't looking when they tried to get in. We were seated promptly in a very dim atmosphere. I always get edgy if a place is too dark. Do they not want us to see our food? Our order was taken relatively quickly, and then it was a lot of waiting. The soup had a pleasant, if mild, vegetable stock, but the veggies were overcooked and the chicken tasteless. More waiting later, and our "Native Thai hot" curries arrived. Tthe vegetables were so overcooked as to be nearly tasteless. I've had crisper out of a can. To their credit, the scallops were perfectly textured, but that's not enough to make me go back. There was no heat to the dish whatsoever. If I took a mouthful with basil on it, I got some flavor, but nothing near what I've had in a multitude of places. I shudder to think what I would have tasted if I'd ordered "mild." The spring roll was nothing special, not detracting from the meal, but not adding to it either. Go to Golden Thai down the street for a much better experience.
label: NEG

text: Since my friend and I were going to spend all day downtown, we decided Rooster would be a great place to fuel up for our long day. With a restaurant.com coupon in hand, we got to enjoy one breakfast entree, a savory crepe, a dessert crepe, and a cup of coffee all for just $22 (tax and tip included). My friend opted for the rooster slinger, a smorgasbord of eggs, andouille sausage, and breakfast potatoes served on toast and ladled with sausage gravy. I had a few bites and it was spicy -- not too spicy that it had me grabbing for my water but just enough that I could feel the burn. I had the marinated spicy chicken crepe, served with arugula and fontina cheese. The size of the crepe was perfect -- I didn't get sick of it and didn't wonder halfway through, "geez, when's this crepe going to end?". Plus, it left me just enough room to enjoy a dessert crepe with my friend! And on to the star of the meal: the smores crepe. Just as delectable as it sounds. Crumbled cookies, dark chocolate, and marshmallow all wrapped up in a crepe. Every bite was just as delicious as the last. Rooster has a pretty extensive menu of savory and sweet crepes -- and for those who don't want to eat things wrapped in a thin pancake, Rooster also offers a variety of salads, sandwiches, and breakfast entrees. I will definitely be back to try more of their other food offerings and to have another one of those delicious smores crepes!

text: My first trip to Pappy's was all that I had hoped for and more. I stopped in with my son on the way out of town to grab a late lunch and also some takeout for the family. The staff is extremely friendly and helpful and the cashier was very patient while I placed my extensive fat man order and quizzed her on the options. Our lunches were delicious. I almost wept with joy after taking my first bite of the pulled pork. It was un-sauced, and naked with only the sweet pork goodness and smoke to caress my tongue. Even my son abandoned his hot link sandwich to partake of the pulled pork. All three sauce options (original, sweet, and hot) were enjoyable, but I think I prefer the original. No real reasoning here, I just enjoyed the flavor paired with the pork. The beans are sweet and molassas-y, and the deep fried corn is crispy on the outside and succulent on the inside. I have heard the crowds are tough to deal with but going off hours on a weekday had us walking straight up to order and our food out within minutes of settling into our table. The guys are right next to the cashier making your order while you are ordering. I recommend an off hours trip to Pappy's where you can baste your insides in deliciousness.

text: Like a sharp slap to the face, it has just come to my attention that 2009 is the year of my 20th High School Reunion. Its hard to believe that Ive been out of school almost twice as long as I was in school. As many who follow the message boards may know, while my dammned body has aged 2 times over, my mind is still that of the 16 year old that roamed the halls of Haverford High School. Cenzos Pizza was the only nearby place that tolerated and thrived on the masses of High and Middle schoolers who pooled their change together to buy a few slices of pizza. I havent been back in the entire 20 years since graduation but im pretty sure its still there and im pretty sure some sadsack teens are still suffering with burned roof of mouth, unable to quench it with cola because they couldnt afford both pizza and soda. As I remember, the pizza was exceptionally good. Thin and floppy with good cheese and somewhat sweet sauce. We lived in their delivery range and when it was my turn to order pizza, I always went for Cenzos and invariably, the delivery driver was always someone I knew from school trying to pay off their car, and i felt obliged to tip them well. Cenzos was somewhat of a safe-zone, as the owners tolerated normal teenage nonsense but didnt tolerate acts of violence. More than once, I fled to the safety of Cenzos , pursued by kids who meant me harm, to wait out a beating. What can I say, much like a few times here on Yelp, my sass has gotten me into some trouble. Our HS Reunion isnt planned just yet but I hope, on that evening, we can make a trip to Cenzos for old times sake. Who knows, I may piss someone off at the reunion by calling them fat or old and have to make a break for the safety of Cenzos. Ill just have to remember to bring enough for a slice AND a soda.

text: Casa De Oro just opened in the spot where Panderia Azteca used to be. I'm not sure if these are the same owners or not, but the menu is sold as "Salvadorian food" with a minor Mexican section. I'm not sure when this restaurant opened but it had to be fairly recently - it's just a cloth banner for the store name. I wasn't very impressed with my visit. I placed my order to go and ordered the Churrasco for $8.99, which is listed on their take-out menu as "carne asada, casamiento, chorizo, queso y ensalada fresca" - translated on the same menu as "steak, casamiento, chorizo, chimol, cheese and fresh salad". As you can see some of the words weren't even translated... I also ordered two pork carnitas tacos as well. The order took about ten to fifteen minutes to cook, which I was surprised at since there were only two other customers in the restaurant (and they were already eating). I work right near this restaurant (not even five minutes away) so the food could not have suffered much on the trip. When I opened the container I found two small six-inch tortilla tacos (not surprised by that, because the tacos are only 99 cents) but the chorizo wasn't even a quarter of an entire regular sausage link and the steak was probably about four ounces of beef total. I will say both meats were very flavorful, but for the amount of money paid I expected more. The salad was pretty small, the beans (I'm guessing that was the casamiento?) were a bit watery, and there was no cheese. I think the chimol was the green salsa that was included, but I'm not sure. The pork in the carnitas tacos was also tough and chewy - not good, even if it was only 99 cents per taco. I may give this place another chance with their breakfast menu - but for lunch, it probably won't happen.

text: I recently found out that Buddakan was copied after NYC's China Grill (and actually all of Stephen Starr's concepts are imitations), but I don't care, because there is nothing that compares to Buddakan in Philadelphia. Period. I don't think I have EVER had a bad meal here. Dishes are served family style, so plan on plenty of sharing. For starters, the edamame raviolis are amazing, and you can't go wrong with the crispy calamari salad. On my most recent visit, we tried the tuna pizza, which is worth a try if you like dishes with a kick. On to the entrees....good staples are the cashew chicken and the Japanese cod. The steak here is also tasty, but make sure to get it medium rare. When ordered medium, I found it overcooked and dry. I always like to get a glass of Tawny port when I am here to go with dessert. It pairs well with the creme brulee and also with the chocolate caramel tart, which was smooth and sweet, but the oreo-like crust gave it a crunchy contrast. Service was great. Our waiter even divided up the tart for us precisely into 4 pieces. I would come close to saying Buddakan is a Philadelphia institution, even though there are now Buddakans in NYC and Atlantic City. Whether you are a Philadelphian or a visitor, you MUST go here at least once.

text: How do you rate a place that's unique in St Louis? I'm not aware of any place that compares to La Vallesana. I'm one of those people that thinks 5 star reviews are too cheap on Yelp, but when it comes to Mexican taco shacks, I don't know how La Vallesana could be improved upon. I LOVE this place. It is so simple and basic and wonderful. The closest thing I've found to actual Mexican food. The chicken burrito will change your life. Seriously, you will be a different person when you have finished this burrito. Your mother won't be able to put her finger on it, but when she looks at you she will know something is different. They take a whole skinless chicken breast and cook it on the grill with very little oil and place it in a warm burrito tortilla with just a dab of bean paste, sour cream and lettuce. This burrito is all chicken and not full of beans and or rice. The burrito comes with chips and fresh guacamole for $5bucks. It's the best deal in town. They also sell great Mexican tacos. You know those little tacitos you get on the street in Mexico with shredded beef, a little cilantro and lime in a soft taco tortilla? Awesome. They have a great smokey (ancho I think but more heat) red chili sauce for the tacos which is the perfect compliment. La Vallesana has a large menu. They make giant Mexican style sandwiches (with authentic bread) which are popular in the neighborhood and look amazing. All kinds of Mexican dishes in chicken, beef and pork. I just like the chicken burrito and tacos so much I haven't tried anything else. The also sell Mexican sodas and flavored ice. I have no idea where they get this stuff in St. Louis but it doesn't appear that they have any problem finding everything they need to create a Mexican taco shack right in the middle of South St Louis. The restaurant is in an old Dairy Queen like building with only counter seating (facing a wall) inside and tables outside weather permitting. I've eaten outside and enjoyed it, but mostly take carry-out. Some people might think the restaurant and neighborhood are a little rough but I've never had any problems at all. When I first started coming here only one of the girls spoke English. They all seem to speak English now but Spanish is still the preferred language and that suits me just fine. The food is inexpensive so bring cash. I don't think they take credit cards and even if they do, don't ask people that sell food so inexpensively to pay credit card fees from their profit so you don't have to carry a few bucks in your pocket.
label: POS

text: Amazing. This was quite honestly one of the best meals I've ever had. If not *the* best meal ever. The boyfriend and I spent nearly three romantical (yes, I'm that cheesy) hours here drinking and eating. and eating. and eating. The service was great, thank gawd, because we were not the easiest customers. First we ordered a bottle of wine (when in Rome, right?) from their solely-local-wine list. We'd spent a few hours that day wine tasting so I got to show off my newly acquired sniff-n-swirl pretentious wine moves. While I was busy gargling my wine, I noticed a waiter (towel over arm) display a customers' 2008 Amstel Light bottle to him before unscrewing the top. 2008- good year. Classy. Next we had the tomato duo for an appetizer which was a warm tomato salad with basil and goat cheese (yum) accompanied by a thick smoky tomato soup (frankly, the soup I didn't get). Our waiter told us the chef literally takes a wheelbarrow to a local farmers market every other day and trucks back all of the produce on the menu. A vegetarian heaven.... except for the fact that there were no vegetarian entrees on the menu, typical French restaurant - but wait! The waiter then told me that the chefs love creating vegetarian entrees to order. Meaning, I could scan the menu and offer up some suggestions to the chef and he would create something special for me. How ridiculous is that? I felt like I had my own personal gourmet chef for the evening, which was essentially the truth. Too bad I'm not creative - my only suggestion was that I love *all* vegetables. All? Yes, all. Yup, I'm as helpful as I am creative. So our perfect tomato salad was followed by my surprise entree- a cheesy vegetable risotto filled with a medley of their local fresh vegetables - a few different types of mushrooms, squash, and peas topped with grilled asparagus and baby carrots encircled by a lovely pesto sauce. Colorful. Delicious. And again, perfect. My boyfriend had the chicken but wanted all the sides that came with the steak. (Why? Because we're both difficult like that. Birds of a feather... except he eats birds and I don't. We're both difficult, but one of us does have a heart. Kidding. Tangent over.) Fortunately, the chefs were so accommodating and surprisingly unpretentious that they didn't mind us being picky at all. After we practically licked our plates clean we ordered a dessert to share. We ended up with two desserts because the waiter admittedly forgot what dessert we ordered and accidentally brought us the wrong one. Best mistake ever. So we had a warm peach/blackberry crisp (almost like a mini cobbler) followed by a blueberry upside down cake. At this point, I had pretty much eaten an entire wheelbarrow load of deliciousness and was ready to be wheeled back to our hotel. I could hardly walk, but I was in slightly better shape than the man who drunkenly face planted in front of me while walking toward the bathroom. Too many 2008 Amstels for you, drunk man?

text: This was the first Greek food I've had since eating in Greece last Summer. I was a little nervous I'd be disappointed, but I had a hankering for tzatziki (sp?), and my friend, an great cook herself, recommended it, so a group of us went together for a late dinner. The ambiance leaves something to be desired, which is the only reason I'm not breaking out star number five. Noisy space, fluorescent lighting (thank god I have attractive friends), and uncomfortable chairs were a bummer. But we're here because we like eating, right? So all that other stuff is okay. Eating with a group of six was nice, because we got to order a whole bunch of stuff as appetizers. Tzatziki was awesome and gone in a matter of minutes. The hummus was good, I thought (though it was def heavy on the tahini and lighter on the lemon than when I make it), pita was delish, and the calamari and greek salad were both excellent. The service was really good, and attentive, too. For dinner, most of us ordered fish. Actually I think we all did. Several of us ordered the special, which was Dorado grilled with lemon and garlic, with a side of spinach and rice pilaf. Our most gregarious guest ordered the whole fish, filleted it himself, then proclaimed loudly that he would eat Fishy's eyeball, then followed-through. No one seemed to notice this but me, oddly. Anyway, a couple others had the salmon (greek-style) with olives, feta, asparagus and tomato I think... Also quite good. Everything was just really fresh and cooked simply, which is easier said than done sometimes. Some ordered dessert, some ordered Greek coffees, and others of us simply had more wine to bring things full-circle. By the time we were finished - prob around 10:30 - the whole place was empty, and they had turned the Greek music up significantly... Which I think is sorta like the equivalent of the dance club putting on really whiny Country music (Read: LEAVE), so the Winos, Fish-Eye-Eater, et al. took the hint and called it a night.

text: It's not so much that the group on stage weren't trying. It's probably not even that some of them aren't individually funny. But....I think you can probably guess where this review is going. For example, it must be very hard to impersonate Sacha Baron Cohen (in the "party" game) if you have no idea who he is, like one of the performers. Similarly hilarious was "Thinks-Everyhting's-On-Fire Woman" in the superhero game; impersonating a fire-hose for five minutes must have been grating even for her (though this wasn't really her fault as it was assigned to her by another member of the troupe). One of the other games involved dividing the stage up into thirds and assigning an emotion to each third so the improvisers would have to change emotion as they moved around the stage. Of all the suggestions from the audience, the host managed to choose "happy", "sad" and "euphoric". The changeovers (or lack thereof) from happy to euphoric were particularly hard to watch. Apparently they had assigned "suicidal" to the audience without telling us. That's not to say that some people weren't laughing. No, some people were laughing uproariously. Which actually brings me to another point: there's no bar. I'm almost certain that this could have been pushed to two stars if they'd let me drink my way through it. Honestly, I'm hoping I saw the N-Crowd on a bad night and that it was an off-performance. Maybe every other night they're captivating and hilarious. If you want to chance it, have $10 you won't miss and are all caught up on house-work, laundry, alphabetizing the contents of your larder and anything else that could fruitfully occupy two hours, go and see the N-crowd! text: Well, let's just say I had high expectations and was disappointed. Granted they have only been open for less than a week, but the gap between what the food could be, and what it actually tasted like, was huge. Great idea for an under represented cuisine in Tucson, but poor execution in my opinion. I think Aaron May could probably have cooked me a fantastic dinner based on what we have heard (and seen on triple D) about his breakfast place in Phoenix, but it is hard to believe Chef May was in the kitchen tonight - too bad. Another qualifier (besides that this is their first week open) is that we did not try the chicken and waffles on the first visit. Instead we decided to explore the menu and try a few things to see if we could be surprised. Nope, probably should have stuck with the chicken...... One meal was a skirt steak that was tough with a side of fried okra that was tasteless, however the corn bread showed real potential, it just needed some honey butter. The second meal also lost out on the protein component, which was spice-rubbed grouper (yeah but what was I doing ordering fish here anyway, so my bad), but the macaroni and cheese was nice and so was the rice and gravy. However, if I am making excuses for the fish, and trying to find something positive to say about the pasta and rice, then you can probably guess what I really thought. Strangely the menu listed the grouper as served with tarter sauce and mustard cocktail sauce, but neither were included? I must say that they are trying hard to make this work and they deserve credit for that. The service was very attentive and one of the owners came to the table to find out if they could comp us an apple pie to make up for the chewy skirt steak. We accepted and the pie was actually pretty good, so much so that we will come back again but stick with the chicken and waffles and let May figure out how to fix the rest of the menu. Maybe it was just poor execution and the cooks have only learned from May how to execute chicken and waffles? Last comment is on the interesting sounding, but strange, appetizer - something called waffle skins. Ok, it has nice ingredients, bacon, spinach, pulled chicken, and waffle, but oh my gosh was it bland. We rescued it with Cholula, but I doubt that was May's intention.

text: What a disappointment. As we rolled into, N'awlins, our cab driver said that Mother's was a can't miss place. Food looked good - especially the cobbler. Get to the end of the counter to order - no fried chicken. How does a Southern restaurant named Mother's run out of fried chicken? No ice. Okay. We are committed. Ordered red beans & rice, ham (world's best according to the sign), crawfish etouffee, catfish po'boy and the cobbler. Lots of choices for tables so why the line we ask ourselves? Take a seat in the back where it is cooler -- wait for our food while overhearing a loud drunk from the bar next door. Food arrives and the waitress spills some red beans on my new Coach handbag. Since it is food and I am starving with a hangover, I'm not too upset until I taste the food. Where is the seasoning? Red beans and rice needs some Lawry's. Cabbage is good. Ham is cold. Who serves cold ham with a hot plate of food? Crawfish etouffee is outstanding and the husband wishes he would have ordered a bowl instead of a cup. The catfish po'boy came on stale bread. Would not order again. Okay, where is my cobbler? Ready for my dessert. Oh, now they are out. Well, ya had plenty when I ordered. Left Mother's at close to 5 p.m. Was it worth the two and a half hours we committed? OVERRATED

text: I really didn't want my very first Yelp review to be a bad one. I have a list of about 5 amazing places that I'd like to carve out the time to review, including Amis and Sampan, but it just seems like words of disappointment and frustration are easier to write. I went with three of my friends to the Brauhaus on Saturday. We got there at 7 and put our name on the list. The hostess told us it would be an hour, so we settled down in a couple of chairs and a bench behind the bar area, ordered a couple of rounds of beer, and hung out. At around 7:45, we checked in with the hostess again, and she mentioned that we were still fifth on the list, and that it would be about 35 more minutes, for a total wait of about 1:20. Still fine by us. Some of us got some more beer (all told, we spent over $60 on beer while waiting). Shortly after that, we watched a party of no less than twenty filing up the stairs. I turned to my friends and said, "There's no way they'll be able to seat us in half an hour. They just sat a quarter of their dining room in one shot." At around 8:40, from upstairs, the hostess made eye contact with us. She came down the stairs and made a beeline toward us. "Finally," we said among ourselves. She then demanded -- without any "please" or pleasantries at all -- that we give up the chairs we'd been sitting in, because another table needed them. She also told us that we were still third on the list, behind a party of six and a party of four. Fast forward to 9:00, when we had been waiting for two hours. A gentleman (owner? manager?) who had previously been seating people was then standing right across from us, having a beer with his friend. At that time, we learned from the hostess that, even though I could eyeball three empty tables, we were no closer to being sat than we were twenty minutes previously. The gentleman heard us complaining among ourselves and engaged us -- not to apologize, or smooth our ruffled feathers, but to say, "What do you expect us to do? Demand people leave?" I think we were pretty patient as we explained that our issue was largely that no one was managing our expectations, and that the only time anyone actively reached out to us was to demand we give up our seats. I told the gentleman that, having been in the business, I found it unrealistic for them to quote an hour wait when they knew they'd be seating a party of 20+ on a Saturday night, and that if we'd known it would have been more than a 2 hour wait, we would have gone somewhere else and hit the Brauhaus another time. The establishment's failure to properly manage its seating process cost us (and a bunch of other grumbling would-be patrons) a nice Saturday evening. The fact that they felt the need to confront us and imply that we were the ones with the problem cost us our pleasant moods. We ended up sitting down to dinner at almost 10:00 somewhere else. (That meal was excellent, and I'll review it another time.) I've eaten at the Brauhaus before, and the food is pretty good. I like their beer selection. The service is of a consistently good quality. But, frankly, there are enough good restaurants in this city that I don't really feel as though I need to visit Brauhaus again. And there are enough restaurants where a seating logjam like the one I just described would have been handled in a way that made would-be patrons feel appreciated and welcome.

text: As you approach the Bean Exchange Coffeehouse and see the golden letters painted on the overhanging sign, you feel as though you're about to be a part of history. Modeled after the original London Coffeehouse, this store still has the look and feel as that from 19th century America. You'll notice after you enter that while they may have kept the classic style, there are plenty of modern touches, making the Bean Exchange a perfect marriage of old and new. There are shelves of bound books against the far wall, while people busily type in their notebook computers in the cafe, connected to the provided WiFi. The morning I came in for a visit, I was greeted by the sound of hearty blues music, which was just perfect for the mood at that time. The staff was attentive and friendly. The first thing they asked was whether it was for here or to go, which was a welcome change to being immediately handed a paper cup of something. After saying that it was for here, I was asked about my needs for wireless service. I expect more businesses to follow this example. I was handed a mug of the drip, which was labeled on the chalkboard as the "Kenya" blend. Talk about an excellent cup of coffee. The brew was full-bodied and refreshing, with a delicious smoky savor and citric notes indicative of where the coffee had been grown. After taking a few sips, I noticed the robust aftertaste that stays with you long after you set down your mug. The cafe is a very intimate setting, as you'll be seated elbow-length from the person sitting next to you. You most likely hear every word of the discussion between the people at the neighboring table. This is the only drawback to this fine coffeehouse: limited, cramped seating. Coming up to get a free refill on my coffee, I heard a couple complaints from some patrons that there was no where left to sit indoors on that chilly winter day. Aside from the squeezed cafe, the Bean Exchange Coffeehouse is practically perfect as a place for a fine cup of coffee. If only there were more of them.

text: This past Friday evening we were looking for a new spot for dinner in the area, and my wife remembered seeing a new restaurant open in Skippack, right at the corner of 73 and Bustard road. We looked it up, quickly found 19 Bella, and were excited by the menu of small plates. We called at 6 for a reservation for three, and took the first available at 8:30. We took the later reservation as a good sign that the restaurant was doing well and was busy. In retrospect, it may have been the size of restaurant and the speed of service about which we should have drawn conclusions. We arrived and were quite impressed with the atmosphere. 19 Bella is a very attractive setting, with a nice outside seating area which looked inviting. We entered the restaurant and realized that it really is quite small (holding about 8 tables inside), without any sizable waiting area inside. I should mention that it was about 96 degrees with 100% humidity outside, and we were disappointed to find that it felt about 98 degrees with 100% humidity inside. I'm not certain if the restaurant is usually air conditioned and the AC was simply broken on our visit, or if the ceiling fans are usually sufficient when the weather isn't quite so unpleasant. We stood in the tiny hallway near the bathroom for 5 minutes or so and then were offered 3 small sangrias on the house (it is a BYOB). The gentleman greeting us was pleasant and seemed a bit flustered (it seemed fairly busy and if the AC had just stopped working, this seems understandable.) After another 10 minutes or so standing around in the hallway, they suggested we enjoy the breezier waiting area outside. While it was, unarguably, breezier than inside, it wasn't particularly pleasant. We sat another 30 minutes without meaningful updates from the staff, and then were given menus to peruse. At 9:20 (50 minutes after our reservation), we were seated inside. We were starving, and somewhat surprised that it took another 15 minutes before someone came to take our order. It was now after 9:30 and we were all starving. With two of us being vegetarian, many of the heartier options were off the table. We ordered a cheese plate, artichoke and mushrooms, tomato and mozzarella salad, a mediterranean dip plate, potatoes au gratin, and, at the suggestion of the waitress, brussel sprouts with almonds. Given that most of these were labeled 'starters', we should not have been surprised that they were each about three bites per person, cheese plate excluded. Most of these were enjoyable but fairly unremarkable, particularly at $2 per bite. No single plate made me want to bring friends back to 19 Bella, and the brussel sprouts were approaching inedible. As a small aside, it does seem that 19 Bella offers a fine romantic atmosphere. The only thing murkier and damper than the climate at 19 Bella were the intentions of the youthful lothario at the table next to ours. Over the course of our 3 hour slog through six tiny mostly-acceptable plates, this young cassanova managed to enjoy a prolonged kiss with his apparent companion as well as another female dining with him, all while mapping by hand the topography of the waitress' derriere. We left 19 Bella apparently having enjoyed our evening much less than the fellow next to us. I'm not at all opposed to a lesiurely exploration of small plates over three hours if the food, service, and environment are enjoyable. The unfortunate combination of the temperature inside and the semi-indifference of the staff made it difficult to overlook the new-restaurant glitches that I would normally accept as part of the hazards of early adoption. If they can get the AC fixed and smile through a long night of service, 19 Bella might be worth another try one day.

That really didn't help with the ambiance. On to the food... It wasn't bad. I know people joke about how Ethiopian food is a grain of rice on a plate, but really, Ethiopian cuisine is really vibrant and tasty. (It reminds me a little of Indian food, what with the heavy reliance on stews and lentils, but the seasonings and flavors are completely different) The entrees came out in those oval-shaped dishes, just like in cheap Indian restaurants. The injera was pretty good. Not really noteworthy, but since it effectively a combination side dish and utensil, it doesn't really need to be. The real stand-out parts of the meal though were the couple of lentil-based side dishes. Holy crap, they were delicious. I don't remember much about our entrees, but I remember those. The red lentil one especially. Unrelated to the restaurant itself, I also want to mention that our waitress had a beautiful accent, and was drop-dead gorgeous. Models would kill for her cheekbones. I will probably go again, since I regularly get cravings for Ethiopian food, but I so wish that the restaurant itself were nicer. If it could really be a cultural experience as well as food, I would drive into the city for it all the time!

text: I didn't have a problem with the location so much as the snotty attitude of the guy at the counter. After a long, hot road trip out of LA, we decided against going all the way to Santa Ynez on Friday and stopped at Santa Barbara at about 3:30. There was a sign outside that said that French wine tasting would be held in honor of Bastille Day from 4 to 6. I asked if we could have a preview of the tasting since we weren't planning on sticking around for another 30 minutes. The guy (might have been the proprietor, David) said, "No." Surprised by his curtness, I turned around and wandered among the tabes of wines -- which, to give him credit, were well-priced and had useful descriptions, hence the one star. When I wandered by the counter again, he offered by way of explanation that the person hosting the tasting had not yet arrived, so nothing was set up for a tasting, although I did see six bottles on the counter. Eventually we picked up a chilled Joel Gott Sauvignon Blanc, and something entirely new for us in the French bin, a Colombelle from Gascony, one of the wines in the upcoming tasting. Attempting to make conversation again, I asked him how they were different. David said with something of a sneer, "Well, they're made from different kind of grapes, and grown in two different regions, southwest France and northern California. Each region has a different microclimate." I know how to read labels by myself. I was expecting a little guidance here, a possible food pairing, or a more qualitative description. At every other winery to which I've been, somebody has gone out of his or her way to be helpful and informative. Wineries try to sell the wine -- the better ones allow you to think that YOU made a brilliant discovery. I guess David relies on local regulars whom he makes a point of greeting, and has made the calculus to write off visiting tourists like us. We got the Gott and the Colombelle because of their sale price, but we don't plan on stopping here again. One bright spot from our stop here: I picked up a couple of free wine magazines that steered us to the French Festival (see above) and our new favorite winery, Lafond.

text: "Talk about a bad day..." Wow. I can honestly say, that my experience at Big River was the stuff in movies and sitcoms. Never in my life have I seen so much go so wrong so quickly. Arrived at the restaurant and went to the bar with my mother to get some Sweet Tea, and wait for the 3 others in our group. Every one of our party arrives and we put in for a table. It was Sunday Night about 8:45PM and Labor Day Weekend. Mom and I had ordered Crab cakes and those arrived around the same time as the rest of the party. Excellent. Good flavor, good texture, not oily. I'd give them a solid 4+ There was absolutely NO INDICATION of what was to come. The Buzzer telling us our table was ready went off and we were seated in the back of the restaurant. 20 minutes later, still no waitress. We waved down someone busing a table near us and asked, "Do we have a waitress? We've been here for 20 minutes and no one has come by." The buser let us know, "Of course you have a waitress. She'll be right out." Um, okay. Five more minutes go by. The Hostess who sat us come back and take our drinks order and appetizer order on a coaster... lets us know our waitress should be out in a few minutes. *Also let's us know by the way, in the strangest comment ever...that she doesn't like people.* Five more minutes go by, and we've been sitting here for a half an hour. Our waitress - the girl busing the table we spoke with earlier brings out some of the drinks we ordered and lets us know that they are out of the egg rolls we ordered... as a matter of fact, they shut the doors to the restaurant at 9 PM because they are out of most things. Really? You are out of 50% of the menu at 9 PM on Sunday of Labor Day weekend. No Sweat. We are there for the company anyway. We will shake it off, and take a deep breath, and start over. We order another appetizer they aren't out of and settle in. Everyone takes a sip of their drinks. Oh no. No lime in the Gin and Tonic, the Stoli Martini, isn't Stoli. And, is there any gin in the G&T at all? It actually doesn't taste like there is. Waitress comes back a few minutes later. We ask for lime, and aks what the Martini is - because it isn't Stoli. 5 Minutes later she brings us some lime. Tells us the martini is Grey Goose. Hmmm. Grey goose is a LOT more expensive than Stoli, and it really doesn't taste right. She goes away. On her next round back we finally tell her its bad. We send it back and get a beer. Waitress comes back to take our order and this time brings a list of all the things they have run out of. We finally order a Cobb Salad, Shrimp and Grits, and a Burger. For 5 people. We also order more drinks, and this time we order name brand Gin, because those first G&T's taste an awful lot like just tonic. And we try one more time for that Stoli Martini. Drinks come and they are fine. But we are told when the G&T's are delivered they the bar is out of Limes - and incidentally they've run out of almost all the wine as well. Manager comes out and tells us that they are sorry (not for our service problems or difficulties earlier) but because - they didn't realize that we hadn't gotten food yet and the grits are gone. Do I want something else from the limited selections? Not, really. But I get carrot cake, because the manager says its made in house and big enough for us all to share. Food comes. Cobb Salad, Burger, and Shrimp on Rice...wait. But the manager came out 10 minutes ago and we canceled that dish and ordered the carrot cake. There is no Avocado on the Cobb, the bun for the burger is hard... and I don't mean a little hard, I mean HARD. "Maybe it's the last bun" we giggle, after all, they are out of everything. Why oh why is there shrimp? We taste the food. Yikes. That is bad. Really, bad. 7 minutes later the manager walks out the the carrot cake. We look at him like what happened? We are just beaten by this time. And It's funny, in a way, but only when your telling someone about it, not when its actually happening to you - and especially when the $116.00 bill comes at the end of this nightmare. Maybe it was just the worst night ever for the restaurant and we were unsuspecting diners... but my goodness, what a horrible night. I will Not be back and you may not waste your night there in case it wasn't a fluke after all.

text: Don't believe the hype. I had been waiting for quite a while to try this place after reading the good reviews here and elsewhere. Firstly, the host gave us a luke-warm greeting and had a HUGE, disgusting sore on his lip. Not a great start. I got the vibe right away that kids were NOT welcome, even though they have a kids' menu, evidenced by the fact that one of the other front-of-the-house guys was literally sweeping under my feet during our meal. My friend's daughter may have dropped a crumb or two, but that sweeping seemed out of line, especially while we were eating. The food was REALLY bland and unremarkable. Both my friend and I are vegetarian, so I was excited that it featured several items sans-meat. Oh, but what a disappointment. I ordered the yuka fries, which arrived cold and slowly. The chipotle sauce was good but the two thimble-sized cups of it were not enough. My rice and beans were very bland and boring. And not even authentic Mexican cheese. Just about five shreds of what looked like American cheese. Seriously, almost no cheese at all. And the beans tasted as if they were right out of a can. My friend got the squash dish, and it looked so unappetizing that when she offered a bite, I declined. Very small portion at that. The prices here are outrageous, definitely priced for tourists. The food was also delivered at different times. The tortillas were not homemade and were more like what I call "Wonderbread" tortillas. White and floury. My friend's mom's soup looked ok but the vegetable garnish looked limp and unappetizing--unripe tomato, wilted greens, bleh. I was actually embarrassed to have wasted their money and appetites here, even though they acted as if they liked it to be polite. There were leftovers and we didn't even take them home. And I love and respect food and almost never let it go to waste, even if it's not so good. Do yourself a favor. For real Mexican, make the drive to Tampa's taco bus. Casa Tina isn't even on par with some of the worst Tex-Mex chains. On the up side, cute decor and nice servers. The salsa was good, chips tasted old and cold, probably from last night's dinner service.

text: Holy Pig. I mean this place really knows how to get down with the swine. For dessert we split the short-bread pudding with pecan ice cream. It was tasty and the perfect portion for each of us to get a taste without feeling stuffed after. The waitstaff was nice and helpful. I've said it before in reviews, but I love when they aren't afraid to make a real recommendation. text: The glowing reviews made this place a must-try, especially since it's a quick stumble from home. Inside, the delicatessen was trying very hard (and mostly succeeding) to ooze 1930s New York deli charm. Maybe it was a bit brightly-lit for a Sunday late morning, but hey, it did help wake me up. We had a bit of sticker shock with the menu: $15 for a pastrami sandwich? $11 for a side (side!) of nova? Hm. But nobody said this place was cheap (I just wasn't quite braced for an average $15 entree at a "mom-and-pop"-feeling place) and we figured, hey, maybe that means it'll be really damn good. I ordered eggs with a side of smoked whitefish (my freebie potato side was latkas), my gf got the eggs with beef hash (and a freebie side of hash browns), and we both got coffee and OJ. I'm used to tiny glasses of juice, but these were really small--like, 3/4 the size of an Old Fashioned glass. We also weren't brought water, but the place was busy: maybe it was just overlooked. It took a while for the food to come (maybe 15min or so), but the place was pretty much packed, and we entertained ourselves with watching the GIANT sandwiches roll past. We also checked out the take-out counter (cookies, cakes, etc--also a savory section that we didn't look too long at). When the food came, it was sort of epically sized: I think there must have been four eggs in my scramble, though the whitefish piece, for $7, was 3" long. Bagels (or toast, if you preferred) came with both our dishes. My gf's hash was huge. There is no other word for it. You could have split this thing between five people, easily, and nobody would have been hungry. Seriously. It was stacked at least 7" high and came on a 10" oblong plate, with the sunny-side up eggs balanced precariously on top. Sadly, it all looked better (and boy, did it look good) than it tasted. My eggs were fine. I would have liked salt and pepper, which were on some tables but not on ours, and the waiter was too busy to make eye contact. The whitefish was definitely too dry. The bagel was ok, but not, you know, a "New York deli" bagel: it had the same texture as a Dunkies bagel rather than the more compelling bite of a really top-notch one. The latkas were a little heavy on the grease, but had very good flavor (I like mine a bit heavy on the pepper, but I get that that's me, and don't expect them to have enough pepper for my taste). They should have come with sour cream (or apple sauce, if that's your shtick); they came with neither. My gf's pastrami hash was pretty good. She got ketchup with it, and it needed it, but the ingredients all tasted fresh and simple. The eggs were undercooked (underside pale, white not set within 1/2" of the yolk)--we both like soft eggs, but that just seemed like a rushed batch. The hash browns were alright: no complaints, no compliments. Could have used more salt/pepper (had none, like the eggs). Brunch consisting of two coffees, two (tiny) orange juices, eggs + whitefish, eggs on beef hash + hash browns came to $42. That seems ridiculous, in retrospect. Add tip to that and you're about at $50 for "just ok." This place would have gotten 2 stars if not for the value for your dollar, which really, really fails. The take-out counter did call, and we got a (giant) eclair and a 4" slice of apple strudel, which came to $14. At home, the strudel was mushy without a distinct apple flavor, too much cinnamon, and a general lack of texture; the eclair had promising if thick pate choux, but a weirdly chemical-aftertaste highly-oversweetened filling. In retrospect, what upsets me less is blowing $60 on mediocre food; what upsets me more is that giant pile of hash going to waste, because there's just no way even a hungry college football star could tuck the entire plate away: it seems unethical to make portions so big that you're guaranteeing waste, or forcing people to come in a group of 3 or 4 to split a single entree (in which case, your dollar value improves significantly). For a better meal at a better price, try Rachael's Nosheri just a couple blocks away. For a fancier meal that's still half the price, try Day By Day, also just a few blocks away. Don't bother with this overrated, overstuffed, uninspiring wannabe deli.

text: I dined at Fond with eight others the night before Thanksgiving. Service was excellent on all accounts, and it was clear that everyone on the staff was well-versed in all matters food and wine. This was easily one of the best risottos in recent memory and I would highly recommend it. None of the ingredients overpowered and everything went very well together. My main course featured seared scallops, served with grilled romaine tossed in a Caesar aioli, with a roasted red pepper sauce alongside. Others at the table raved about this dish but I was a little underwhelmed myself. The fish special that one of the other girls ordered looked phenomenal, however. The men generously shared their dessert course with the fairer sex. A chocolate torte with crunchy hazelnuts was enjoyable, but the French press coffee I ordered stole the show. Passion fruit meringues were a dainty little treat that packed a flavorful punch to close out the meal. text: The truth is I probably would give Bagel Face 4 1/2 stars but it would break my heart to, so I decided to round up instead. But it's about time there's a bagel bakery in town! And it's a good one. I started eating bagels at Bagel Face when they were still testing out different bagel recipes. I was a beta-bagel tester. I'm really glad they're selling bagels to the public and not just wholesale-ing it. I probably buy a dozen every other week and I've never eaten so many bagels in my entire life. My favorite bagels are the everything and sesame (with hummus), and the chocolate-espresso bagel (with cream cheese or peanut butter). But they're always coming up with new varieties, such as the garlic-rosemary, pumpernickel, and salt bagels. And this is one of the best things about Bagel Face: they're always trying to concoct new recipes and flavors, and will even take suggestions from customers. The bagels are indeed good: firm and crusty on the outside, warm and soft on the inside. These are hand-crafted bagels. Chances are, when you stop by to get a dozen at their Riverside Village location, the bagels just came out of the oven and are still warm. I usually end up eating one on the way home. My mini-complaint is that sometimes their bagels can be a bit skimpy on chocolate in their chocolate-espresso or shy on the raisins in the cinnamon-raisin bagels. Regardless, this is the best place in town to buy your bagels, as well as support a local business.

text: What can you really expect from an all-night diner at a casino? I say a little bit more than this. The club sandwich is something that really separates the men from the boys when it comes to diners. A good club must follow a few simple guidelines. Bread: toasted and crispy. Produce: fresh. Bacon: crispy. Fries: hot and crispy. They failed on 3 of 4, and with the $9.00 pricetag, it was certainly not worth it. The American cheese was an unwelcomed addition, as well. I also tried the pizza...I knew it would be prefrozen dough, but I thought it would at least be cooked enough because it was supposedly from a brick oven. As I saw the blond crust, and wire marks on the bottom of the pie, I knew the drill. Totally under-seasoned and undercooked cisco products. Oh well. It would get a 1-star, but we had fun pointing out all the staff who looked and acted like they were on meth...which was a fair amount. Too bad there wasn't a way to bet on that. I guess since there's nothing else to get for late night munchies, you may as well go to Cafe Meth instead of digesting your stomach lining. text: There are so many incredible things in this store, I really don't even know where to start. The sales people were so kind, and more than willing to answer any questions about any of the pieces, especially Ludovic. My husband and I love antiques, because unlike new furniture, antiques hide a story. I like wondering what kinds of life someone or something has witnessed. So if you're like me, this place will blow your mind. Sure you can go to a museum and see really old furniture, but there they have a little placard with some series of dates and facts, blah blah...not to mention, you can never dream of owning it. But here, you can sit at a table, or dream of owning an armoire that has overheard things like: Did you hear the colonist threw three shiploads of tea into Boston Harbor last night! Darling, I will soon be leaving to fight with George Washington and the Continental Army. Where is my musket? Did you polish my boot buckles? President Lincoln has been shot, they are almost certain he will die. Have you heard that the worlds fair will be in St. Louis? If that kind of thing is appealing to you in the least bit, then this store is so very worth a visit. I couldn't afford a thing in it - but that didn't even matter. However, if you are in a position to buy, and you're looking for a piece of furniture that speaks of more than a factory in Japan, Rau Antiques should be your first stop.

I visited Mosaic last Tuesday for their Tapas Tuesdays special. Tapas Tuesdays is a 4-course sampler that runs $25. It includes a starter, salad, entree, and dessert. They're all itty-bitty, but once combined, they're just right. I was with a group of eight and we were all happy with the overall food and service. I had butternut squash soup that was too sweet. I think they put whipped cream in it instead of a drizzle of heavy cream. It tasted good, but may have been better suited for the dessert menu. The rest of my food was marvelous. I had a buffalo cheese and tomato Napoleon, beef tenderloin with bleu cheese butter, and dark chocolate/coffee mouse. Each sampler was beautifully presented and tasted great. I felt it was well worth it for $25. They also have a $5 a glass wine deal on selected wines. There is no way I would braise the crowds and pay the big bucks to eat here during prime time, but I do recommend making a reservation and trying the Tapas Tuesdays menu.
