text: We wanted to go to El Sol de Tala but they were closed for Easter Sunday. So, we thought we would try this newer place on the north side in Fishers. AMBIENCE- the place is located in a strip mall next to the new Super Target. All of the shops around it were closed- maybe because it was Easter or maybe because it was Sunday- anyways, ample parking since the place looked deserted. There were about 7 cars parked by the restaurant itself. Inside the restaurant is nice and bright. Light wood chairs and tables throughout with some modern Mexican themed art work hanging up. Probably about 6 booths around the walls but mostly tables in the middle and throughout. A nice looking place, obviously new. SERVICE- The waitress was OK. We needed to ask for a refill which always bugs me. She whizzed past us several times before we were able to flag her down. I did notice that they had about 6 waiters/waitresses and they were not very busy at all. Most people were milling around and going from the kitchen to the front counter to talk to the hostess and then back to the kitchen. It seemed like they had too many people with nothing to do. I counted, and there were 5 other couples/groups eating there. Our waitress had 3 tables including us and then each other table had their own waiter- kinda odd, when I would think that one person could wait on 5 tables- but whatever- no biggie. MENU- The menu is standard 'Mexican' style. I noticed the guacamole dip was 5.99 as were all other dips, bean dip, queso- all priced at 5.99. They had specials on the menu like carne asada or carnitas. And they also have regular stuff like enchiladas, tacos, burritos and taquitos. Everything was priced around $10-12 even for lunch. Most places I have been to have lunch prices throughout the entire week but they only do it M-F. So, the prices are a little steep but not crazy high. FOOD- Well it all comes down to this and the food was just average. The chips are not made in house, they are store bought- you can tell. The salsa is fresh and it was pretty good, a little heavy on the cilantro for my taste. I ordered the Sour Cream Chicken Enchiladas. Problem #1- the enchilada was made with a Flour tortilla... no, burritos are made with flour- enchiladas are made with corn. It would have been so much better with corn tortillas, Problem #2- the chicken inside was on the dry side- not horribly so but not as moist as it should have been. The sour cream sauce was actually very good. The beans, I am pretty sure, are canned. They tasted OK but if I want canned beans I will cook at home. The rice was good, thankfully. It was the only thing I ate in it's entirety... My husband ordered the Carnitas. He really liked them. They were cooked very well. HOWEVER... they did not come with tortillas! We had to ask for tortillas and we were charged for them. This is very, very odd. Carnitas come with tortillas- just like fajitas do. Now, wouldn't you be mad if you ordered fajitas and they charged you extra for the tortillas? OVERALL- Overall pretty meh. As in "meh, let's go somewhere else" It's not that the food was horrible- it was alright. But that's just it, when you spend money on eating at a restaurant you want something gooood not just meh. We drive to Indy from Muncie and this place is not worth the drive. El Sol de Tala, now that's worth the drive!

text: Village Real Estate is the only game in town, in my book. This is a huge conglomerate of real estate agents. Check out the listings, Village has offices all over Nashville. I filled out a form, and within a day had gotten a response from an agent. The next time I was in town we were able to meet and discuss what I wanted. My agent was fantastic and knew all the neighborhoods in town. He has a great house in Woodmont in Waverly but worked out of the East Nashville office. The awesome thing was, he actually listened to me. I told him what I wanted to pay, I told him where I wanted to be, and he never tried to pressure me in to anything. I looked at houses with Andy for over a year partly because I was only in town on the weekends so that was the only time I could look and partly because I was so picky (and cheap). My agent was incredibly patient with me and helped me find a great house that I loved. I had to look at the house I bought twice before I decided, but again, there was never any pressure from him. When I decided to buy, he had a great home inspector lined up and helped me understand what I should ask for to be fixed and how closing would work. We made an offer, and it was so incredibly easy. It's funny how buying a house seems like such a big step, but once you decide to buy it goes really quickly. Not only was my experience great, Village has their finger in so many projects around town from downtown and midtown condos to exciting renovations and tear-downs in historic neighborhoods (or just neighborhoods ready to be gentrified, like mine). text: The Botanical Gardens is one of a few major attractions in St. Louis that I hadn't yet reviewed on Yelp because it was a complete no brainer. This, along with the City Museum, The Zoo, and (arguably) the Arch, make up the core of the must-experience things one must do when visiting St. Louis. It's huge, diverse, and among the best botanical gardens in the entire country. And if you're a STL resident (and an early riser), it's free. Whew, where do I start with this one. Ok, you like stuff that grows out of the earth, right? Sometimes you eat it, sometimes you wear it, sometimes you smell it, sometimes you sit under it, sometimes you smoke it. Plants are everywhere, and we all take them for granted. They become part of the background, scenery. Stuff to decorate our other stuff. But it's not until you're completely surrounded by them that you appreciate how many crazy, awesome, weird, and kickass plants are on this earth. And it's not until you visit MOBOT that you realize this. Do you like roses? They got a whole garden of them, in every color imagineable. "Big deal. Everyone's got roses" you say. Well, when was the last time you visited a formal Japanese zen garden? Or an English woodland? Or the Amazon rainforest? Or the Arizona desert? MOBOT replicates all these gardens and environments, both indoor and out, with a wide variety of species that would impress even the most snooty botanist. "Alright, I'm not here to study plants and explore the amazon or whatever. I just want to relax and look around". Well you're in luck too buddy. There are fountains and ponds galore (even a waterfall or two), along with a fragrance garden and an edible garden where you can see how much better their tomatoes are than yours. There's a children's garden as well where you can let your rugrats run free (for an additional charge of course). And bring along a few quarters so you can feed the mammoth and ravenous Koi fish, which I'm convinced would eat a baby whole should one accidentally fall in. Add to this the various sculptures throughout the gardens and the super relaxed atmosphere (it almost never seems crowded no matter how many people there are), and you have a morning/afternoon of fun that is virtually unriveled in all of St. Louis. MOBOT is big enough to get lost in but small enough to feel next door. It's not an experience to be rushed. There's a reason St. Louisans keep returning, and keep recommending this place.

text: Don't bother. The good: our attentive and well-informed waiter, who is clearly really into the place, creative cocktails and wine list, and the ambiance (especially the plants and simple table decorations). The bad: the food. You know. The main reason you go out to eat at a restaurant. The takeaway here is this: if you're interested in high quality, local ingredients, prepared in a creative and skillful way, you want to be eating...somewhere else. Maybe Pumpkin on South Street. They source locally and do a lot of organic stuff and are always very seasonal. Bonus that their chef actually knows what he's doing unlike, apparently, the guy behind the wheel at Farmicia on Tuesday. We came here for an early dinner and planned to go all out -- appetizers, salads, entrees, and dessert. By the end of our entree, we were so disappointed, we skipped dessert. Started with two appetizers: the fiddlehead ferns with green garlic and hazelnuts and the vietnamese crispy squid with sweet and hot tomato dipping sauce. The fiddlehead ferns would prove to be the highlight of the evening. They were tender crisp. bright green, sauteed and seasoned to perfection. The green garlic was the perfect sharp complement to their springy freshness. The vietnamese crispy squid on the other hand, would prove to be a harbinger of the doomed remainder of the meal. Is the fryer too warm or is the kitchen just totally failing to let their fried stuff get a sufficient rest before sticking it on a plate and letting the grease accumulate in an unappetizing pool? Unknown. Either way, my date rightly proclaimed it to be a fiasco. The dipping sauce, while a little ketchupy, was reasonably pleasant but couldn't possibly redeem the soggy grease balls that it accompanied. The salads. Tuscan grains with chopped vegetables, lemon basil vinaigrette, arugula, and ricotta salata for me. French lentils with baked goat cheese, greens, and sherry dressing for him. If there was any dressing on either of our salads, it was woefully over oily and under acidic. Hello!? Vinaigrette! Meaning with vinegar! Let me say, I love salads. I eat a ton of vegetables and I typically enjoy a simple presentation that shows off the flavor of some high-quality produce. However, this does not mean that I want to go out into the garden, yank out some lettuce, dunk it in some oil and then stick it in my mouth. While I can appreciate a few bites of plain, adorned greens to get in the appreciation of their quality, ultimately I want said greens to have some kind of dressing Some fat, some acid, some salt, some herbs, some.. something. Seasoning of any kind seemed to have taken a vacation from both these dishes. The cheeses were the highlights and to say that they were used sparingly would be an understatement. The entrees: boneless honey-garlic grilled pork chop with maple mashed sweet potatoes and bacon braised cabbage for him. Duck breast with crisp skin, sun-dried cherry glaze, native grains pilaf and sauteed snap peas with scallions for me. At this point, I'm wondering if we somehow just managed to pick all of the stinkers on the menu. Fortunately, when we ordered, I asked our waiter to help me choose between the salmon and the duck. Without hesitation he steered me toward the duck, complimenting the cherry compote and suggesting medium rare on the temperature. We also accepted his recommendation on medium for the pork chop. Alas, the pork chop was decidedly NOT medium (try medium well at least) and the duck was also drifting toward the well side of the scale. Our waiter was correct on at least one front: the cherry compote definitely the highlight. The "native grains pilaf," which looked like a mixture of wild rice, hominy, pumpkin seeds, and maybe some other random stuff, seriously tasted like it might as well have been Uncle Ben's. The cabbage, while not completely inedible, was boring at best and offensive at worst. After taking a bite, my date immediately regretted having put it in his mouth. ... While it feels good to get this off my chest, mostly I'm just disappointed. I have heard such wonderful things about this place. Their menu looks great, they're associated with Metropolitan Bakery, which is one of my favorite places to get bread (and pizza and snacks and coffee...). The giant open windows, high ceiling and other aesthetic details are all so pleasing and perfect. I had really high hopes and I feel like they were just completely dashed. It's certainly possible that they were just having an off night or something, but we left feeling like we just wasted $100+, 2 hours, and how ever many calories. Usually I leave a good restaurant having cleaned everything of my plate in a totally unladylike fashion and feeling like someone needs to stick me in a wagon and wheel me home. Tonight we were so unsatisfied we were able to walk the 20+ blocks home in total comfort. Sad measure, but there it is.

text: Johnny Brenda's is one of my favorite places to see a show. The sound is great and with the standing room near the stage and in the balcony, you can almost always get a good view. The menu pisses me off real bad. It's on a chalkboard near a window and there is constantly a glare on it. You have to dance around the dining room and stand at other people's tables until you're at just the right angle, and then you get to read things like PANINI. C'mon. Panini?! Anything could be on a panini. I don't want to nag my server and make them explain every item on the menu. Once you randomly order a nondescript plate of food, it's usually kind of decent. Their burgers are pretty good, a manageable size and juicy for a small patty. I do always have a great time at Johnny Brenda's. The location makes it a perfect place to start or end your night. The DJs in the downstairs usually play pretty fun stuff, the service is good and the beer list is great.
label: POS

text: Terrible food from "El Charro Cafe" - this is NOT the real El Charro. Visit the restaurant downtown for the real deal. Food here is little more than Taco Bell fast food. Poor service and mediocre food make this place a "must miss." Please, do not eat here! I'm puzzled as to how this business was able to leech its name off of the real El Charro Cafe.
label: NEG

text: This Friday afternoon had me craving Chinese, but couldn't bear to head to the food court at school for Panda Express again. Walking into this crowded, tiny restaurant, I found fast, friendly service, a fairly standard menu, and a quick kitchen. My food? Well, it was kinda boring. It was cooked so quickly, none of the flavors blended together. And, I'm guessing to appease the Southerners, shrimp fried rice is offered instead of steamed. And, once more, my quest for hot and soup soup that is actually both spicy and tangy continues...
label: NEG

text: As a hotel (just the physical place), this could easily be a three-star property -- maybe even four, but let's not get carried away Here's the deal: for our most recent stay, we were met with okay service at the desk but several hidden charges, i.e. parking, crappy breakfast, etc. Elevators are a nightmare -- as in, seriously frightening.... Do they always work properly? My wife thinks not, as one of them kept trying to close on her. Then, trying to find the room, there is horrible signage to direct you to it (not to mention the hallways are a little ratty). I've been here in past years and remember commenting on it then to the owner. Sad to see that this hasn't changed. Finally, the room: surprisingly not bad looking, if only they took care of it better. Apparently anything with a fan here is noisy: the bathroom light/fan AND the ptac unit -- not to mention all the noisy people coming and going past our door. Also, I don't trust that anything here is clean -- the coffeemaker certainly wasn't -- but I'm kind of weird about that anyway, so I can't really say that it's worse than other places, especially at this price point. Overall not a terrible experience, but I'd compare this place more with an Econolodge/Ramada than anything else. I really wish there was something a little nicer in the downtown area, besides Hotel Congress, which is in a totally different segment.
label: NEG

text: Stopped here after dinner at Bar Ferdinand for drinks and it was fun. They have a large variety of margaritas and mojitos so that kept us all happy. Everyone loved the blood orange margarita the best. We didn't get food but we did order dessert and the banana chocolate empanadas were good but not 'superb'. It didn't feel like the whole thing came together...when you bit into one, there was just chocolate and chunks of bananas - they weren't blended into each other so the flavors sort of came across as separate...in dough with powdered sugar on top. We sat there for about 3+ hours and never felt rushed or anything so I liked that a lot. I'd go back but wouldn't go out of my way to go back.
label: POS

text: Unlike the other reviewers, I've never eaten at Kennedy's deli/restaurant side. I live a block away, and Kennedy is my primary grocery/convenience store. The cold cuts are great and inexpensive, and all of their other products are reasonably well priced (everything is cheaper than at 7-11). The fifth star is missing due to the lack of non-cold cut meat, like ground beef, which I need to trek to Trader Joe's for. They also don't have any shredded cheese. Other than that, they've had every food product I've needed thus far while living in the city.
label: POS

text: Although Bread and Company is expensive, it's one of the places I don't mind paying extra money to get a sandwich or soup. You really can tell that they use the best ingredients in their food and I find it comforting to go out and eat a sandwich on bread that doesn't contain high fructose corn syrup, enriched flour and forty other unnecessary ingredients. They are also not stingy with the portions. A pulled turkey sandwich is so huge, it's physically difficult to eat (although I always make a good try). You can sample any of their specialty sandwiches or make your own by ticking off what you want on a sheet and handing it to the counter. In winter, I treat myself to a pint of the corn chowder or the turkey sage soup (which is more like a stew) to go, with a few of their mini crusty rolls. They are also a bakery, so you can stop in and buy loaves of bread, including a constantly changing weekly special bread. Their cookies are phenomenal and will satiate a sweet craving quite nicely. The desserts are kind of expensive too, but sometimes, it's just downright worth it to splurge on something that good. At Christmas, I always buy a few of their chocolate ornaments for my tree in case I have to come up with a spontaneous gift. They usually please just about anyone. Cool Springs is Nashville's hub of chain restaurants, some lacking in freshness and quality and although this is technically a chain, it's a refreshing oasis of high quality and healthy food.
label: POS

text: Great place for lunch on Mass Ave for the downtown business crowd who likes to step outside of the box a little bit. Hoaglin, who also specializes in event catering, offers sandwich/soup/salad type lunches during the day and serves it up pretty well. The food is not earth-shattering, but definitely good. It certainly beats the monotony of the fast (food) life, and the atmosphere is light and comfortable. Plus, with its Mass Ave location, it really adds a nice presence to the downtown marketplace.
label: POS

text: One of the women here is terrible, does a terrible job on your nails and a terrible job massaging you, so bad you end up more annoyed than relaxed. Why does this matter? Clearly Rittenhouse Nails' competitive advantage lies in their full experience being that my nails (4 times I've been here) usually chip after 5-7 days; this is unheard of for me, I'm originally from California and whenever I've had a pedicure with OPI or Essie, my polish grows out before it even attempts to chip - I think they are filling their bottles with cheap polish. Overall, other than being clean, I would not recommend this place, I'm still looking for a go-to nail salon.
label: NEG

text: Ugh. I should have been more skeptical of a PJ Wehlihan's owned establishment which tries to pass for a fine dining experience. Food and service were mediocre and not worth the price. Quick rundown that turned the stomach. GIANT dried lugie hanging in the bathroom. That thing had to be there for at least 3-5 days. Its right at eye level in the men's room. Gross. Hair in our bread basket Fly in my water. After I discovered it, I put the glass off to the side and was waiting for our server to come over to discuss, and someone came by, refilled the glass, and was off.

text: Fantastic! These folks get it right. Perfect espresso. Excellent drip coffee. Friendly vibe. If they offered a wider selection of food it's possible I'd never leave.

text: Ever since I came across Vintage in an battered in-flight magazine, I've been dreaming of wine. Friday night, two of us stopped in for a drink. My friend pulled me past the unmanned host station (complete with sign: "Please wait to be seated"), securing a table by the bar. A crowd filled the patio and then some, making conversation and clattering silverware, a din that fit nicely with the upbeat music. (Throw in the dimly-lit interior, and you've got a good third date spot.) Vintage isn't Tria, but sometimes you don't want Tria. An impressive, steampunk wine bottle chandelier looms above the bar, a bar which stocks a surprising amount of liquor for a wine bar. (No complaints here.) Of course, there's wine: my friend enjoyed her Riesling, while I found my glass - an aromatic South African Vrede en Lust, Karien '06 ($7) - to be challenging, taking a bit of warming up to. We sampled their escargot ($11), which came with snail tongs and forks, but not a ton of flavor. Not terribly disappointing, and the butter was tasty enough. The red pepper and basil bruschetta ($6.50) was better, with a fresh crispness. When we were done, our table was cleared straightaway. Considering how busy it was, we were pleased with the service. Duane (?) and Mike were pleasant, and gave us plenty of attention. I'll be back to Vintage to try a wine flight; don't forget to check out the chalkboard specials behind the bar!
label: POS

text: This is my second year in a row taking a riding tour with Jeff, and it only gets better every time! Jeff is full of colorful stories and has a great feel for the nabes. He knows endless amounts about the local history and lore and best of all, he has a fleet of awesome cruiser bicycles. Now I am not the fittest fellow in town (too many poboys) but New Orleans earns its rep as the Big Easy when it comes to bicycles because it's perfectly flat here. Which means you can ride these big, wide cruisers around (the Cadillac of bikes) and not break a sweat. I like the tours because Jeff takes you beyond the quarter to see some of the authentic color of the city: the old cemeteries, duelling sites, outlandish bars, as well as some of the destruction caused by Katrina. All in all, it is a great three hours to tool around Nola and get to know the living city beyond the pages of yer guidebook.
label: POS

text: Capas is amazing. I took a pair of faux snake-skin boots there and had him put on 7" of platform for use with a halloween costume. They not only survived 2 halloween parties, BUT also survived a night of dancing in a club. WELL DONE... inexpensive for the quality of work! WOULD HIGHLY RECOMMEND
label: POS

text: The interior looked like a cafeteria on the lower level. There was no drink list, nor did the waitress know what liquors they had in stock (turns out they had only two bourbons). Ordered a perfect manhattan with a twist, got cherry juice & bourbon. When my friend, the cocktail connoisseur went and complained, they fixed it, but the bartender pretended that he didn't know who'd made the drinks and proceeded to get his boss. His boss made them right. I don't know who thought this place had "classic" cocktails, but they must have been high. The menu was all over the place. They need to figure out what kind of food they serve and then redo it. My friend had the spinach artichoke chicken; it was tough & incredibly flat. A real loser. We had the crab-stuffed portobello appetizer and it was nice. My Kansas Strip came well cooked with nice mashed potatoes and a vegetable side, but then the staff brought a little bowl of gravy out that looked and tasted like that brown instant gravy from the store (read: terrible). My girlfriend had the beef stroganoff and it turned out to be another real loser as well. It tasted as though the ingredients had been cooked separately and then lumped together and served. Stroganoff should be simmered together. Also, for all the trouble, the place was incredibly expnesive. I won't be back to give it a second chance.
label: NEG

text: Huge waste of space. The display was pretty neat and informative, but all and all it was a huge waste of money. We paid 12 doll hairs to walk around through a single interesting area. Maybe if they had all kinds of things going on it would've been worth it, but with what they have right now, it isn't. The building is huge though, so hopefully they will improve on what they have going on there.
label: NEG

text: Often overlooked, like the bigger, clumsy, unkempt sister of Audubon Park, City Park is going through some exciting, albeit slow, changes and will one day outshine that Uptown princess. The bike path is making its way around the perimeter one chunk of smooth, lovely sidewalk at a time. The new exercise track was the centerpiece of Voodoo Music Experience and a fine place to try out your new jogging sneaks. One of the 2 golf courses has re-opened, and NOMA as well as the tennis courts and Storyland continue to draw crowds of families and field trips every day of the week. I love coming to read or hula hoop or walk my dog under the moss draped oaks of City Park. It is one of my favorite places and I just hope the rest of the city sees what a treasure we have in so much gorgeous green space.
label: POS

text: My Husband decided to take me here on a whim, we were looking for something "different" and boy did we ever get it. First impression, the first waitress we saw sat us in the other waitresses section, we are positive she did this because she thought we could not pay for our meal. The place was no where near full. (total of 5 tables) The second waitress was nice, although we kept getting looks from her like she was afraid we were going to skip out. We placed our order, My husband decided on the calamari to start, with an entree of Halibut and fries, and I decided on the crab and shrimp. The waitress brung out my husbands calamari (I'm not a fan), the flavor was okay and the batter was heavily seasoned, but the squid was not cleaned properly and my husband kept pulling long strings of skin out of his mouth. They weren't very crispy and overall the dish looked rushed and sloppy. My husband commented he was certain that it was frozen calamari. The waitress came back with our entrees and at first glance we were VERY disappointed. My husbands halibut was flavourless and the batter was heavy with grease. The fries were okay at best and again the dish was plated sloppily, and my husband was certain the halibut was frozen. My dish was terrible, the shrimp were blatantly overcooked and tasted and felt like chewing on deflated balloons. They used pre-minced garlic and oil instead of butter to flavor them, which stole any of the good that was left to be had in them. The crab was a joke, a real joke. It was cold and the meat was tough and did not stay together but rather flaked away weirdly. The melted "butter" they gave me was surely oil with "butter" flavouring mixed in (which settled to the bottom). The legs themselves were painfully small and some even had weird "sores" on them like open brown rotting spots on the shells!! It was obvious that these too were frozen. We paid our tab, giving our waitress a good tip so she could rub it in the others face and left, never to return again Keep in mind my husband and I are from Nova Scotia, so we know decent seafood and Joey's Only is not the place to get it. Everything is previously frozen and overcooked and it is a waste of money to consume any food out of this restaurant. For anyone who knows and loves seafood, I would never ever recommend Joey's only.
label: NEG

text: I have ordered food from this place several times. I think the taste of the food is OK, especially when you are hungry after shopping :-)). I should say the food tastes very similar to the food from other Chinese eateries in the mall food court. They served chicken teriyaki, orange chicken, spicy chicken, maki chicken ( a.ka. bourbon chicken) and many more. They also serve sushi during lunch time. The price is comparable to other places $5.99 for 2 entrees, or $7.99 for 3 entrees. The steam rice was cooked too dry the last time I went there. My biggest complaint is that they do not offer FREE water to their customers. I have tried to ask for water everytime I go there, and the answer is (always) the same that they only have bottled water. This makes me really unhappy because other places usually let their buying customers have a cup of water for FREE.... Watch out Maki of Japan! I can easily go to Cajun & Grill (which is surprisingly serving Chinese food???) or Asian Chao when I am hungry for Chinese fast food next time I go to the mall.
label: NEG

text: Open every freakin day of the year? That's gotta suck for who ever has to work but good for me if I need a drinky. Anybody from St. Louis has probably been to this joint.....especially if you were a Wash U. student. What's the attraction? People watching, food, cool memorabilia, alcohol, and oh yeah....Chuck Berry plays here sometimes! Don't hate me for saying this, but wasn't this place a bit cooler before the expansion remodel? Meh. Regardless, this is a good place to kill time and drink every day of the year.

text: Prices were good. Beer was terrible. It tasted sour -- and I'm not a picky drinker. And I NEVER send stuff back unless I have to. But we tried two separate beers, and they tasted like sour mash mixed with beer. I don't think that they clean their tap lines very often -- or at all. What was really alarming was when I complained to the bartender, he poured himself a sip in another glass and claimed it tasted fine to him. If that's their quality control expert, count me out of a return visit to Vic's Kangaroo bar.

Gave me her cell phone and said to text her if I needed her! I haven't been to the other services, but she also has a nutritionist, fitness center, and even a medical spa.

text: Paul Mineo's Trattoria has sub par customer service. One of the many examples is when the a waiter rolled his eyes when my friends and I requested separate checks. The service is also very slow. I tried this restaurant three times just to make sure I was giving it a fair chance. I know what it's like when you have an off day. But it seems like this restaurant is constantly having an off day. The food is mediocre. It isn't great and it isn't bad. They do have a yummy chicken cheese steak sandwich though. When they opened their doors several months ago, salad was served as part of the entrees. Now, they charge extra for the salad. Although I work right next to Paul Mineo's, I now avoid going there.
label: NEG

text: Good old Wal-Mart: even the Yelp reviews cannot help but become a polemic on the race/class/aesthetic/urban issues central to the Beast from Bentonville and its continued success. And despite the unavoidably ...uh "problematic" nature of many of the comments, I found myself really intrigued by the idea that this particular Wal-Mart might be the WORST one. Also, the whole post-apocalyptic Wal-Mart thing sounded pretty cool, I must say. Except then I realized, "Oh, I've been to that Wal-Mart. A few times, actually." Yes, it sucks. Wal-Mart always sucks. But, really, there is honestly nothing all that extreme about this particular Wal-Mart. So I guess that's why I am writing this: the next time you find yourself wanting to save money on, well whatever, don't worry. You will almost certainly, or at least probably (it is NOLA, after all), not be shot here. But you might want to shoot yourself afterward.
label: NEG

text: When somebody asks me where they should go for a great cheese steak, I always send them to Tony Luke's. But while Tony's cheese steak is arguably the best around, that's not even the best thing on the menu. His best sandwich is the roast pork Italian with broccoli rabe. This sandwich is everything a sandwhich should be. And the way you know it's good is that nobody will be getting close to you during or after your meal (thank you stinky cheese and garlic!).
label: POS

text: Holy crap, what a great find! Stumbled upon this place randomly after a detour put us in this neck of the woods on a Sunday. It was lunchtime and we were peckish, and the restaurant name had the magic word "coffee" in it, so what the heck. The Coffee Station II (apparently the original one is in Morton, PA) is clearly a family-owned mom-and-pop sort of place that only serves breakfast and lunch; if memory serves, they close at 2pm on Sundays, and 3pm on Saturdays. On Sundays, you can only order from the breakfast side of the menu. This is perfectly OK, because the menu is full of delicious stuff (and snarky quips). My boyfriend ordered the sausage breakfast wrap, and I ordered a swiss cheese omelet with tomatoes and green peppers... it was really great. They slice their red-bliss homefries fresh each day, and you can tell because they're leaps and bounds better than your average diner spuds. They brag about using real butter-- my kind of place. Inside, there's counter service available as well as table service, and the waitstaff is comprised of friendly high school kids who are already learning about providing good service. The tables have a mug of Trivial Pursuit cards to pass the time, and live music as well-- can you stand it? It was awesome! The musician of the day played a sweet combination of singer/songwriter favorites, and the volume was loud enough to enjoy it, but you could still have a conversation. He seemed confused but appreciative when we applauded. :-) [EDIT: No more live music. No worries.] This place and menu was clearly designed by someone who gives a crap about good food, cheery ambiance, tasty coffee and quick service. The Coffee Station II is now officially part of our restaurant short list. We'll be back, and often. [EDIT: We just went there for lunch today (a Saturday)... whatever you do, make sure you get an order of sweet potato fries with the cranberry dipping sauce. Hallelujah!]
label: POS

text: Hype, hype and more hype. My wife took me here for my birthday in January and my memory of the experience is still strong enough for me to write here. We dine out quite often and know quality food and service. Unfortunately, we chose Vetri for my birthday only to be served ridiculously small portions (an entire order of tagliatelli was two pieces of pasta) that were DRENCHED in truffle oil. If you are interested in paying a premium price for ill executed culinary attempts in pea sized portions, this is your place. Perhaps it was an anomalous event, but at the price charged for meals here, there should be no such thing. We actually went to Barclay Prime afterwards for some sliders that delivered in all the departments Vetri didn't: taste, portions, value.
label: NEG

text: My fiance' and I have met up at Stratton's a couple of times because it is in between my office and his school (Webster). The first time, I had mayan hot cocoa (delicious!) and the peppered feta turkey burger, which was surprisingly bland given that "peppered" is in the name. I much prefer the turkey burger at CJ Mugg's up the street, and you get more food at CJ Muggs for maybe $1 more. On our second visit, I got a caffe latte (okay, rather plain) and some mint oreo gelato. I really wanted to try the gelato and asked the cashier/barista for a recommendation. She looked at me like I was crazy and listed off the flavors I could plainly see for myself. I was craving mint, so I went with it. Probably not the best choice, as it basically tasted like Baskin Robbins mint chocolate chip. meh. I've heard good things about other sandwiches, and they have a wide variety. I'd say Stratton's is an okay place to grab a quick bite if you're in the area, but there are many other more delicious options in the same price range within a 1 mile radius.
label: NEG

text: Y-U-M-M-Y! We sat inside at the bar area because it was cold outside, and we were able to watch the guys cook. So that was cool. We ordered steamed clams, steamed mussels and an order of their special that was on the chalkboard - abalone on rice. That abalone was yummilicious !!!!!!!!! It hit the spot right on. Darn, we should have ordered 2 of those. The baked clams and mussels were yummy too. Broth was good. Staff was accomodating and took care of our requests. He also knew what was good on their menu etc. Prices were reasonable. Overall a great experience. :) Will definitely return to eat there again.

text: Ugh! I can't believe they sell food here! Not the cleanest or friendliest place at all. I have to go here to pick up prescriptions for my In-laws. The pharmacy is great and friendly, but the food/grocery part of the store is pretty gross. stick to Raley's for a better alternative.

text: Service was fine, red beans and rice were a healthy portion, but mediocre. Drinks were *very* watered down.
label: NEG

text: Did Urban Outfitters just throw up in here? Good Lord, I thought I was in a commercial yesterday as I drank my $5 Fleur de Lehigh draft on Swift Half's cooler-than-thou outside space. I had high hopes for Good Dog's new transplant, as I was (and still am) fiercely loyal to the original. I wasn't overly impressed. First, the interior was one big, generic suburban yawn. There was no sizzle, no personality and with all the cool galleries and shops nearby, I thought this place could have turned up the decor a slight edgier notch. Second, the atmosphere here was definitely more club-ish than laid-back bar. With four security personnel (in not to be missed fluorescent yellow t-shirts) in two's, flanking both the entrance of the patio and the interior of the bar, you'd think there were some big diplomats imbibing inside. I wasn't crazy about the DJ spinning club-ish tunes outside either, although mercifully, a live band later graced the stage and provided a better ambiance. The level of sound too, is on par with a club. Because of Swift Half's proximity to the stage and speakers, it was a bit too loud - the whole time, our server had hard time hearing us and we hearing her... Further, though the food was decent, I found that the portions were itty bitty - (cheese plate: miniscule, ditto with the cone of fries) and overall, I found the menu selections (both small plates and entrées) entirely uninspired (cucumber sandwiches? fish and chips? really? That's the best they could do?) And on a side note: was it just me or are their pint glasses smaller than your average bar pint glass? I love my neighborhood and I believe NL prides itself on businesses (restaurants and bars alike) that are a little different, unique and that boast individuality and a local patronage following. Swift Half just didn't measure up in that way for me. Only the ample outdoor space, prompt and attentive service saves the experience here.
label: NEG

text: I was traveling to Philadelphia and saw the recommendation from my hostel that this ice-cream restaurant was quite famous, so I decided to give a try. It was quite a tiny one yet a very old-school atmosphere ice-cream restaurant. I felt like I was in a maybe 20s-30s periods because all the servers wore their super old-school outfit. It definitely was a very interesting experience for me and I could think of how the owner of this restaurant wanted to create a feeling like going back to those old times. I was totally amazed by their antique cashier, it wasnt working at all but it was one of the important equipment in this restaurant. I finally ordered a Franklin Fountain, which contained some mint chocolates and cream. It tasted good generally but it made me full so easily. It was quite pricey too, it was around $10 for a medium-small sized bowl of ice-cream. Their customer service was satisfying and they smiled all the time. I recommended this restaurant, for its old-school atmosphere and its nice ice-cream.
label: POS

text: My aunt treated us here a few years back and it was really good. Everyone thought their meals were SUPERB! The staff was nice and we got to walk through the kitchen....there were some cute cooks too. The dessert was AWESOME I had the creme brulee and OMG I just remember it being magically delicious.

text: We have ordered from Lovash for years. The owner used to greet us in my husband's native bengali when we would come in or caller ID noted it was us. Recently we have been disappointed. At first we noticed the owner wasn't answering & the food had slipped a bit. Hoping it was temporary, we tried several more times. Last week's delivery was $5 more for one less dish and so tasteless that we only ate a few bites and tossed the rest. Sorry to have lost the original!

text: Tanners has been a stop for me for probably the last 35 years or so when my mom took me there to get ice cream and get milk in a plastic bag that you would put into a plastic container at home. I guess you can call me old. How times have changed, what has not though is their ice cream which makes this place a stop when i drive into that area. The produce is fresh and they have an ample selection. I can't say much has changed in their store since I went as a kid but it has a old school feel to the days when stands were more the norm.
label: POS

text: Like many, I am a fan of Iron Chef and Chef Morimoto in particular. Stopped by last week, a barely half full dining room made me a little nervous... perhaps a sign of the times? But then again, we were having an earlier dinner on a Thursday. Enjoyed chef's combination sushi, which consisted of 9 pieces of nigiri and 1 roll for the price of $30, quite reasonable. Fresh and quality slices of fish but I thought the sushi rice was a little hard. Miso black cod was on the menu, so I had to order it. It was flavorful, crisply charred on the skin side and definitely delicious. The dessert special for that day was an homage to back to school: ice cream with peanut butter, jelly and cheese crackers (perhaps goldfish crackers?). Sounds strange, but the combination worked and it was tasty. Who knew lunch box goodies could be a scrumptious dessert? Great Service. Our server was professional and friendly, dishes were presented at a nice pace and the manager stopped by to check up on us.
label: POS

text: They've got some good Tea. Really nice vibe, free wifi, a book swap shelf, and its very spacious. If I were a student I'd camp out here. Its quiet and doesnt suffer the same fate as other coffee shops in there area. There is plenty of room to sit and spread your shit out. I think I'll swing in from time to time to have a post work tea. You know, for the days where I dont need that post work drink.

text: I've given this place a couple of tries, hoping that it will get it's act together, but so far, no luck. text: I was eager to try the newly opened Bibou and went to dinner there tonight with three friends. The old Pif space has been lovingly redone, with dark wainscoting contrasting nicely with the elegantly set tables. Charlotte Calmels is the perfect hostess: the welcome is warm and charming, and everything is done to make you comfortable at one of the very closely spaced tables. The menu is short but diverse, with some dishes hinting at the Burgundian origin of the chef (snail ragout with fava beans). We tried the soup of the day, made with corn and lump crab meat, its velvety creaminess nicely contrasted with tasty kernels of roasted corn, the foie gras, unctuously rich as expected on a port and cassis reduction, and the beautifully textured rillettes terrine. For our main dishes, we had the deftly prepared duck breast special, the richly tasting hangar steak (both meats perfectly cooked rare to medium rare), a moistly sweet halibut on basmati rice with ramps, incredibly light and deeply flavored, and the breaded veal scaloppini, correctly done but my least favored dish of our order. The desserts, as well as the cheese plate, need some tweaking. The $12 cheese plate came with three small pieces of good but hardly exceptional cheeses, a few grapes and some salad greens - serviceable but not up to the high standards of the first two courses. Similarly, the desserts are all good - a nicely caramelized apple Tarte Tatin with chocolaty ice cream, a "chocolate millefeuille" that brought miniscule layers of creamy chocolate on crisp puff pastry - but they too are not in the class of the appetizers and main courses. The price/quality ratio is excellent, most appetizers are under ten dollars (the exception, of course, is the foie gras) and the most expensive main courses are in the mid twenties. You can end the meal with a rich French Press coffee and a couple tiny madeleines (the latter compliments of the house). Lovely! The service is professional and diners can have a quick conversation with chef Pierre Calmels when he briefly leaves his kitchen. It is simply marvelous to go out in South Philadelphia and sit in a restaurant with such amazingly sophisticated food at such affordable prices. Word has already gotten around, the restaurant was full at all times with content diners, enjoying the good luck of having a place like Bijou join the list of fine Philadelphia BYOBs. My rating is 4.5 - when the cheese platter gets better, it will be a 5 star place!

text: Pop Shop is a place of promise. It staged a coup of sorts when Bobby Flay had the establishment on Throwdown for their grilled cheese, which in the end came off more like a turkey sandwich with melted cheese. That should have been a signal that a book should not be judged by its cover. There must be something under all the diner-like bright lights and chrome, and substance under all those heavily-described menu items, right? I revisited Pop Shop today for the third time, with the hope it would be a "charm," but alas, I was left again with disappointment after only mediocre expectations. The first visit a year ago had me introduced to their milkshake, which was fine; the second was for my niece's 5th birthday on a Sunday in January, which found the place in a madness of noise and young children, and waitresses stumbling over each other, with meals taking too long to arrive, and sloppily presented. Today I was only one of three tables at about 11:30AM, one of which already had their food. I perused the menu, which is too voluminous for any diner to make a reasonable decision (I wonder how a kitchen keeps all these ingredients on hand - makes me wonder how much of it is frozen and pre-packaged!), and I ordered the California Eggs Benedict, which promised house roasted turkey and fresh sliced avocado atop toasted ciabatta bread with homemade hollandaise. Sounded promising...but the Shop didn't deliver. While waiting for almost THIRTY MINUTES for breakfast, my dining partner and I noticed both the disgruntled-looking floor manager and the dirty floors underneath our table. Our server didn't help the setting much either, coming off as very baffled and unsure about many things, and actually taking my coffee mug from the table to refill it (why?). I received my dish and it looked unappetizing. I wondered why 2 breakfast dishes took so long when a normal diner (Pop Shop comes off like a diner's stepchild) would have them delivered within 10 minutes. The hollandaise looked and tasted more like turkey gravy and the two poached eggs were severely undercooked. The avocado was barely ripe and hard, and the potatoes were unseasoned and undercooked despite the appearance of a dark crust. The ciabatta was presented open-face style and was not toasted, too soft to cradle the turkey and eggs handily. The turkey looked like turkey, but had minimal flavor for being home- roasted. The meal was bland and boring, despite all of the descriptors on the menu. Every time I cut through my meal, the unstable table shook and my coffee kept pouring over the edges. It was not an enjoyable experience overall. Tasteless food that took too long to deliver handed to me by a poor server (I don't expect genius at this place but this was bad). I was never served water and no extra napkins ever showed up. Perhaps the reason for the delays was the fact that they were closing on Thursday April 23rd for kitchen renovations. But that is no excuse...and the service was an issue for me the second time I visted, and for many other diners who have written about Pop Shop on Yelp. Unfortunately, the third time was no charm, and I hate to say it, but my new name for this place is the "Poop Shop." Not so nice... but I will not be returning. I would rather make breakfast at home for the 12 bucks wasted. Head over to Philly to Honey's or even the Collingswood Diner on Rt 130.
label: NEG

text: It's not that I overly hate White Dog. Far from it! It's just that a 20 year history in an ever evolving spot like West Philadelphia can make a place feel like a withered dinosaur. It's always been a great restaurant with a lot of cool innovations (and some interestingly themed dancing nights) But in the span of it's 20 year existence Philadelphia just happened to see a Steven Starr who WASN'T involved in the restaurant business. His first Restaurant (The Continental) opened in 1993. 15 more restaurants since, a few Zagat ratings here and there, and I think you've heard of the guy by now. So what am I saying? even Timely old Philly institutions like Silk City have seen significant face lifts since then. The overall face of Philadelphia restaurants have seen some milestone changes ever since the days that White Dog has been on top, and thats the only thing that really hurts it. But it's still a great spot. If your looking for the fanciest of restaurants that provides you with a work of art that you can eat go elsewhere. But if your looking for timely old food that you can easily recognize on your plate. And a cool Philly restaurant with a tiny bit of history (and some fun nights) then this is your place.

text: Yes Virginia, it is a chain restaurant! And I am NOT a fan of the Olive Garden, nor the Red Lobster or many of the other chain restaurants including Carrabba's sister store, the Outback Steakhouse. Carrabba's Italian Grill was founded in Houston by Johnny Carrabba and Damian Mandola in December of 1986. Both Johnny and Damian have extensive restaurant experience and belong to one of Houston's most successful restaurant families. Many of the recipes on their menu are those of Damian's mother Grace and sister Rose. Damian has preserved the Italian authenticity of Carrabba's food by traveling the world in search of unique Italian dishes and by taking numerous trips to his grandparents' native Italy. After many travels to the Houston area, Carrabba's caught the attention of Aussie-themed Outback Steakhouse, Inc. owners. A joint venture partnership was formed in January of 1993. Under the joint partnership, 10 locations were opened in Houston and in Florida. In January, 1995, Outback Steakhouse, Inc. acquired the rights to develop Carrabba's nationwide. There are currently over 200 Carrabba's Italian Grill locations. Okay, since they say it so much better than I can, that of course was copied from their web page, but I personally can attest to THE BREAD is the very best around! You know all the sauces are homemade. The marsala sauce is as good as Vin & Eddies or any great Italian restaurant. I personally love the Pasta Weesie, except I have them serve it over linguini instead of fettuccine. I really do get a good filet mignon here. The lobster ravioli is a good choice and one of hubby's favorites. The Calamari Ricardo is wonderful with a spicy red pepper and lemon butter sauce. They also have hand tossed and made to order personal pizzas. Check them out @ http://www.carrabbas.com/menu/pdf/M60.pdf Don't boo them until you have tried them!

I had the lunch special ($6.99) with three baby back ribs and fries, which doesn't sound like much. I added a side of the BBQ beans and snacked from someone else's mashed sweet potatoes (very tasty). The ribs were great, the fries were crisp, the beans were overly sweet. Someone commented here that things seemed too sweet all around, and it's true: the beans, the cornbread, the potatoes, the BBQ sauce are childrens' level sweet. (Hope it's sugar and not HF corn syrup . . .) The sushi eater had a salmon roll that was huge, with some kind of jalapeno spread inside, and liked it very well. Next to us a guy had something the server told us was a Mountain Roll--it looked yummy. Kokopelli has a sushi bar for a more authentic and less schizophrenic sushi-eating experience. (Raw fish and smoked ribs together don't make a lot of sense.) Pulled-pork eater was thrilled with her dish and so am I. She's in a hotel without a fridge so I got to take her remainders home. Server was excellent though stretched a little thin. It WAS after the lunch rush and the crowd was light. She cheerfully took three credit cards so we could split the tab and otherwise took good care of us. Tracy by name, good job.

text: We drove by here trying to find the infamous hot dog spot down the street but it was already closed. So we turned around to scope this place out since it looked lively when we drove by. Upon arrival, the place was packed. There were drunks that looked like they just came from clubs, families that probably just left a quincinera, and even a drunken cowboy with a freakish looking black cat (that looked like he was electrocuted) on his shoulder dancing and singing in the parking lot. Wow, reminds me of King Taco in East LA at 3am on a Saturday night. I used to be one of those drunks in my old partying days so I wasn't really intimidated but for others I can see that it can be. I was craving a Sonoran dog, so I ordered that. The BF had a Chicken Torta. I also ordered a Carne Asada Caramelo to share because I was curious and never heard of it before. Sonoran Dog, ehh... Chicken Torta... slightly above average. Good bread. Asada Caramelo... Yum! So freakin' good! Two tortillas with melted jack cheese and carne asada in between and crisp up on both sides. The carne asada was really tasty with a hint of lime just the way I like it. Now, if we would have got the torta with asada it would have been way above average. There was also a condiment bar with 5-6 different types of salsa, cucumbers, guacamole with cottage cheese, onions and cilantro to garnish to your liking. We liked the Caramelo so much that we agreed we would stop by for lunch before our trip to Sierra Vista in a couple days... Fast forward two days... What a long two days it was. We came here for lunch on a Sunday morning/afternoon. The scene was definitely different. Seemed like a whole different restaurant. There was lots of families with little kids and different ethnic backgrounds. The other night I was the only non-hispanic there. We shared a carne asada burrito, a Pastor torta, and a Carne Asada Caramelo (large one this time). Yum, yum, yum... Caramelo was as good as I remembered. The pastor torta and asada burrito was also tasty. We ate til we were put into a food coma. It was that good. This is probably one of my favorite mexican restaurants ever. Only second to my beloved King Taco (LA chain).

text: Overall: overrated. St. Elmo is unequivocally an Indianapolis establishment, well-known for everything from great steaks to a posh, yet unpretentious atmosphere, with a shrimp cocktail that is nothing short of a local celebrity. Taking advantage of Devour Downtown, I decided after 2+ years as an Indianapolis resident that it was time to see what all the talk was about. If I had only one word: "meh." Fortunately, I'm not so limited ;-) Before I say anything specifically culinary-related, our service was impeccable. Our server, David, brought a warm personality and classy charm -- leaving us with the impression he was as happy to be there as we were. Unfortunately for the restaurant, that's about where my "wow"ing ended. The much-celebrated shrimp cocktail seemed a tad over-the-top. The otherwise unique flavor was all but trounced by the overpowering Horseradish. While I understand they're going for "fiery" -- you don't have to completely kick my ass just to take my lunch money. But, if that's your thing, go for it! Finally, the main course. Ultimately, I simply expected more from my 10oz filet mignon. First of all, everyone has the right to a well-prepared steak, regardless of preferred temperature; mine is medium to medium-well. I ordered mine MW, based on their menu description -- not only was it charred on one side, it was very unevenly cooked throughout -- reddish pink in some parts, well-done in others. It was not butterflied; I would have been fine with that had I been given the option. In the end, it tastes the same; we're not there to look at it. A wedge salad, mashed potatoes, and green beans accompanied the filet; all of which were very good. In the end, however, all I've heard for 2+ years is that this is the destination for a good steak in Indianapolis. My final opinion, which (sadly) hasn't wavered much with regard to fine dining (especially for the money): if you really want something done right, do it yourself.
label: NEG

text: J-Bar is probably my wife's favorite restaurant in Tucson. And that's not a bad thing. There is much to be liked about J-Bar. The appetizers are great (especially the nachos!), the entrees are flavorful (try something of the Recession Busters menu) and the deserts are unique and delicious (yum!). Throughout the summer they have a concert series that provides a perfect soundtrack to their menu. All in all, it's a pretty great place to eat. There really is just one thing that keeps me from giving J-Bar a 5-star review: the waitstaff. I don't know if their sections are too big or if their training is lax or if we just happen to continually catch the one bad one that night, but we've never had a waiter/waitress who is even decent at the job. Giving a table time to peruse the menu before ordering is one thing, but making people wait 20 minutes to order is another. On our most recent visit, we waited about 20 minutes to order, another 20 minutes to get the desert menu after we were clearly finished and 15 minutes after desert was finished to get the bill. We were really thankful that a separate person came through the room with water or we'd have not had anything to drink for most of the meal. If they can get their waitstaff straightened out, this place'll be just about perfect. Unfortunately the waitstaff ruin what would be a great dining experience.

text: I'm usually too lazy and unmotivated to write reviews longer than a couple sentences, but I'll make an exception here. I wish I'd noticed that the more recent reviews have trended lower than the overall number of stars indicates. My friend and I arrived at just before 9 pm on a Friday night. There were at least a few empty tables with half-full glasses and used napkins still on them which should have been the first clue that the restaurant was understaffed. We were offered an outside table in what appeared to be an alley where the Prince of Demons and his minions lived. No thanks. After being seated, we realized that the greeter was also the only waitress working that night. And the music? It was coming from a clock radio at the rear of the restaurant w the time blinking. WTF? I had to resist my OCD tendency to set the clock. We waited at least 10 minutes before the greeter/waitress returned to pour water into our glasses and offered to open our bottle of wine. By now, my friend and I had discussed leaving for another restaurant because we were both starved and presumed it would take hours, if not days for our food to come out. We were reassured that they were no longer seating new customers and that it wouldn't take too long for our food. After placing our order (two apps - dumplings, chicken nachos; two entrees - pork tacos, burger), she began to open our bottle of wine. We saw her struggling w it and then she came back to inform us that her corkscrew had probably broken and that she was still trying to open it. By now, the cork was at least a centimeter into the neck and appeared to have been mauled by cheetahs. She returned to inform us that her corkscrew was officially broken and asked whether she could filter our wine so that we did not drink the cork residue. Why yes, we responded, that would be quite nice. What a generous offer from the person who had just mangled the cork w a broken corkscrew. Fortunately, our (inexpensive) wine was salvaged. But why she poured the filtered wine into a metal pitcher intended for ice water was beyond me. The food was unremarkable, but not awful. No offer to somehow compensate us for destroying the cork, but that's alright because I'm letting everyone know what happened on Yelp. Shame on you, Paul. Here is an unsolicited, but short list of small steps you can take to improve: - At least set the correct time on your clock radio so it doesn't blink. - Provide your staff w corkscrews that work. - Update your lame website. As it is right now, it's an embarrassment to the World Wide Web. Otherwise, I wish you all the best keeping your restaurant in business during this recession.
label: NEG

text: Even though I work/live in Dallas, being a native Philadelphian I can't help but not tune into this station especially during football season. I have mixed emotions about the hosts, but they do offer the latest news on my Eagles, Phillies, and Sixers so I can't help but listen. Here are my thoughts on few of the hosts.... My knock on the Morning Show is they don't break down Sunday's Eagles games as much as I would like. Yes, they tend to talk alot about the Birds the morning after a game, but they don't do a good job of breaking down each phase of the game to help fans truly understand what went right or what went wrong. They tend to make known the same things most people actually noticed while watching the game on TV themselves which really doesn't tell me more than I already knew. Living in Dallas its easy to compare Dallas sports talk to Philly sports talk & I must say the Dallas radio personalities do a better job breaking down the Cowboys than the Philly hosts do with the Eagles. I wish that were not the case, but I gotta be honest. Angelo Cataldi adds NOTHING in the way of interesting sports talk, however he's a genius when it comes to pulling in listeners & ratings based on the fact 610, until recently, has been the only all-sports station in town. He's been able to successfully build loyal listeners on his style which can be a bit too negative at times. And after 20 years of listening to him, many folks are sucked into believing his style makes for the best sports talk around. Here's another problem I have with Angelo...he's NOT FUNNY. In my opinion the show is soooo much better when he's on vacation. AL Morganti & Rhea Hughes with the help of Keith Jones and Hugh Douglas do a great job. Believe it or not I enjoy Al's non-sports related commentary. Just when you forget he's part of the show, he jumps out with strong opinions about other issues in city which I love. Rhea is great!!! She holds her own, is as knowledgeable as any sports chick I've heard on the radio and is just as passionate as any Philly sports fan, male or female. I hardly listen to sports radio on the weekends except in the spring during Rhea's Saturday show. She's that good. Joe Conklin, although a great impressionist, isn't funny. I tend to think he's probably much better on stage and amongst a live crowd which is more of his element. He does a great Iverson, Barkley & Merrill Hodge as well as others, but his segments which feature these voices are whack! But you wouldn't know it by listening to Angelo cuz he laughs at everything Joe does. Other hosts I enjoy are Anthony Gargano and Ike Reese. Anthony's probably my WIP host and Ike continues to impress me with his knowledge of Philly sports. I mean, even though he's an ex-Eagle, I like the fact he follows the Sixers & Phillies and appears to be as interested in both teams as much as I am. Anthony's host, Steve is pretty decent and I especially enjoy the 'Whose That Guy' segments. He does an excellent job with that as well as with his Saturday show with Ray Diddy. Garry Cobb is another host I enjoy. I just wish he was on more often & during hours when I listen. I give props to his website. Its very informative. And lastly, lets not forget Howard Eskin who I love to hate!!! One of the most arrogant radio hosts around. I love the fact he's in tune to the Eagles, but hate the fact he hardly ever faults Andy or Joe Banner for making bad decisions. Howard never admits he's wrong and he never gives credit to others when they call him out on a bad comment & when it becomes obvious the caller is getting the best of him with a valid point, Howard hits the dump button. Other things I notice about him is he ALWAYS has to remind you that he's been friends with a 'fill in the name of a famous celebrity' for years....so what Howard??? Also he lets it be known he HATES Allen Iverson, Michael Vick , and Terrell Owens without admitting that's actually the case. Personally I think Howards still bitter Iverson sued him so he has voice his displeasure with him every chance he gets. Again, I only listen to him for his knowledge of the Eagles and his ability to get the 'breaking news' about the team, but thats about it. All things considered I enjoy the station, but think they could do even better if they made a few changes.

text: El Greco is a neighborhood shop, and it's just a few blocks from my workshop. I stop by every once in a while, and it's an experience. Today, as usual, there were a bunch of people inside. Three behind the small (but tall) counter, a driver or two outside, and three or four customers in the long, narrow area inside. I order two slices, which are put in a box. (A bit of a downer for me - what, they don't want me eating in front of the shop? Put it on a plate, please...) I go outside and stand by my bike and eat them - warm, gooey, and very sweet. The cheese is thick and chewy, the crust is soft and light, and the sauce is sugary and squirmy. The slices are floppy - they fold, and don't crease - and drip red-orange oil as I squeeze the fluffy crust to keep the whole package together. The first bite requires me to hold the crust side above the rest of the slice, so that it doesn't unfold and go limp. Eating the slices produces a texture that resembles, almost, mollusks. As I stand there eating, I observe the scene. A tall, gaunt man sits on the stoop, then stands and mills around the storefront, smoking a cigarette. Three customers who came out of the shop just as I was entering sit on a stoop next door eating their slices and talking. The traffic on 2nd St. whizzes by, passing the small community at Jefferson - the slice shop, an auto tag store and a barbershop. I like El Greco in a way. It's not exactly gourmet, but talking about the quality of the food misses the point of the business. It isn't quality - some might go so far to argue that it's hardly pizza. Either way, it's food, it's part of a neighborhood. And sometimes that's all you need.

text: Hungry Cat is probably my favorite restaurant in SB. From the outside, the atmosphere in Hungry Cat looks very hip and fun, and there always seems to be a decent sized crowd which is always a good sign. Luckily, inside feels the same. It has a cozy, classy, metropolitan feel, refreshingly unlike most places in SB. The place is tiny, so get here early or make reservations if you want a table, especially on the weekends. If you do get a table, don't expect a lot of elbow room. If you don't have a reservation, sometimes you can grab a few spots at the bar and watch the cooks and bartenders work while you drink and eat. If you don't mind throwing down $10 for a cocktail, they're AMAZING. They always have a new infusion cocktail of the day, and several seasonal options in their cocktail menu. Best drinks in SB in my opinion! I know they have a happy hour also. If you're a foodie, this is also the place... assuming you love seafood. If you feel like splurging and you're willing to eat raw shellfish and uni, go for the seafood tier! Such a treat. I've heard their pub burger is also delicious but I've never had a chance to order it yet. Definitely on my to-do list.
label: POS

text: First off, I will say that the price is phenomenal. I pay $29.99 a month for unlimited classes. I joined because I wanted access to yoga classes without paying yoga studio prices. I had to pay a $39.99 fee additionally after three months membership to "secure" my monthly price. Another thing that I like is the atmosphere, as another reviewer said it is not too commercial. It feels non-judgemental and "normal". A lot of the people who work there are really nice, especially Ellie, Carl, and Sam. Now onto why I chose 2 stars, instead of 3. On any other day I probably would have chosen 3, but right now I am very upset at their spin class policy. Because their spinning classes fill up so quickly, they have recently instituted a call list system in which you must call and reserve your spot in class. On Friday I called at 3:30 to reserve my spot in the 5:30 class. I was told I called too early and to call back later. I called back at 4:14 and was told the class was full, oh well. Tonight I had planned on going to the 6:30 spin class. I called at 5:03 and was told the class was full up and that I could not attend. I asked them how it was possible that in 2 and 1/2 - 3 minutes 20+ people had called and reserved spots. The girl on the phone told me that there are three phones and three people answering them and that 6-7 people on each line had beaten me to it. Then she told me I could go to Zumba instead if I wanted. No thanks. That annoyance aside, spin class is usually great. Carl and Ellie are my favorite spin teachers, as they are both fun and challenging. Ellie is really the best thing that gym has going for it. Not only is she a great spinning instructor, she holds other classes, like "Sweat, Tone, Sculpt", which is a combo of aerobics and light weight training. She puts 100% into every workout and doesn't allow anyone to slack. She is the best fitness teacher I have ever encountered, anywhere. If it weren't for her classes I might have just told the gym to take their spin classes and their 29.99 a month and shove it up their toned asses. Clearly I do it for the classes. That being said, I'm not an expert on the quality of the weight lifting machines. They seem pretty normal to me and are never very crowded. The treadmills, eliptical machines, and bikes are not many in number. If you are someone who prefers to run on the treadmill but can only get to the gym after a 9-5 job, this is very challenging. Often times on week night evenings all of the machines are taken and people stalk them out like a parking spot at the mall at Christmas.

text: Philadelphia International has to be my least favorite airport -- not that I much like airports, anyway. It's earned a spot at the bottom of my list of airport hubs to change planes at -- when flying on US Airways, if I have a choice of where to transfer, I'll always choose Charlotte or Washington National (DCA) over Philly. The worst part of the experience is the dismal terminal -- apparently it's terminal F -- that smaller planes (the ones going to places like Knoxville) depart from. I'm don't think I'm being unreasonably picky. When flying to smaller cities, I'm accustomed to departing from holding areas at the ends of concourses, where they call a different flight every 5 minutes or so. Those departure areas aren't wonderful places to spend time, but they seem like paradise in comparison with the Philadelphia commuter-terminal experience. The commuter terminal always feels poorly lighted and dirty. Worse than that, there's nowhere to sit. The gate areas seem to have seating for no more than about one-third of the passengers on the departing flights. Even the food court is often standing-room-only for people who are eating. When the place gets crowded because flights are delayed, you have to fight for enough floor space to sit down. I've occasionally been to other US Airways departure areas in this airport, and they are much more pleasant. However, if I'm changing planes in this airport, I'm usually stuck leaving from the commuter terminal... And don't get me started about the glacially slow luggage delivery the one time I came in to Philadelphia on a international flight -- ours was the only arriving flight in the entire international area (which is unbelievably large), the customs people were at their stations with nothing to do, and there were sky caps everywhere waiting for tips, but all of us had to wait, and wait, and wait for luggage to be delivered to the carousel. (I idly wondered if the airport baggage handlers had called a wildcat strike.) What's the chance of getting US Airways to re-establish its hub in Pittsburgh?

text: Here is a synopsis of my experience at Osteria: We arrived for our reservation about 15 minutes early, and were delighted to hear they could seat us. We expected to have to have a drink at the bar first, which we did not mind at all. We were seating in a back room that lacked ambiance. There was very little decoration or personality, and the room was empty. When our server arrived, we asked as kindly as possible if it would be possible to move to the main room, we didn't mind if we would have to wait longer. (It was a special occasion and we were looking for something more lively and inviting, especially since we don't often go out and spend a lot on meals) She got a manager, and they said it would not be a problem at all. We could go to the bar and get a table in about 20 minutes. All was well at the bar, we ordered cocktails and wine, all expertly chosen and enjoyed our time chatting. When our table was ready, we sat down and our server came over and told us about the specials. The menu looked lovely. When we were ready to order new glasses of wine, our server immedietly reccomended the sommolier come by and make reccomendations that will work with our meal. One of my companions appreciated the offer, and the sommolier went to bring her a small sample of wine based on what she was looking for. Unfortuantely, she wasn't crazy about it, so she asked if she could try one more. She enjoyed the second wine and ordered it, but the sommolier acted as if she was being unreasonable and rude. Normally, I am overly polite and just take what is first offered, even if I am not crazy about it. But as a sommolier, is it that big of a deal to offer a second small sample? It wasn't even as if we were bothering our server asking her to do a million things when she needs to take food orders from the other tables. Her job is to assist tables in chosing wines. It seemed like a reasonable request. But we moved on. The sommolier was annoyed but we were there to have a lovely time. We all ordered, and two of my companions ordered a $36 special - a 1/2 pound of lobster and pasta. Appetizers came and were delicious, although the antipasta is charged per person and was not a lot of food. When the entree came, the two companions that ordered the lobster dish looked suprised. They were literarly fishing around to find lobster. Soon, the four of us were trying to assist, to try to find the lobster because we were so afraid of asking for the server. All in all, pieces that add up to about 1/2 the size of my tiny palm were found. We did not ask for the server or even steal glances across the room to find her. She stopped back to see how things were and we said everything was very good, and they hated to complain, but there was barely any lobster in the pasta. Immedietly she became very annoyed. She pointed to a small piece and said "There it is!" My companions said they understood, but they have ordered lobster many times in their lives and 1/2 a pound never looked so small. She said there was nothing they could do and if they wanted she would get the manager. What were we to do? We said OK. The manager arrived and said basically the same thing. He said they weight each lobster and it is always 1/2 a pound. We decided to let it go and just ate. Then things became incredibly embarassing. I was facing the room and saw our server, the manager, the sommolier and the bartender talking and pointing at us. I felt like that "nightmare" table, like I was in some kind of Twilight Zone episode. I always consider myself to be a great restaurant customer. I myself worked in the industry for two years. I know what they deal with. When the check arrived it was tossed at us. She did not look our way at all, just got close to the table and tossed it in the center. We paid, but only left a 15% tip, which is something we never do. So that was my experience. We did call and leave a message the next day and did not hear back. Obviously to many this is an amazing restaurant. But I can't return. We spent over $260 there (not including tip) and I have received better service for a lot less.

text: In town for a convention (read: boring), and I was charged with finding a spot for my group to eat dinner. We had eaten at Broussard's the evening prior, and I figured I'd find a place that would provide a contrast to some of the formal dining we had enjoyed the night before. After reading several reviews, Cochon appeared to fit the bill perfectly. Although it was fairly easy to make a reservation just a few hours before dinner time, I was pleasantly surprised to find that when I arrived, the place was packed and really kicking. The vibe was great, and the ambiance could be described as modern, yet inviting, and just the right blend of casual and formal. First up were a couple of drinks, and I had a specialty cocktail made with Gin (yes!), lemon bitters, blueberry infused simple syrup, and a lime wedge. I really enjoyed this cocktail, although it could have been less sweet, but this is the South. Of course, we ordered the fried alligator, boudin, and roasted oysters. I'd skip on the oysters next time, and focus on that boudin for sure. What a great tasting sausage! The fried alligator had an interesting texture, on the tough side for sure, but the flavor was great and definitely worth a try even if just for the novelty. I perused the entrees on the menu, and quickly settled on the Cochon, which is perhaps one of the most tender chunks of pulled pork shoulder that I have ever sank my teeth into. It was truly amazing. Everyone in my group was in a sharing mood, so we sampled each other's dishes, which included a delectable red fish, rabbit, beef brisket, and goat. Besides my cochon dish, the beef brisket was something to write home about, and the red fish was a close 3rd place. The entrees stole the show at this restaurant. The desserts did not seem to be a strong point here, yet they managed to be quite palatable and enjoyable. I ordered a fried peach pie with cinnamon ice cream. The pie shell and chunky fruit filing was good, and the cinnamon ice cream was delicious on its own, but I felt that its nuanced flavor profile was overwhelmed by the pie. All in all, I had a wonderful dining experience at Cochon and it was a nice change of pace for sure. My choice was also a hit with my coworkers, so I feel good about that, too!
