text: Whyte Knight is one of the coolest stores on Whyte Ave--well, it's cool, if you're a geek like me. Unlike your average comic store, that usually has more new merchandise than old, Whyte Knight has a lot of vintage items. Their collection of action figures and toys is quite impressive, and I've been whisked back in time on more than one occasion after seeing one of my old toys from childhood. I've considered buying some of these, since I do collect toys, but they are almost always out of my budget. Whyte Knight also has a good selection of comic books and a few vintage video games, but what really sets this store apart is their incredible collection of medieval and war items like weapons, medals, and armour. I've also seen some beautiful statues of dragons and gargoyles. Every time I go here, there is always something new--the store is constantly changing. I've never participated in one, but I've walked in on more than one occasion when there was a role-playing card game going on. If you're into this kind of thing, they sell tons of stuff for role playing games as well. Even if you only have a little bit of geek in you, this store is definitely worth checking out!
label: POS

text: I love Willie Mae's Fried Chicken. It only compares in deliciousness with the chicken at Praline Connection and Coop's Place. I am a local and fried chicken is something I grew up on, so I consider myself somewhat of an aficionado. The price is a little high, but the portions are good. The sides are really spectacular, as well. I like the butter beans but my mom likes the red beans and rice.

text: Just got back from the store as I needed some quick things and didn't feel like going to acme. A loaf a bread, a jar of peanut butter, a pint of milk and a squeeze thing of honey = 14 fucking dollars. No lie.

text: If you have a craving for the prefabricated goodness of some far off chain restaurant but don't want the hassle of figuring out which one - just go here. It's closer than Cherry Hill. They have a basic amalgamation of the all the crappy chains greatest hits all the rolled into one. Chicken tenders, ribs, Mexican inspired French dishes, things made out of pasta, things made out of shrimp. You know the drill. You'll like it especially if you love tons of televisions blasting at top volume with all kinds of sports (you can even watch TV in the ladies room) and fresh pimply faced servers. Probably a good place to take sticky-fussy eatin' kids though I wouldn't really know. I hate sticky children. If you hate sports like I hate sports - this is a very bad place. If you like run-of-the-mill chicken fingers in a basket lined with paper and dipping sauce from a jar, then this is in fact, the place for you.

text: Fun place with excellent staff! Recently I visited Tucson and tried Nimbus Bistro with my son. The interior is decorated well, there was live music and the beer batter dipped onion rings were amazing. We shared a beer/ale sampler which was great as well. I am now fan will visit whenever I am in Tucson.

text: The Ridge, offers golfers a fairly memorable 18 hole golf outing at a decent price ($24 all you can play after 3 w/ cart). The course is kept up very nicely on the fairways and greens, but the tee boxes can be taken for granted by the grounds crew. The actual golf course set up is pretty good for a public golf club. Doglegs on most longer holes, hills and valleys throughout the course. It has water on several holes that make for risky shots, and demands club selection a little bit harder. The scenery is also pretty simplistic, but most of the course is wooded and seems natural. The club house is fairly small, but the food is better than expected, and the beer is cold and cheap. If in the area and are looking for a decent place to play, definitely worth checking out.
label: POS

text: We were visiting Philadelphia from our home in San Francisco and looking for some Chinese food. This place is a bit off the beaten path, but still we walked here with ease from Market East train station. Saw some good reviews on Yelp so came in. We were a bit early and seated fast with four waiters waiting, but by the time we left there was a nice crowd. I found it reasonably priced, I think I spent about 20 bucks for three dishes and the bathroom was clean. The food was excellent. The namesake says DUCK and we could see in the window it was great duck but we wanted to try other things too. I ordered the clams with curry sauce, some fried rice, and my wife ordered the mixed bbq with duck, chicken pork. Everything was really good. My clams were plentiful and had the curry flavor permeated throughout. My favorite thing is to then put the curry sauce left in the bowl on top of my rice and let it soak in. Nothing goes to waste and the flavor is complete. Go here, try it.
label: POS

text: Exceptional bakery for good ol fashioned sweets. Prices are excellent and there is a good rotating selection. Definitely a place you want to hit early, if you go to late (especially on the weekends) you might miss out on some great stuff. The coffee lovers coffee cake is about the best thing you can have on a Saturday morning. Other recommendations are the cheddar cheese scone breakfast sandwich, the Cinnamon-chocolate-banana cake (the exact name escapes me) and the grittatta. Really you can't go wrong no matter what you choose. One thing to know ahead of time is that they do not have bread, so don't expect a french loaf and sourdough. This is strictly for the baked goods that you could make yourself, if only you were a baking genius and woke up everyday at 3:00 am like the Einsteins.
label: POS

text: Located opposite the McDonalds and beside a Galaxy Land entrance, there is no better place for quick Japanese food. The staff here are very friendly and I never have to wait long for my order, even during peak lunch rush hours. Sitting area can be a bit of an issue, as this is a popular place to eat, but just be patient and do not be discouraged. I typically choose the Teriyaki Chicken and Beef on rice. Their servings are quite generous that I'm usually quite full for the rest of the day. During really busy lunch period, I do notice that they sometimes might not be as generous with their portions, but I understand they have a lot of people to serve. The smell of their food on their grill wafts through this area and I often find myself craving their food even when I'm just passing by. I also like how you can add extra sides such as tofu or shrimp, or get other dishes like their curry chicken.
label: POS

text: I went here for a friend's birthday on a Saturday night. For Flanders, this is a very upscale place, as the area doesn't have many places like it. Their menu was pretty varied, offering steak, chicken, pasta and seafood, including sushi. This was the first place I ever really tried sushi and I thought it was pretty good. My friends said they have had better, but I didn't have anything to compare it to. Our waiter was a ditz. He didn't offer any help when we asked questions about the menu and said the restaurant's policy on a busy night did not allow guests to order appetizers while they decided on their dinner choice. I thought that was bogus - I mean, I'm paying for the meal, let me order when I want, it was like 8 - 8:30pm - I don't think you were going to get bum rushed where you couldn't take our app order separately. We waited forever for drinks and didn't have bread plates, water or sauces for the sushi for what seemed like hours. The waitresses and hostess noticed our concern and tried to salvage as best they could. Things started to look up from there. The food was ok, It wasn't anything to write home about and it came out a bit cool, but we didn't want to deal with any issues with the dumb waiter. I had the tuna and my friends had the filet. They said they enjoyed theirs and mine was pretty tasty too, but like I said, nothing spectacular. The bar is very inviting, but a little small. Drink prices are also a bit high, at least for the area I think. They also closed at 11pm. They let us stay while we finished our drinks and the bartender bought us each a round. But I think this place could do great if they stayed opened a little later and took advantage of their bar. Bottom line, I enjoyed my night, more because of the ambience and company than the food and service. But if you are looking for a night out in a small town, give it a try - maybe we just had an off night!
label: NEG

text: Tasty interesting food - check Nice atmosphere (especially if you are a fan of Dias de los Muertos) - check Good service - double check Great inventive drinks - triple check My husband and I stumbled across this place by accident the last Dining out for Life; we forgot to make reservations, and attempted to try to drop in a grab a table at Atomic Cowboy which was not happening (we are stupid). So ravenous and desperate, we began wandering the Grove and came across Sanctuaria "Wild Tapas," which we had seen driving by (and may have made a few jokes about the name). They had open tables and man did we luck out! Fried plantains and chorizo sliders? Yes please. And the drink menu is extremely well curated, completely creative and tasty. We have been back (highly recommend the late night happy hour) since and enjoyed it every time. Matt the bartender rocks and is an absolute mixology genius.

text: As a chef, you sometimes walk into a restaurant and think to yourself, "Whoa.. I want to own a place like this someday" A restaurant where the service matches the ambiance and the ambiance matches the food. After many years of cooking and traveling, Chef John Harris has found a home at 3637 Magazine Street. Chef Harris' vision has turned into a reality named 'Lilette'. For the first course we had the Braised Veal Cheeks with Baby Greens and Horseradish Vinaigrette. The Veal Cheeks were cooked and seasoned perfectly. Only one problem, the portion size.. it's never enough!! But still very good! The first of the two entrees was the Roasted Muscovy Duck Breast with Creamy Polenta, Fennel and Coriander Jus. The combinations of the rich Roasted Duck along with the Fennel and Coriander really set it off.. And the finish it off with the Creamy Polenta helped to mellow it all out very nicely. The second entree was the Pan roasted Alaskan Cod with Mushrooms, Roasted Potatoes and Marsala Butter. I loved everything about this dish! The crispy, tender and moist Cod left nothing to be desired..the rustic sauce along with the mushrooms and roasted spuds were all definitely worthy of praise..

text: This was my second time at this restaurant. The first time we had arrived late and only ate off the bar menu; The food was flavorful and the only down side was the horrible tasting drink I decided to get. After talking with a bartender they agreed to replace the repulsive concoction that tasted like dirty water and old champagne with another choice. The dinner was horrible from when we sat to when we exited the building. When we walked in we were not greeted the hostess stared at us as if she had no idea why we were standing in front of her. When we were led to our table I asked if we could sit in the bar to watch the game and she seemed bothered by that request. We sat and waited and waited when our waiter (9 min later to be exact) decided to come around and take our drink/appetizer order. Another 10 min passed before we saw our drinks, he then took our order and seemed annoyed with our questions about items on the menu. Another 10 min passed before we saw our appetizer which was there guacamole and chips I had spoke so highly of. He also brought my friends food (two carnitas tacos) but didn't bring out my carne asada tacos so I was bothered by that. The guac was very bland no flavor at all and nothing like what I had had the first time, I was extremely disappointed. We had asked for limes for the tacos and instead of getting them he went behind the bar and chatted it up with some other workers. After we flagged him down and asked again he took at least 5 more minutes and still no limes so we asked another waiter who brought them right out to us. My food came out, cold and raw, my meat was still very pink. So I asked if it could be cooked longer, when he brought it back out it was still too pink for my taste and still cold...very odd. The meat had no flavor whatsoever, and by now i lost my appetite and I just wanted to pay and get out of there. We couldn't find our waiter so we had to go to the bar and ask for our check...I think I forgot to mention we were the 3rd table of people there and our waiters ONLY table. To sum it all up, we had HORRIBLE FOOD, HORRIBLE SERVICE, I feel our food was OVERPRICED and I will never eat there again.

text: I found out about Jedco when I asked my Edmonton Twitter friends where a good place was to find reasonably priced gold jewelry in the city. More than one person recommended Jedco, which I had previously never heard of. A small shop on the second floor of the Melton Building on Jasper Avenue, Jedco is full of gold and silver chains, pendants, and rings galore in a variety of styles. I was looking for a specific length and style of gold chain and I found it - at about half the price of a similar chain in another store I was in recently. Jedco manufactures a lot of what they sell and their prices are well below retail. The staff is very friendly and helpful. They have layaway, which I took advantage of. I look forward to bringing home my beautiful chain in a few months!
label: POS

text: I overate. But it was worth every bit of discomfort I felt. If Emeril's was the best meal I had, Cochon was a very close second. These guys put out some very tasty food. Between my wife and I, we managed to eat at all three of the Link/Stryjewski restaurants and never left disappointed. So what did I stuff myself with? The Cajon gumbo, for starters. It was a rainy day and this was just what I needed. It was rich in flavor, studded with sausage and chicken. Man, was it good. Not wanting to commit to just one entree, I cobbled a meal together by ordering two apps: the fried boudin and the meat pie. The boudin was delicious. The loose sausage was rolled with rice into balls, then battered and fried to a crisp. The empanada-like meat pie was also a great choice. Flaky on the outside and wonderfully unctuous on the inside, it was a filling -- and pleasing -- dish. Much like the gumbo, both of these were perfect for a stormy Tuesday. Nova, conversely, probably had too little to eat. She ordered the smoked brisket with potato salad. While it was incredibly flavorful, the portion size was also a little modest. So maybe my approach wasn't so bad after all. That said, you might want want to order an app with any entree you get.
label: POS

text: Best cannoli EVER. My favorite is the vanilla, which is hard to find elsewhere. Everyone else has cheese and chocolate, but vanilla? That's what puts Termini Bros. ahead of the pack in my book. text: My mistake for coming here during a world cup game. The lady who did my pedi seemed more interested in watching the tv than actually doing a good job on my nails. Um, I'm sorry I had to cut one because I have weak nails and it broke. But isn't it your job to even it out or at least make it look as good as possible? I've never had this issue at any other nail places and I've come out with fantastic looking feet. So I said fine and she said she'd choose a color for me-- old lady bright red. WTF? I was trying to go for a classy French and she brought me to trashy red? Nice. I'm guessing she didn't want to take the time to make a French pedi look good and just wanted to slap on some solid color. Again, she was trying to concentrate on the game (and interrogating the other nail tech next to her) so I had no bottom coat and no top coat, though my nails were painted nicely. She quickly rushed me to the dryers and plopped down to continue watching the game. I'll give it another try, as many people come here and seem to be happy, but I definitely won't be asking for her again.

text: Apparently, Odunde, Inc does many things. The only thing that I've experience is the Odunde festival, held in June on South Street near Grays Ferry. Like many ethnic festivals, there were vendors selling trinkets. but there were also lots of African and African-American themed products. Lots of Caribbean and soul food for sale, and great entertainment. There were capoeira, drumming circles, African dance, breakdancing, and even hip hop dance by some adorable girls from a local dance troupe. Authors were on hand to sell their books. There were hair stylists doing amazing things and beautiful clothing for sale. I'm told Odunde hosts the biggest African American heritage festival in the US. It was definitely packed with people. Check it out next June! (As you can see by my photo, you don't have to be African American to have a great time at the festival!)

text: I have been to this place a bunch of times and feel somewhat guilty for not getting around to review it yet, because I LOVE it. It's definitely one of my top 5 in Tampa. The local/sustainable concept would be worthless if the food weren't good, but it is. Oooooh it is. I have had a killer meal the every time (10+) I've been here, and for how often the menu changes, that's no small feat. The service is fantastic, the prices are VERY reasonable, thanks to the locally-sourced food (for dinner, a couple beers and/or bottle of wine, your tab will be less than or equal to any of those big box "high end" chains like pf wang's or skeezcake factory but for far better food), and I have not eaten a single thing here that didn't please my palate. I've been here for dinner and brunch and always been delighted. Actually, if you love homemade jam and perfect biscuits like I do, brunch is a must. Their savories and their pancakes are also awesome. I don't know what I love better here, the dinner or the brunch...but I'll take either!

text: Uffff, where to begin? Well, for starters, I was excited to be staying here as I thought it would be a pleasant experience. Boy, was I wrong! It started out bad and ended bad. When I first checked in, the heavily accented (and not easily understood) clerk first started telling me about the complimentary breakfast and the free happy hour. OK, I says, sounds good to me. Then I realize she is trying to sell me an upgrade for a few hundred more. No, I tell her, I want to stick with what I reserved. Then (amazingly), she tries to sell me a "downgrade!" She says I can save $10 or $15 a night if I opt for a smaller room with (get this!) no bed! I am incredulous! I mean, even Super 8 rooms got beds in 'em. (I later hear that the pull out sofa doesn't even have sheets!) I'm like, "do you have a room with a bed? because it is late, I am sleepy, I just want to check in. Are you telling me I don't have any rooms with beds?" Well, luckily they do have a bed, so I get my key and trudge upstairs. I get off on the 7th floor and instantly am hit with "eau de 20 years worth of cigarette smoke." Yikes. I go to my room, open the door and of course the stench is even stronger. Now I'm pissed. I specifically requested non-smoking when I called the reservation line several weeks ago, and I renewed my request moments earlier when I just checked in. Again (and this is the theme for my whole review), this isn't Super 8, this is the Hotel Intercontinental. C'mon dogs. If you be charging $559 a night (as per an advertisement last week in the NY Times), you got to step up your A game. Cuz this ain't going to cut it. (for the record, I paid well below that, however that doesn't excuse sub par service). Anyway, I changed rooms and it was okay, well, until I found the pack of (luckily unopened) condoms in the nightstand drawer. Ummnm, do you all actually clean shit around here? My list of complaints could go on and on, but I will try to just hit the low points. The fridge with goodies in the room is heinously overpriced - think $3.75 for bottled water. Luckily these nitwits are too stupid to count apparently and fail to charge me for the one bottle of water I had on the first night when I checked in and was too parched to seek out any other form of hydration. And the room service menu is insane - a breakfast with 2 eggs is like $16, plus a $3 delivery fee and a mandatory gratuity. Oh, and coffee is an additional $7. Enjoy! Hmmm, can you tell I am not liking this place? The elevators are slower than molasses in January and there always seem to be a queue to use them. Oh, and for some reason, they don't go to the ground floor, they start on the second. Though the building is tall, I only have a view of the top of a nearby parking garage, which the local inbreds seem to delight in using as a place to noisily make donuts with their cars at 3 a.m. I was really hoping to see one go careening off the side and plummet to the street below, but as usual, I was disappointed. I will fast forward to check out - a minor question about the bill and the clerk says that I will have to come back on Monday morning and talk to the accounting department. Well, duh, we are checking out, so we won't be here on Monday. With that, she disappears into a back office until I leave. Again, Intercontinental, $559/night service? Methinks not. I don't recall having such an unpleasant stay even at a Super 8. And I have never ever found condoms in a room anywhere else before. Tip of the day: there is a really nice looking La Quinta on the other side of the block where you can doubtless receive much better service at a much better price. P.S. - One of my friends, who frequently travels both at home and abroad, disabused me of my notion that this Intercontinental was perhaps a post-Katrina anomaly and said that it was pretty much par for the course with other Intercontinental properties that he has stayed at.
label: NEG

text: Tons of bang for the buck - I've had good luck with the chop shop. $10 has bought me cuts that were awesome and a few that were not as awesome but still cute. If you're seeking that kind of attention, creative artistry and inspired hair, choose your stylist carefully and tip well - or go to The Alley or AmMo. This is the kind of place where you need to bring a picture and a verbal description of what you want. And once you find a stylist there who fits, request them next time (it's worth the extra $5). text: When I worked down on Second Avenue, we probably ate here once a week. They have some great lunch specials that won't break the bank and good prices on lunch portions that are very ample. My visit Friday for lunch was the first in a long time. I can't wait for the Lunchline to start running by my work so I can go more often. Demo's manages to accomplish what seems to be so hard for most restaurants - consistency at it's best! The place isn't fancy but it's nice. The wait at lunch can be long unless you get there early so be warned. As crowded as it gets, they do a great job of getting folks in and out as quickly as possible. I even noticed that one fo the waitresses that used to wait on us before I stopped working downtown in 2006, is still there! I am a creature of habit here pretty much always ordering the lunch portions of mediallions of sirloin, medium rare. Most of the time I order the house soup which is a lemon and rice chicken soup and is fantastic! But their salads are good also - nice and cold and crisp with house made dressings. I usually go for the baked potato but they also have these incredible hash browns and their steamed broccoli is also very good. The bread is great too. I've also had the hamburger steak and I've tried other people's baked chicken and have to admit it's very good. At any rate, it always tastes the same. The quality is always there. I've rarely had any problems with service that I can recall. As we were talking about at lunch, it would be nice if every restaurant was this dependable and onsistent.

text: I don't want to do a negative review. Really, I take no pleasure in slamming a local business. I feel obligated to warn you, though. The fact is I went there two months ago with family and I still vividly recall how bad of an experience it was. In the interest of "full disclosure", I used to work in a mid-priced Indian restaurant and have certain expectations for how things should be done. There were five of us total when we visited Taste on a Sunday evening. There was only one waiter to work the take out orders, the seating, the busing and the lassi making. But the place only had a handful of tables. Also it seemed very unkempt. After a loooong wait the waiter finally came by. The waiter was in such a hurry to take our order and move on that he literally ran away before we got through half the stuff we wanted to order (1 appetizer, 5 mains and some naan). We had to tell him to "hold on" multiple times so we could finish telling him what we wanted. This guy was so unbelievably inept at customer service throughout our meal that it became hilarious by the time we left. Most Indian food is made from a pre-made base that various sauces are added to when ordered. This is why every other Indian place in town can get your order out in about 15 minutes. We waited, and waited, and waited at Taste for food to come out. For that amount of time (and after all the hype) I expected something fresher. Food was not good when it finally arrived. The tikka masala and korma cream sauces were obviously cut with water or milk or something and they were runny and separating. Everything was under seasoned. The whole spread was pretty dismal. Both the fiancee and I were sick by the time we got home from dinner and had to fight over who got to use the restroom first. Yuck, I know. I don't know where the much-talked about benevolent owner lady was that night or why Taste feels like they have to cut corners with their food. If you want solid Indian food with a nice ambiance and attentive, friendly service, pay the few extra bucks and go up the street to India Kabab & Curry.

text: I ate here one afternoon when I had time to kill before my flight home. The menu consists mainly of Belgian meats, cheeses, and beer--how can you go wrong? Ambiance is very casual, with street-side window seating and also a darkly-lit area in the back. This place was a borderline hole-in-the-wall, but clean, and the service is the kind I like--functional and unobtrusive, but attentive. We sampled a bunch of the appetizers, including the charcouterie plate, which had some kind of delicious loaf-like meat (rabbit terrine), assorted sausages, fruit, and delicious soft Belgian cheeses. Also tried the barbecue wings (not the HOT HOT HOT wings the menu warned us against--but they were still very hot) and fresh cut fries; also partook of the smoked trout with toast points--that and the meat plate were far the best items we chose. I drank copious amounts of Allagash White (a Belgian wheat) whilst eating and conversing in the darkened bar with a coworker. We emerged into the daylight again some four hours later, refreshed and ready for the airport.

text: Terrible service, mediocre food, middling beer, and rather high prices For appetizers we ordered chicken wings and seitan wings. The chicken's dry rub was good, but the protein itself was cooked to a consistency that one might call "slimy." The seitan on the other hand was nicely flavored and crispy. We also had chips and salsa, which any Mexican restaurant should be able to do. It came with 2 salsas: smoked and verde. The verde was an abomination: ground up tomatillos...no salt, no spices. The "smoked" one was far from smoked- just chopped tomatoes, onions and a bit of cilantro and salt (essentially a basic pico de gallo found at a condiment bar like Fuddruckers). I ordered from the "Texas" menu with the wagyu beef brisket and ribs with spicy sauce. The sauce was good, and the meat was smoky,moist,and mostly acceptable. The brisket however was very fatty. My boyfriend ordered an $11 barbacoa burrito and upgraded to the plato for an extra $5. When one thinks of a $16 burrito meal you'd imagine a formidably sized Mexican wrap with all the fixins. This alleged burrito turned out to be two finger-sized tortillas (slightly larger than a 7-11 taquito) with a tablespoon each of what tasted like dry shredded pemmican meat crammed into only one end of each little tube. There was nothing else in these odd little "burritos"- quite literally, the only ingredient beside the meat was a flour tortilla. The rice and beans addition to this "meal" were mushy, unseasoned, and revolting in appearance, texture and flavor. That being said, the meat dishes there are passably executed, but the price tag should command a higher level of quality for everything on the plate (and some sides should be included). If you are not a tasteless aging hipster sheep, and must still go to this place for whatever reason, I suggest you order an all-meat item from the Texas side of the menu. * Pros: mostly good smoked meat, decent atmosphere if you don't mind hipsters * Cons: service (extremely slow), value, food selection, "Mexican" menu

Also, there are no noisy ice machines...instead the ice is in convenient bags stored in a freezer drawer located in a hallway alcove. The hotel is a Green Hotel and 100% smoke free. So yeah. 5 Stars! Unfortunately we only stayed the one night...but if I'm ever in Nashville again, this is where I will stay. It's also why it's in the middle of absolutely nowhere, which is a key component to its' charm. And some of the same "native" vendors are still here week in and week out, year after year. You can get great deals on the typical eclectic mixture of who knows what, and I dont believe I've ever left without picking up something. text: I'll admit, I have a tough time with shaving products. Men have to be trained to shave by those they grow up with, and for those of us who weren't taught properly, all I can say is, thank goodness for Art of Shaving! Their process is amazing, and I'm happy to say its all available, relatively inexpensively, through this great King of Prussia store. The store holds everything you'd need for men who need help grooming their non-scalp hair. There's a wide variety of shaving creams in different scents, including lemon, lavender, and sandalwood. Sandalwood is my favorite. There are matching oils for pre-shaving lubrication and aftershaves in the same scents to keep it all in the same family. What's more is that they have a great selection of shaving brushes to make lathering more effective. All of these products may give you sticker shock when you first walk in. $20-some for shaving cream?! Okay, but it comes in a big tub, and it's not the GEL kind, so you only need a VERY little dab of it on your shaving brush, and it lasts for months, so it's even cheaper than something from CVS. $100 for a nice shaving brush? Okay, but, they last for 10 years, so that's really $10 a year to give you a far closer shave. The store is set up with wonderful displays on dark mahogany shelves which gives you a classic and manly feel. There are big starter kits for around $100 which includes the oil, a large shaving cream, aftershave, and the lowest-end shaving brush, which makes a great gift set. text: I would agree with Daniel's assessment of Cottage Hospital's inadequate facilities for labor/delivery. I am the proud father of 2 beautiful babies. We had 2 babies here in the past 15 months, both 15+ hours delivery. Out of the many different nurses/staff members during both deliveries, I would say 80% were great. However, both times I was sent home around 2 hours after delivery because they did not have enough rooms. For the first baby, when my wife delivered at 2:15am (hadn't eaten since 11am the day before) the nurses didn't get her any food until the 8am breakfast time - close to 6 hours after 15 hours of delivering a baby - unreal! Couldn't believe with our 2nd baby when they said I had to leave because visiting hours were over (my child was just born 2 hours prior). Also on the 2nd delivery we called ahead and tried to get in at 10pm when contractions had picked up. We waited in the emergency room for at least 20 minutes for someone to get to us. Luckily they had masks and signs instructing people to wear them due to the risk of swine flu and seasonal flu - great to see right before delivering a baby. Talking with a colleague in the Bay Area...they had a private room the whole time, bathtub in the room for the mom relax during labor, meals for both people and most importantly - they did not kick the father out after the birth of his children. This is how a birth should be treated at minimum. When I returned to "visit" the day after my second child was born I asked to pay for my meals so I could spend more time with my family - of course they missed the lunch I ordered and I waited over 2 hours as they kept telling me "it's on it's way." Ate lunch around 3pm and of course they were going to charge me for the meal. People come in from Santa Maria, Lompoc, Santa Ynez, Goleta, Santa Barbara, Ventura and even Oxnard to have their baby in this city and after Cottage shut down the Goleta labor center it is a mess. If you have the option, go somewhere that keeps up with the current standards of care.

text: Somehow, Complete Music DJ's claim they are "North America's #1 DJ Service". I am baffled by how they won this acclaim. I booked Complete Music DJ for my wedding May 2010. Initially I was very impressed with their customer service and they came highly recommended from a friend. I booked them, received the planning paperwork, and put them in the back of my mind until about a month before the wedding. Something came up and I tried to cancel my services. Holy rude cow, they were so mean to me. Immediately threats of lawsuits came flying at me as they explained I was contractually bound to them and would have to pay in full if I chose to cancel, even if I received no services. Okay, how about you say that nicely? Everyone I talked to from Complete Music from then on out, except our actual DJ, was rather horrible to me on the phone. Less than a week before the wedding they informed me that they require you to pay them to be set up 30 minutes prior to the event. If you are requiring you be set up by then, but I did not ask you to, why should I pay you for it? It felt like they were grubbing money from the frazzled bride at the last minute, and I told them that. To be "nice" the guy split the cost with me. argh. I could not get out of it. Our DJ, Kenny, called us prior to the event, met with us in person, and was courteous and professional. Unfortunately, Kenny and Complete Music DJs had VERY few of the songs we requested to be played. Kenny tried his best to get them, but Complete Music only uses CDs and will not obtain additional music for you. So we ended up downloading and burning our own music onto a CD for our DJ to use. What did I pay for again? And we had a few very specific requests for the DJ to say. He forgot some of the very important stuff on the actual wedding day. He was nice and accommodating though, and brought me a rose for my new husband to present to me at our first dance. Nice touch, but otherwise, I was not overly impressed. I would never recommend Complete Music DJs, and I totally disagree that they are #1 in North America.

I only gave Lonnie's 2 stars and probably 4 visits ago I would have given it a full five, so here are my issues: The last time we were there.... so were the cockroaches. I'm itching just recalling the experience. Now, I know... it's a dark, back alley place and they don't serve food so it didn't make me leave, but come on. Cockroaches are unacceptable in any establishment. Being a KJ is an art.... truly. What a lot of the decent Nashville area singers don't get when they accept a job as a KJ is that this is NOT a concert. We are not buying buckets of beer to hear YOU sing... we want to sing! We may not be as good as you aspiring country singers (and most of your are very good), but we want to sing none the less and when you sing more than 1 song at a time or put yourself in the rotation more than once... that sort of sucks for the folks buying the drinks and tipping you. We aren't tipping you because you sing well, we're tipping the KJ's who are good at working the rotation, don't sing too often and keep the crowd going. So seriously sing lots when you're out with YOUR friends... not while you're hosting, it's bad taste. The song list... Lonnie's used to have everything! I do LIKE Lonnie's and always have fun putting beer tops on the ceiling and singing like a karaoke rockstar, but they do need to really make some improvements, especially with regard to the cleanliness. If you're looking for some quality karaoke in downtown Nashville... I still think Lonnie's is the best bet! text: Man, this place is old. As in, it's been around since the mid-1800s. I visited the market on a Friday morning and am reserving further judgment for a weekend visit when the stalls are apparently all full. That's not to say there weren't plenty of options on a weekday--fresh produce, herbs and flowers abound in the outdoor stalls, while the indoor portion of the market houses a lovely spice shop (it also sells artisanal cheeses and some meats), a bakery, a few butchers (some even had boudin, which I rarely see outside of Louisiana) and a fish stall that I hear is totally phenomenal. I'm looking forward to visiting the fish guy the next time we're in town. All the produce we bought for dinner that night was wonderful and I liked the old-school feel to the market. One thing grossed me out, though--there's this one stall that's pretty out of the way (thank goodness) and I guess it's a pet store. It has loads of bunnies that I think were crammed a bit too close together and pigeons for sale for $5.50. text: Worst service I have ever experienced. I brought my scooter here to have the rear tire changed after driving over a nail. My brother and I loaded the scooter into his van and pulled up right in front of the shop to unload it. We were obviously struggling trying to keep the rear doors open and get the bike on the ground. I noticed a guy leaning against the store and watching us, and he offered no help, but I figured he's just a random inconsiderate bystander. Not the case. Once I entered the shop, I discovered it is the OWNER of the scooter shop. Seriously? I am struggling to unload a scooter in front of you and you can't even hold the door for me? It was so difficult just to get it there that I didn't have much of a choice in whether to leave it there or not. I was told the tire was in stock and they would probably get to it that day. 4 days of unreturned phone calls later, they told me they had to order the tire. 2 WEEKS later, they had managed to change the back tire. Unfortunately, this is not the end of the story. I've ridden the scooter three times since getting it back and it is getting progressively worse to the point where I am afraid to even ride it back to the shop. It is making a rubbing and clunking sound (coming from the rear tire) and when the rear brake is applied it makes a horrible grinding sound. The owner told me the following: 1. They can't even look at it for a couple of weeks. 2. He doubts it is because of something they did. 3. "They test drive all the scooters after changing a tire." This is absolutely not true because when I picked the bike up, they told me it needed a new battery because they couldn't get it to start. The kill switch was on. I turned it off and started the bike on the first try. This means they either don't know their stuff or they were trying to con me into buying a battery from them. 4. "I'm not going to argue this with you over the phone" 5. "Don't take this the wrong way, but a lot of people need their bikes fixed" Lastly, while I waited for an hour to pick up my bike, I heard the employees arguing with several people over the phone and telling them "We have a policy not to discuss prices over the phone." So, they want people to come all the way to South Philly, and then not be helpful, or truthful or even knowledgeable about service. Awesome. Stay away from this place at all costs.

text: Wow, this place was HORRIBLE! I am sure lots and lots of people have gone here and had the time of their lives or something like that, and maybe if I had gone on another night my experience would have been different. But with the experience I had, there is no way I will EVER go back. I made reservations for a party of 6 at 9:30 and arrived by 9:15. I elbow my way through the very very crowded bar/waiting area to get to the hostess who is inconveniently in the back. The Hostess was very flustered and showed very little interest in checking on our table. We find a nice little corner for all six of us to stand in a wait... and wait... and wait... its ten o'clock... still not seated. I ask how the table is coming along, and the hostess says only "it's coming", as if I had asked her to bring me the head of her first born child. I go back to my corner to wait some more and get elbowed by drunk people... and I wait and wait. it's ten-thirty... still not seated... the hostess buys us a round of drinks to "make up for it". Very nice, thank you! I ask if they are running out of food because it is getting so late, and they say "Oh No! everything is available! There's plenty!"... Now more waiting.... it's eleven...... it's eleven-thirty... ALAS! Our table is ready... TWO HOURS after our reservation! with not a single "I'm sorry". Wait for it! we get to our table.... it's in a tiny awkward room that is around 42 degrees, we all need to huddle to stay warm, so we ask if they can turn off the air conditioning that is blowing directly on us... nothing happens. The waiter shows up and starts rattling off a list of things they are out of.... out? I thought there was plenty!!! I am left to choose from the general rejects of the menu (they were out of everything i wanted)..... I find something after a little debate, the fried chicken dinner with mashed potatoes, sounds tasty enough. Around 45 minutes later, our food arrives with no mashed potatoes. They regret to inform us that they ran out and that we all had to choose a different side. So we all do... and the new sides never show up... ever! Oh and by the way, the air conditioner was never turned off, so we ask again to have it turned off. my chicken was dry... the air conditioner is still blasting.... we go tell he hostess that we are freezing, and she comes back to our little room and looks at us and says, "you should have told me earlier". Ummm... this was attempt #3 to turn the damned thing off. This is the point where I stood up handed her my credit card and told her to charge whatever price they were going to make me pay for the worst restaurant experience I have ever had. They charge me fully, which is perfectly fine, I am not one to try to weasel my way into getting a free meal. This place needs to fire it's entire staff and start all over again. And on top of that, the food was extremely mediocre and very overpriced...

text: I visited Tampa in the end of March 2009 and on my last night stopped into the Leeroy Selmon's Restaurant for dinner. I was hungry and craved barbecue! -Atmosphere- While waiting to be seated, I peered into the bar area and saw one of the nicest projector presentations in a public place - bright and sharp. The ambient lighting levels were a good balance for the game on the screen and the ability to see in the bar. This is kind of a strange thing to point out, but I think it speaks to the attention to detail in the experience. Lee Roy Selmon's is like the localized offspring of Texas Roadhouse and the 99 Restaurants. The place is well-lit and very family friendly - it is the basis for the restaurant, afterall. There is a collection of photos and memorabilia on the wall, not only featuring Lee Roy but also of Mama Selmon and other sports figures. -Food- We shared the Selmon Family Platter featuring a sampling of ribs, pulled pork, chicken, and meat loaf. All the meats were relatively moist and had a great smoky flavor. Our server asked if it was our first time (it was) and gave us a tour of the four barbecue sauces that were available. The sauces range from sweet to spicy and some stops in between. I had the bottomless Arnold Palmer to drink and it became an instant favorite! -Conclusion- If I'm ever in the area again, I wouldn't mind a return visit (maybe even step into the bar next time).
label: POS

text: We stayed at the House on Bayou Road in January and were so impressed with the place. This place was perfect! It was a short cab ride away and only cost a few bucks. It was a great place to retreat to after a long day of playing tourist. And Frank, the caretaker, was awesome! I was glad to see from the previous poster that he is still running this place. He was so friendly and helped us with any questions we had on the area. And the breakfasts he prepared were amazing! If we need anything he was so easy to get a hold of and he left out snacks and drinks for guests during the day. We would definitely stay here again if Frank is still in charge the next time we're in town!

text: For RR I say four stars, only in that I have a single experience there. My story follows: Sleeping on the train home, my custom always of the evening, my friend Max did stole, with juice of cursed hebenon, and in the porches of my ears did pour the leperous distillment. That, obviously, awoke me. "What say you!" I started. "Leperous distillments are for the gullet and not the porches of one's ears!" Max heartily agreed and humbly apologized. Thus, with the accompanyment and the suggestion of Lady Pennywort, we proceeded to the Ranstead Room. A second, lesser known custom to many, is our tradition to drinking one's supper during midweek. We arrived at the RR shortly after opening, which during summer, was still bright out. After entering, our eyes slowly became accustomed to the dimly lit, speakeasy environment. Our elbow rested on the pillowy bar. Drinks were ordered, and we had the pleasure of watching the bartender at his craft. Recommendations: As with the other posters, the bartender's choice is highly recommended. Our barkeep had mentioned his former profession as barkeep at other establishments was about mass production of drinks, and the bartender's choice allowed his creative juices to flow. I had asked for a bartender's choice similar to a standby of mine, a Manhattan. He came back with the Wicker Park, which flowed like quicksilver through the natural gates and alleys of the body. After two Wicker Parks, my blood was properly thinned, and my mind properly subdued. Price, it is on par with other fine drinking establishments like Franklin and Apo. You receive well prepared, strong leprous distillments for the price. Ambiance: I cannot say what it is like during the later hours. If you want a relaxed style and conversation with the barkeep, you can drink your supper like we did. I agree with Brad P. that it may become rather trendy if it hasn't already, being a Stephen Starr.
label: POS

text: One of the first hotels I stayed at in the city, the Hilton does not fail to live up to the prestige one would expect. That said, I felt the experience was worth it. This location is right next to the Circle, downtown. This place is full of cute shops, restaurants, one strange biker hangout, and picturesque landmarks are just a staircase away. In the other direction, a slightly more hefty, but still doable, walk away, are the clubs and liquor-themed restaurants. But none of this seedy type of traffic would ever pass by the Hilton, it's simply out of their way. A horse-drawn carriage ride to another location in downtown would be entirely possible. text: I agree with the descriptions by previous reviewers. This is a combination Japanese (not pan-Asian) grocery store and restaurant. There's a small dining area with some tables-for-2 and a couple tables-for-4. You can shop for groceries: dry, packaged, fresh, refridgerated, or frozen. You can order a meal-prepared-to-your-order to eat-in or to carry-out. You can get pre-packaged fresh sushi/sashimi in the cellophane wrapped containers, or you can order sushi/sashimi freshly made to order. This place is spotlessly clean, very neat, shiny, brightly lit, tidy and organized. Noticeably cleaner than most Asian grocery stores. The unisex restroom in the back was clean too. I had the Gyu Don beef bowl, $7.95 plus tax. Thinly sliced beef and sauteed onions over short grain rice, and I think it was shredded ginger as the garnish. Excellent. The rice was perfect, and the flavors just right. It came with miso soup, which was also among the best I've had, and it had some ito wakame type seaweed in it, which I love. Service was cheerful and friendly and they have that common Asian trait of being ultra-polite and having a deferential attitude that makes you feel respected and important. They sell alcohol by the bottle in the grocery section, but you're not allowed to posess or open any alcohol in the dining area.

text: Despite the lack of shade, the lack of seating in the Beer Tent (it's usually pretty crowded), and the occasional mudfest should the weather be rainy, this is by far the best long weekend event of the year in Edmonton. The volunteers, the performers, the artists in the crafts tent, the board, and the audience all know it -- this is a world-class event. Yes, you have to either take the bus or ride your bike or get someone to drive you there. Yes, you have to buy your tickets on June 1st at 10am or risk not getting them. Yes, the food and water can be over-priced (so bring your own!). Yes, there's hardly any shade. The ski hill is a natural amphitheatre, the organization of the festival is top-notch, the mood/culture of those who attend is kind, responsible, kid-friendly, trustworthy, fun, and just darned wonderful. If you live in Edmonton, if you have ever lived in Edmonton, you will see many people you know at the Festival. It's like a reunion -- plus, you'll make new friends, too, if only your tarp neighbours. Tip for getting a tarp location of your choice on the weekend: show up at 7am sharp (not early!) in order to get your coloured/numbered slip of paper (which also has an artist's name) and group up with friends in order to get the largest number and most diverse group of slips so that when one of the colours/artists gets called out as the first group of 25 people who gets to line up, you or your group representative (hopefully with long legs for the speed walking - no running!) gets to line up early/close to the front of the line. Doesn't make sense? Just show up at 7am with a bunch of friends who are going. If you don't know anyone else who's going, maybe go anyhow and make friends in the corral (that's where you wait from 7am to 7:30am while the colours get handed out) and see if they'll group up with you. Don't bring your dog -- it gets crowded in the corral. You can leave after 7:30am and return anytime, so long as you have some way of contacting the long-legged person who placed your tarp. What did we do before cell phones? *smile* There's a Safeway in Bonnie Doon -- you can pick up food and beverages (in plastic containers only) there should you wish. Bring lots of sunscreen, reapply it often over all exposed skin! Wear a long-sleeved shirt, wear a hat. Bring layers to put on over your base layer in the evening, because it gets really cold. Some folks wear toques, really. Bring a book or a craft. Bring a comfy chair that isn't high -- look at the website that will give you guidelines re: how tall a chair can be. If you're part of a big family, bring a tent and set it up at the top of the hill -- there's a great culture of tent-dwellers at the Folk Fest and they all lookout for each other. Your kids can nap while you continue to watch the performances, plus there's a tonne of room (well, relatively) up there. Expect to be crowded if you prefer your tarp location to be close to the main stage. Buy at least one raffle ticket. Volunteer at least one year -- the folks who volunteer are *so* much fun, plus they get to go to the nightly parties that happen when the folk fest ends -- which is where the performers go to keep on playing ... plus, you get your meals for free and usually a pretty cool t-shirt. Bring two tarps at the approved size (see the website!) -- wrap the top one's edge under the bottom one when hammering in your tent pegs -- use it to cover your possessions to keep them safe from a sudden downpour, or yourself, should you be on the tarp. I remember a great afternoon concert by Blue Rodeo when it was raining HARD and there were about ten of us puppy piling under a tarp. Bring a flag and a ski pole -- attach the flag (or very visible object of your choice) to said ski pole -- and plant it beside your tarp. This is how you find your tarp, and what you tell your friends to look for when they're trying to find your tarp. And finally, be prepared to get really tired if you attend the whole thing. I usually take the following Monday off from work; I'm lucky to be able to do so. Have fun!

The pizza places are always just passable. Grandparents' cooking usually rocks but its difficult to meet other sexy fun singles near their china hutch and eating over doilies. So...places like the Backefin Blue Cafe have started to spring up. Its menu is very Floridian w/o the 4pm eating time or buffet feel. text: One of the hidden gems of Chinatown. Great for both spicy and mild tastes, this restaurant showcases the food of Myanmar (Burma) as it is a crossroads between several Asian cuisines. One can find the influences of China, Thailand, Viet Nam and even India both in name and flavor across the menu. Less adventurous diners will find Chinese-American classics like sweet and sour and kung po. Lovers of Indian food will find curries and even samosa. As far as the more unique and regional dishes, my personal favorites are: pumpkin soup shrimp and lemongrass soup thousand layer bread with potato curry mango chicken jungle chicken. There are also a great number of vegetarian dishes. Try the crispy tofu appetizer. And pretty much every stir fry dish has a tofu option. Desserts are a must try and really showcase the pan-Asian mixture of cultures. There is a decent selection of beer and wine as well. I only wish they were open later!

text: I am a big fan of the sonoran hot dog and this is the place to choose, if you wish to partake of one of the best. Since a sonoran dog is essentially street food, originally served from carts, I give this location an extra star for being a hodge-podge assemblage of carts, tents and random structures. It is also in South Tucson, which gives it extra authenticity. There is another location in Tucson proper, but it has been gentrified, sanitized and fully enclosed (the food is equally good, but tastes less so due to the de-tuned experience). The menu has two staples: sonoran dogs and caramelos, which are basically quesadillas with a choice of meat. While the caramelos are quite good, it is the sonoran dog that delights. It is a hot dog wrapped in bacon and griddled. This is nestled in a steamed bolillo (soft pointed, bun with more structure than a normal hot dog bun) on a bed of beans and topped with chopped tomato, onion, mayo, mustard, and jalapeño sauce. The condiment bar offers several enhancements: pickled onions, cucumber slices, grilled peppers, grilled green onions, and a few salsas. The sonoran dog, as is, is a great balance of flavors and textures. It is perhaps the finest use of the humble hot dog. Both Guero Canelos are counter service. You place your order from the small menu and then wait for them to call out your number first in Spanish and then, if you fail to appear, in English. Everyone is friendly enough and they are very quick with the orders. Check it out next time you are heading south of Tucson. It is an authentic, local experience.

Cons Light -Low-key vibe carries over to the service, which tends to be quite hands-off. But this is to be expected if you're looking for authenticity in your Italian dining experience. Just ask anyone who's dined out in Italy. So don't go if you're in a rush. Otherwise, take this 'con' with a grain of salt and finish your wine at your leisure.

The dish I had (which was vegetarian, with noodles, tofu, and vegetables) was very good, and was the sort of thing that is not available at most Americanized Chinese restaurants. The rest of the food, standard American-Chinese food, is above average. The inside is a nice sit-down restaurant, nicer than one would expect from the outside. Service was very good. text: I recently spent a girls' weekend in the Brandywine River Valley that was lovely *in spite of* our two-night stay at the Pennsbury Inn. The Inn enhanced our experience only by providing us with common spaces for gossip and games and ample fodder for stories. A positive Inn/B&B experience depends on the hospitality of the owners, the cleanliness and comfort of the accommodations and the quality of the food. All elements at the Pennsbury deserve only a single star. Upon our arrival, the innkeepers were more harried than welcoming. They claimed they were expecting six of us even though we had made a reservation for eight (which led to a rapid assembly of cots), the very able male innkeeper made no offer to help carry our bags up the narrow winding steps, he declared he would not be putting fresh flowers in our room because he didn't want to go out in the rain to cut them (p.s. we never would have known the flowers were missing if he hadn't mentioned them), and he didn't want to give us the historic tour of the house because the group was arriving in three shifts and he didn't want to repeat himself. (He promised to give us the tour the following day, but the next day he never followed up on the offer.) We had confirmed with the innkeepers well in advance that we would be using their kitchen to cook dinner the first evening. Yet when we arrived the kitchen counters (which look pristine on the website) were cluttered with plants, dried flowers, jamming jars and dishes, and the refrigerator - which released an unpleasant odor - had barely any room for our wine and produce. Last on the hospitality list, we were surprised when the female innkeeper told us to fold up our used cloth napkins at the end of dinner so we could reuse them for breakfast. She told us they were trying to save water. I'm all for helping the environment, but surely they had enough extra napkins to save us from wearing tomato sauce on our lap while we ate waffles the next morning. Like the kitchen, the bedrooms had far more clutter than pictured on the website. (All of those pictures must have been taken a while ago. That, or the owners shoved all the stuffed animals, paperback books, candle warmers and other chotchkes under the bed when the camera crew came.) Only the biggest room had air conditioning and opening the window in the smallest revealed an inside frame filled with dirt and dead bugs. There were teddy bears on our pillows (which I imagine do no go into the washer with the sheets), and in the evening, one innkeeper flicked on a warmer that turned an old Bloomingdales candle into a pool of strong-scented liquid wax that made me queasy in the middle of the night. (The candle was on the bed table next to my head.) Elements of the breakfast were good: fresh bread, miniature muffins, a yogurt parfait. But the coffee was weak, afternoon snacks (such as cheese puffs, chocolate-covered pretzels and animal crackers) were stale, and to top it all off - in this case the topping was for our main breakfast dish - they used fruit that we had brought with us to garnish our waffles. They apologized, but it seems a bit suspicious that they would have forgotten what they purchased at the supermarket.

text: The best bowl of pho, fo sho. Between Reno and SF, it even edges the SF Tenderloin pho joints, which many consider the best on the West Coast. The only downside I can possibly see to going here (aside from the bullshit nitpicky "our table wasn't wiped down properly" reviews also seen here) would be the menu is somewhat limited besides the pho bowls. You have a few appetizers, and maybe 10-15 noodle dishes, including vegetarian options, but the pho is definitely the strong point. I stick to the #1: beef balls (they're just meatballs, not bull testicles btw. duh!!), well done brisket, tendon, tripe, and shitloads of noodles in that cure-all broth, with the side dish of mint leaves, fresh jalapenos, and bean sprouts. Head-sized bowl going for a competitive $5.95. Don't order anything else unless you're sharing or taking some home. All the meat is incredibly fresh and flavorful, and with the jalapenos and a couple scoops of the red chili sauce the broth is a great sinus cleanser. If you do decide to get crazy, treat yourself to a couple of spring rolls stuffed with shrimp, lettuce, bean sprouts and sliced pork. And, of course, the peanut sauce to dip 'em in. These muthas are the diameter of Andre the Giant's finger, you could actually make a meal of two spring rolls. That's just the appetizer. For big appetites and pho purists, I've probably hit 15-20 pho places between Reno and SF and again, 777 comes out on top every time. I kinda liked the old cramped location a little more, when inebriated it resulted in some interesting social interactions around the counter area. Damn you bitch who burned down the Mizpah Hotel!!! If I ever get off that #1 order, I'd probably go for the seafood pho. If the freshness and quantity of meat in the #1 is any indication of how they'd load up that seafood, it's worth a shot. I'll post if I try it, but with the #1 I'm stuck in the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" mentality. Takeout is interesting btw: they give you the raw meat separate from the broth. Once that broth gets boiling it only takes about 5-10 minutes to cook the meat, that brisket is sliced so thin and perfect you could "flash boil" it for like 2 minutes and have it medium-rare, mmmm....

text: For quite a while now, I've been pondering what exactly to say about The Drunken Fish based on the one time I visited the Central West End location. I had veritable writer's block insofar as any substantive, noteworthy observations were concerned. In retrospect, my mental jogging-in-place makes perfect sense, because this restaurant is nothing if not insubstantial. The decor and overall ambiance - if you can even call it that - are more in line with a vapid Wash Ave. club than with anywhere I would want to be caught eating, dead or alive. If the restaurant name wasn't a tip-off, The Drunken Fish basically imports the most boilerplate aspects of Vegas and Ibiza culture and distills them to appeal to self-consciously hip Midwestern college students whose experience with these locations is limited to feature shows they watched on E! I digress, though - good food/service can always mitigate if not supersede lack of ambiance. In light of that, it's doubly disappointing that the actual substance here does nothing to loosen the perpetual eye roll that embodies my attitude towards this place. The staff is functional, but not particularly friendly or efficient. As for the sushi, it's not the worst I've had in St. Louis, but it's the kind of sushi made for people who eat sushi just so they can be seen eating sushi. I can't speak for all of the rolls, but the California and spicy tuna rolls tasted somewhere between "sloppy" and "bland", with none of the smooth, clean sophistication of similar rolls at superior restaurants. Supposedly the happy hour here is legendary but really, too much of a mediocre thing is just that. It's like oil to water anyway, because I don't even drink. I honestly don't understand how this place makes a killing when the much better Chi is mere blocks away. Then again, Chi has been trying really, really hard to emulate The Drunken Fish nowadays. Let's just hope they limit the hero worship to the decor.

text: Stonewood prides itself as an upscale, dinner-only restaurant experience..a bad experience I would have to add. I've been there twice in the past two weeks. Both times the service had been sub-par, which is appalling for a restaurant that dares to call itself "upscale". The waiters are horrible actors, showing a fake kind of politeness to their customers, while still expected a hefty tip once the meal is complete, and that would be a LARGE tip considering the prices of their meals. The meals are like an appetizer at Ruby Tuesday, and don't taste much better than the Olive Garden, for double and sometimes TRIPLE the prices. I've had their Oak Grilled Burger, which had no real taste to it. Compare to the Cheesecake Factory, a real upscale restaurants, Kobe Burger that has a taste in the beef that just oozes out into your mouth without needing to add condiments and you find yourself with a DRY burger that tastes like cooked paper. Condiments are highly needed just to give it some kind of substance. In addition the french fries were horrible, I'd rather have McDonald's, Checkers, or dare i say it, BURGER KING (the most horrible french fry dealer on Earth, now second to most horrible). They had tons of seasoning on them, but the seasoning was of no help to the bland taste that came with them. During my next visit for my Aunt's 35th birthday (someone explain to me why restaurants do so horrible with birthday dinners, where they get so much business from, are they just nervous, or just ignorant of the impression they are making on fairly large parties), I had a lobster ravioli meal with my mother. For twenty-two dollars, we received three (yes three), small raviolis with a small amount of lobster sauce on top, and a kabob with shrimp on it. Frankly, I could have had more food anywhere else I can think of in my head. Clearly making this restaurant a, I'm rich so I'm just going to blow all my money on AIR and dark lighting kind of restaurant. First of all, let me say that we had THREE waiters in the same night. The waiters had no clue what had gone on with the waiter before them, and I'm utterly shocked that we received our meals at all. They actually had us tell them what we had at the end so that they could bill us, it would have been so easy to lie and just pay a small price after they took all our plates away. It's not always to be so honest, but alas we were. I had to track the waiters down for refills. The cup size they give you is slightly bigger than a shot glass, and their food is DRY. It just doesn't make any sense. The waiters half the time seemed to just ignore my glares for them to come and pay attention to me, the person who is controlling their tip. Like I said, I do not understand any of it. The only good thing at this restaurant, saving it from the taboo of one star is their exquisite clam chowder. It tastes amazing, they have the best recipe I have ever had. If I could get the clam chowder, and ignore everything else, that would be swell. I have never eaten clam chowder so quickly and indulged so much into a soup like I did into theirs. They should add a bread bowl and I would be SET. If it were up to me, the waiters would have received nothing in tips and frankly I would have probably complained to no end to the management. Since I was in the party of others, the restaurant was saved of my fury. Of course, I can't let them off that easily. This restaurant is such a wreck that I'm going to give them suggestions to make it better. 1. Get bigger glasses for drinks or make your food more MOIST. There are just no excuses for this. 2. Either lower your prices or add more food, you charge more than the Cheesecake Factory, which is utterly superior to you in every single way. 3. Turn the lights up a little. I didn't see barely any couples there in both my visits, the tables are too big for couples, and you can barely see your own hands in that kind of darkness. Take a note from the Cheesecake Factory, they don't leave their customers blind in the darkness while trying to have conversations and eat their meals. 4. Fire or re-train all your waiters, they suck. They don't know how to attend to peoples needs. That is all. Until we meet again.

text: Bern's Steakhouse is the best steakhouse in the world. End of Review..... Ok I'll explain a little more....I'm not sure how many times I've eaten at Bern's. I'm guessing that it's close to 30 times over 25 years. Their steaks are dry aged 5 to 8 weeks, which is way longer than any dry aged steak I've ever had. Most steakhouses never age them longer than 4 weeks and most steakhouses are wet aged in a vacuumed sealed bag. To dry age a steak, the beef must be hung in a refrigerated cooler and left uncut. This is a very expensive way to age the beef, but way superior to wet aging. The flavor of the meat is unmatched. Because of this flavor the only seasoning that Bern's really needs is garlic butter brushed on. Bern's motto of "We do things differently here" is right on the money. Your steak is not cut until you order it. This means you can order almost any size steak in any cut. For instance they have 17 different size NY strips (from 8oz to 60 oz) available on the menu. That's just the NY strip. There are 34 other size options offered in different cuts (Filet Mignon, Chateaubriand, Delmonico, Porterhouse, and T-Bone). Try getting those options anywhere else. It doesn't exist. My favorite cut is the 25oz Porterhouse. On all their Porterhouse steaks they replace the tail section bone part with a piece of Filet Mignon equal to the weight of the bone. On the 25 oz. Porterhouse, it's about a 4oz filet. Not exactly small. But it isn't just the steaks where they go above and beyond. You like caviar? They have 21 different kinds from 4 different countries. 4 different ways they prepare their steak tartare. The original Steak Tartare Bern is the best I've ever had. Their French Onion soup uses Veal Bones for the Stock and is topped with 5 kinds of cheese. It's amazing. The Lobster Bisque soup is the best I've ever had with a rich dark flavor (burnt butter is added I think) Their vegetables are all organically grown on their own farm, and salads are offered with a choice of 10 different home made dressings. Baked potatoes are cooked perfectly and prepared tableside by your waiter with lots of butter, sour cream, and chives. The Lobster is removed from the shell, claws and all and served in a dish of sizzling butter. The Charcoal grilled shrimp are huge and there must be like 30 of them on that plate served in spicy herb butter. I've also tried the Chicken Bern, which is rolled in sesame seeds and sautéed. It is very tasty. The lump crab cake is good, but not the best I've ever had. The wine list, can't be described. It's the largest in the world. They carry about 700,000 to 1 million bottles of wine on hand. Prices are very reasonable, at least 30% less than the same bottle in most restaurants. In fact for price, Bern's can't be matched. Most restaurants of its caliber are a la carte. Not Berns, for your price of your steak, you get soup, salad, and vegetables. After your dinner, you will be given a tour of the kitchen and wine cellar. Then it's up to your own private dessert room made from wine casks. A 4-page menu of very good deserts with another 1800 dessert wines, ports, and cordials to choose from. Berns is a dining experience like no other. I hope you all enjoy it as much as I have over the years. I just wish Yelp offerd a 6 star rating, because Bern's is in a class all of it's own.

text: My partner and I fostered four kittens from PAWS for three months, and after having a great experience with it, we plan to do it again. Everyone there was incredibly friendly and helpful, despite the fact that they are always swamped with a billion animals who need saving. One of our kittens had to come in for nearly weekly visits, and although we sometimes had to wait a long time to be seen, no one was ever unkind to us and we understood. Dr. Jen did everything she could to help our foster kitten with mysterious blood in her urine, including personally doing her spay surgery so that she could check her out further without having to open her up twice. In the end, there seemed to be no explanation. But after all that she did for the kitten, and the kindness and very thorough checkups that the kitten received, we told Dr. Jen we wished we could bring our adult cat and dog to her! If you're considering fostering for PAWS, I highly recommend it. PAWS takes care of spay/neuter, and the process is relatively simple (email for an appointment, drop them in the morning, pick them up at night). They also take care of their basic vet care on-site, and it was never too hard for us to get an appointment. You're responsible for the finding-them-homes part. Kittens are cute and stinky and fun and troublemakers all at the same time, so if you're prepared for the less fun aspects of pet fostering (giving meds, cleaning up messes, etc) they're worth every ounce of work. PAWS makes fostering pretty simple. We now have adopted out all four kittens in pairs to great homes. All we have to do is drop off their final paperwork, and soon we'll be ready to foster again!

text: I've reserved my first 1-star review for a truly deserving venue. The Gargoyle, hands down the worst music venue in St. Louis. First of all, The Gargoyle is not really a club...it's not even a building. It's a room located in the basement of the Mallinckrodt Center, home of the bookstore and Edison Theater on the campus of Washington University. About 10-14 times a year, this all-purpose room (it resembles a former cafeteria, with low ceilings and tile floors) becomes The Gargoyle, a student-run concert venue that brings nationally recognized acts to town. Since getting only 1 star is a remarkable feat within itself, let me break this down for you. 1. The layout - This is a big, rectangular room with several support poles and a very low stage in front. And when I say low, I mean low. As in, if you're further than 10 feet from the stage, you probably won't be able to see the performers. And if you're short, well let's hope you can sit on your boyfriend's shoulders, otherwise you might as well listen to the CD at home. There's a portion about halfway across the room that suddenly juts out which allows additional room, but no one stands, on account of the fact that the sightlines from there are abysmal. 2. The atmosphere - Have you ever been to a frat party at a morgue? Well, that's what's in store for you at The Gargoyle. Since it's on the Wash U campus, that means they have to play by campus rules, which means no alcohol, no rowdy behavior, and the campus psudo-cops flex their muscle any chance they get. This includes dispersing the crowd immediately following shows. What's that, you want to hang around and chat with your friends? Nope, get out. Oh, you want to talk outside instead? Nah, can't do that either. Doesn't matter if you're a student or not. The second the show is done, the lights come on and you're expected to go back from wherever you came. Of course the students don't help out their own case. Since it's a "dry" campus, students show up already drunk, sometimes not in the best mood. In addition, tickets for students are free, so there are always some people who go for the simple fact that it's free for them. This group of students are almost too annoying to bear, showing little to no respect for the band performing. 3. The management - This is a student-run organization, so in reality there really is no management. 20 year old communications majors who have never run a business don't hold much sway. Whether or not a show is "sold out" depends on the opinion of security, along with the sloppy head counts done while students are stumbling through the door. If a conflict comes up, security and the campus cops take over, and as a result the organizers really have no influence on the show itself, apart from booking the band and cleaning up afterwards. 4. Sound - This is probably the only category that wouldn't get 1 star, technically speaking. But like any small venue, bring your earplugs if you enjoy the gift of hearing. And of course the quality varies greatly based on where you're standing in the cavern...er, room. 5. Parking - Your best bet is the street (good luck) a visitor meter spot (again, good luck), or underneath the visitor center for $1.00/hour. During the school year, Wash U offers the most unfriendly-parking situation of any college or university in St. Louis. If you're brave enough to park in a spot that requires a tag before 10:00PM on a weekday, just assume you're going to get a ticket. I could probably go on, but I'll just let it rest here. I've seen many shows here, just because the band was so good I couldn't NOT go, so I grin and bear it. But I always know what to expect, and always groan when I hear a band I like is playing here. The Gargoyle's worked hard for the worst venue in St. Louis, and it's in no position to give it up anytime soon.

text: I like chain restaurants, but never did I think I'd be visiting three different Ruth's Chris restaurants in three different cities. The Ruth's Chris restaurant in King of Prussia is no different from the rest. Great food and great service. I ordered off the Ruth's Choice menu which is a prix fixe menu of appetizer, entree, and dessert. You have a choice of a $39.95 or a $49.95 menu. Unfortunately the $49.95 menu isnt online but some of the choices on this menu include sea bass, ribeye, and 8 oz filet. I opted for the more expensive prix fixe menu and had the harvest salad (which had dried cherries, bacon bits, goat cheese, fried onions, tomatoes, roasted corn, cajun pecans, and mixed greens), sea bass, and chocolate mousse. The salad was flavorful. The combination of all the ingredients worked well with each other. A mix of sweet, sour and salty. Delicious! The sea bass was the highlight of the meal. It was pan fried so it was slightly crispy on the outside and very flaky and soft on the inside. The sea bass was on a bed of spinach and tomato risotto. I ordered a side of garlic green beans with the entree. It was fresh with big cloves of roasted garlic. Yum! The dessert left much to be desired. The menu online indicated a duo pairing of carrot cake and a cup of chocolate mousse. Instead we got a cup of chocolate mousse and a cup of fruit. It was not very memorable. The Service was good. Since we were stuck in PA for a conference and had no cash, we asked our waitress to split our checks so we could each pay by credit card. They were hesitant at first, but ended up accomodating us.
