text: So our travel book said that NOLA was the place to be for Christmas and, even better, that there wouldn't be crowds in town like during other holidays. When we arrived, it definitely was not overwhelmingly crowded though we were clearly not the only ones in town for the holidays who weren't visiting family. I say all this because, as an out of towner, it was difficult to make dinner reservations a few months ago for Christmas day dinner. We looked online and used the nola.com Reveillon Dinner restaurant list as a place to start. Several restaurants were already booked that we called, so we opened up Yelp and started to make more calls. Several of the most highly rated places like Bayona weren't even serving a Christmas dinner. The Upperline was also not open. So the reviews on Yelp looked pretty good for Cafe Adelaide so we called and made a reservation. Their web site (with the Swizzle Stick Bar) looked quirky so we weren't turned off by the fact that this restaurant was in the Loews Hotel. Typically, unless you're dining at a 5-star hotel restaurant, you're not in for a great meal, but because of the reviews for Cafe Adelaide on Yelp, I thought we would be in for a good meal. We arrived a bit early for our 7pm reservation and were seated in a corner near the restaurant entrance. The hotel service people were outfitted in the exact standard issue hotel uniforms you would expect and many of the busers and even a couple of the servers were clearly high school or college age working a seasonal job, which is generally not the sign of a great place either. Oh well, it was open on Christmas. Our server was an adult, dressed in a non-uniform suit, but the whole time he seemed nervous and not particularly warm. He reached his hand really far out to clear plates as if to stay as far away from us as possible. Granted, the tables were way too large, but still, bizarre. He was accommodating and deferential, but not as professional as what I expect at a nice place. We started with cocktails from the Swizzle Stick Bar--I a Cary Grant and my husband a Sazerac--after perusing the cocktail menu. Surprisingly though, we were never brought a wine list before ordering our dinners and our entrees came out so fast that we were still finishing our cocktails with our meals. Again, not fine dining timing though we paid fine dining prices. We both had the filets mignon with potatoes, green beans and a large shrimp. The filets were fine, but seemed somewhat over-rested and were not very warm. The green beans were advertised as served in a balsamic reduction, but really the beans had been stewed in that sauce so that they were more like canned green beans. Did I mention that these entrees were $36 each? We're willing to pay for a good meal, but for the lackluster quality this was waaaay too much. We tried to redeem the restaurant with desserts--"Creole" Cheesecake (topped with freeze dried raspberries--Why???? Aren't raspberries good enough fresh?) and the Strawberry Shortcake. Neither were earth-shattering. I had an overly strong coffee before we left and went to enjoy a great night at the Maple Leaf Bar. If only we had eaten somewhere else. Come here for a cocktail and eat somewhere else unless you enjoy awkward service and mediocre food at upscale prices. I almost forgot, if you go, don't forget to check out the wood paneled walls. They were lovingly painted to resemble a zebra skin pattern, but again, on WOOD panels in a nice brown wood color, ALL over the walls. Classy? Not so much.
label: NEG

text: Absolutely the worst restaurant steak I have ever had. I'm not even going to waste my time with saying anything more than that. I wrote the above statement a few days prior to today's date (11/26/10). Upon reflection, I've decided that the above statement is not particularly useful, although I still maintain that it is accurate. Allow me to explain further. I know that Charlie's is (inexplicably) a beloved New Orleans establishment. While this is often enough for other mediocre local establishments to maintain a client base (cf. Galatoire's), said other mediocre local establishments normally have SOMETHING worthwhile to offer in the way of cuisine. Not so with Charlie's. Let's talk about the steaks. I had the largest T-Bone that Charlie's offered...my friend had some form of gigantic steak that was, I believe, a ribeye. Having not tried his steak, I can only speak about my own. I get my steaks cooked rare, and this has never been a problem for any other steakhouse in the city. The steak was presented to me on a metal plate and I immediately noticed an inordinate amount of fat on the cut. Worse still, the meat seemed as though it were barely cooked. It was not seared in the least. My suspicions were confirmed when I cut the meat, to discover that it was cold (COLD) in the center. I do not know with certainty what grade of meat the proprietors of Charlie's purchase; however, I do know that it tasted akin to something that one might purchase at Winn-Dixie, or perhaps even Wal-Mart. Perhaps most disturbing, however, is that despite the total lack of quality inherent in my meal, I would have thought that I was actually at Ruth's Chris by virtue of the bill. And that's the thing...I do not go out of my way to bash local restaurants. However, the quality of the food was SO bad, and the cost of the food was SO high that I feel like I need to warn those who haven't been to Charlie's yet. Don't go. Just don't. If you are one of those people who (understandably) cannot bring them selves to eat at Ruth's Chris post-Katrina, that's fine. Might I recommend Dickie Brennan's, then? Or, if you want a steak, and don't necessarily need to eat one in a proper steakhouse, Lillette's hanger steak is absolutely delicious. So, that's that. Bad. Bad, bad, bad.

text: Clarissa J.: *Wanders, lost, through Shop 'n Save like through some horrid nightmare* "Someone help me...please, help me..." Plastic, happy, not-quite-elevator-muzak-but-more-like-sadistic-dentist-office music quietly plays overhead, but with enough pronunciation and cheeriness that it burrows precisely and targetedly into your brain like a needle. This is the soundtrack to a frightening B-movie about grocery shopping where everything is sterile, from the aisles to the music, to the staff -- seemingly in order, but actually in bizarre and utter chaos. What is that stench that emerges from the deli?! The closer you get, the more pungent it becomes. A white nectarine I pick out is hard like an apple, or an uncooked potato. The patrons are brutish and bestial, wearing scowls -- except perhaps when answering a cell phone call from a friend, but once the call is over, proceed back to the sludgy funk with which they began to shop. Price tags on shelves suggest sales, but if you really take a look, everything is actually more expensive than shopping in Chicago. [Clarissa J.: How on EARTH can they use "Save" in their name?] Being set upon the arduous task of finding that "Polar Ice" flavored Eclipse gum that She particularly likes, aisle after aisle offers nothing but Peppermint, Spearmint, Winterfrost, Midnight Cool...everything but the one you were asked to get. [Clarissa J.: Should we risk beheading by buying Her a different flavor??] Our self check out machine is an industrial cousin to HAL 9000 and independently decides to restart after we scan everything in our basket, only to keep us trapped a little longer under the Shop 'n Save's power. And just when you think you've made it out safely, just when you get back to the house and unpack your bags...you realize that, during the awful, cloudy-headed excursion, you'd forgotten the most important item...and you have to go back. *The song "Hotel California" begins to play on the radio as Clarissa J. gets back into the car to return to the store. Or is it really just playing in her mind? "You can check out any time you like, but you can NEVER leave!"*

text: To tell you the truth, I didn't even know that this place had a name, that's how hidden and unrecognized it is. It is a little hole-in-the-wall joint on South Street that you would miss if you blinked your eyes. Aside from the incredible atmosphere that seems like you walked into a time-warp and transported back to the mid-1970s, the food is excellent. When I think of a Philly cheese steak, I think of the beauty's that are served here. Get them with American cheese and fried onions and you will then soon start the conversion. The meat is thinly chopped and the grease seeps into the Amoroso roll providing a taste of the best. If you are really adventurous, or simply starving, be sure to get a slice of the pepperoni and sausage pie. It is a thick slice that gives you the best of worlds, two meats and a zesty sauce. text: Out of all the burrito places in the area, this one is my favorite. The burritos are big and packed with deliciousness. They also have various other standard mexican food items, such as tacos and quesadillas, but I never really get any of those because the burritos are too good to pass up. They have a wide variety of burritos, and you can fill them with steak, chicken, or pork. There are two that are tied for my favorite: the queso burrito and the ancho chile barbecue burrito. The queso burrito is just what it sounds like, a burrito with delicious cheesy queso inside. I'm a big cheese fan and this burrito definitely satisfies. The barbecue burrito contains some sort of spicy mexican barbecue sauce that is packed with flavor. I was somewhat skeptical the first time I tried it, but it tastes great, especially when combined with the shredded pork. They have five different kinds of salsa. My favorites are roja (which is hot) and verde (which is medium). I haven't yet gotten up the guts to try the extra hot salsa, but now I think I'll have to try it the next time I stop in. I'll often stop by to quickly grab a burrito to take home for dinner after work, and the generally fast service makes it easy to do this. They assemble your burrito from the various ingredients while you watch, and they're pretty snappy about it. However, I occasionally happen to stop by during a busy time and have to wait in line, but it's never been a very long wait. My only real complaint is that occasionally the person who is making my burrito will be a bit stingy with the cheese. They'll usually give you more cheese if you ask (like I said, I love cheese) but sometimes they try to make you pay more for it. Come on, just give me a little more cheese. It costs them next to nothing and keeps me a happy and loyal burrito-buying customer. A minor complaint, but somewhat irksome at times. Overall, a great place to grab a tasty burrito, with a convenient location and generally quick service.

text: I have to admit, I am a bit biased about IMS, since I have been to 43 (and counting) 500s, 4 Brickyards, and 4 USGPs. I can't begin to count the number of qual days. I no longer live in Indy, but make the annual trek "to the mount" despite the IRL/CART/ChampCar b.s. of the last 12 years. I have been to at least fifteen other oval tracks (e.g., Texas, Charlotte, Kansas, Atlanta,...) and venues (e.g. Long Beach, Watkins Glen, St. Pete, Laguna Seca, etc.) that I can compare to IMS. IMS is not as modern, clean, and the sight lines can be horrible in comparison to a track like Texas. But the sheer magnitude of grounds is what always brings an "ahhhhh" feeling to everyone new that I bring to the track. The history can consume you as you tour the museum. Be prepared for really lousy, stinking, foul bathrooms and horrible food. At most of the other, newer tracks, food selection is far superior. Always bring your own food but make sure the cooler under 14 inches if sitting in the stands. Best seats in my opinion - and I have sat most places around the track - is the first turn, about 1/2-3/4 up or in the penthouse. Don't sit low along the front straight. You'll see the pits, but that's it. You can always walk along the outside wall to see the pits if you want. The yellow shirts won't let you stop, but you can walk really,really,really slowly.... If in the penthouse, sit in the first three or four rows only. I don't like turns 2-4 because they are open. With the weather the last few years you'll get soaked in the rain or burn to a crisp if it is sunny. Make sure to go to the museum if you have never been. It's open the day before the race which is always a good time to go if you are just visiting.
label: POS

There are all kinds of cool bars and restaurants within walking distance (v important to potential NY ex-pats), and on my most recent visit, we walked to Local 44. Local 44 is the kind of bar everyone wants to be able to walk to. It's laid-back but not divey, and feels like somewhere you'd go knowing that some of your friends and/or neighbors were bound to show up, too. They've got an intimidatingly well-thought out selection of local beers and micro-brews on tap, each listed alongside its alcohol content for those of you who make decisions based on buzz potential. What's not intimidating are the prices--almost all beers were $4 or $5! This...this I like. To wash down my $4 beer, we picked out a couple of snacks from the menu--shrimp tacos and corn dogs (very hip in NY right now, too). Holy moly, these shrimp tacos were some of the absolute best I've had EVER, and this isn't even a Mexican joint! The corn tortillas were warm and fresh (possibly hand made?), the shrimp nice and juicy, and everything was drizzled with a spicy cilantro cream that had a genuine kick. The $5 corn dog plate went above and beyond what any corn dog plate could even aspire to be--EIGHT plump fritters, with crispy, sweet cornbread on the outside and super-juicy dog bites on the inside. Elettaria, are you and your sad, lone corn dog snack listening? If I do make the big move to the 6th borough, it won't be for a year or two, and will depend on me getting a fancy professor job in the neuroscience department at Penn, Haverford, Swarthmore, etc. In the meantime, I have two things to ask of you West Philadelphians: 1. Please keep patronizing Local 44 so it's still in business when I get there. 2. If you happen to know anyone in the neuroscience department at Penn, Haverford, Swarthmore, etc, shoot me a PM, yes? Kthxbye.

text: Ahhh... The Dish. My kitchen away from home for so many years that it almost goes without saying just how much I love the food within these walls! The Latest Dish opened in 1997 and was an instant hit - the food was freshly prepared and served with a smile and a bit of sass to boot! The kitchen became famous for two things; incredible calamari and being open until 1:30 on weekends. Soon after, the upstairs was open as Fluid Nightclub and this little corner of the world became the epicenter for underground nightlife in Philadelphia. DJ icons like Jazzy Jeff, Josh Wink and ?uestlove began nights upstairs - and spent many a night pre-gaming it downstairs with dinner and drinks. The sounds that came through the walls became the pulse of the city and the restaurant was the place to be. Over time things change - however one thing that has remained strong is the quality of food and service you get at The Latest Dish. With the addition of a new head chef, The Dish has transformed what some thought was a stale, but good, menu - into an ever-changing texture of tastes. Along with a list of standard fare, be sure to check the special boards mounted throughout the space to see just what the chef has up his sleeve that night. One night you're traveling south of the border - the next is a trip to New England. Fascinating stuff indeed! A few staples stand out and must be tried - the grilled-caramelized tilapia with green rice, citrus marinated avocado and pinto beans in a tomato chili sauce truly melts in your mouth. Also, even if you're a carnivore, don't miss out on the tofu and miso meatballs; crispy fried tofu balls served on sweet black rice with grilled baby bok choy and a spicy/sweet sauce. It's like warm melted balls of cheese - amazing! Speaking of carnivores, I would be remiss not to mention a true staple of the house - the grilled filet mignon, which comes with white cheddar gratin, seared spinach, fried onion rings and a burgundy demi glace. Rich and heavenly. A nice mix of salads - my favorite is the spinach and arugula salad with toasted walnuts, manchego cheese, red peppers, capers and a sundried cherry vinaigrette. Desserts are hit or miss - but you can never go wrong with their house bread pudding - it's the perfect way to end the meal - it's like a pillow for your tastebuds! So - check out The Dish - - perhaps before you come to the next Sex Dwarf - Philly's nonstop new wave dance party; every first Friday @ Fluid. Doors at 9 - so be sure to start your dinner at the Dish by 7:30, so you don't miss the fun upstairs afterward. **I originally submitted this review to http://phillygrub.ning.com in spring 2008**

text: Let me preface this by saying I was dragged to this place after a 10 hour sales meeting in a hot and steamy conference room. I was starving--and in need of several adult beverages. As this place was described to me I had imagined I'd be embarking on a historical and cultural culinary adventure back through time. You know--chunky bar maids dressed in corseted dresses that functioned for centuries as silicon enhancements holding 8 lead pints in each hand, rogues in the corner laughing and fighting, massive boars heads served on mountainous piles of meat, bards telling their tales of old. And I guess in some demented way this place was just like that....only without the embellishment. Instead of the boar's head we got a small handful of roast beef placed lovingly on a plain bun that was, in turn, placed lovingly on a paper plate of the same size (are we at white castle?). Those Rubenesque hostesses I was imagining turned out to be a friendly--if not forgetful--unceremonious woman who could carry not 8, but 1 pint in each hand. But we did get our Bard. Instead of striking tales of dragons and knights, Mr. J. Alfred Prufrock relinquished a long, tiresome soliloquy on the struggles, tragedies and triumphs that you would expect from a lifetime devoted to being a basketball referee. Now I understand the difference between being captivated with times of yore and being held captive by them.

text: Politicians and pundits often say that small businesses drive America. I think of Rue Lafayette as that quintessential small business. I'm sure there's some official definition of a "small business," but let me break it down as applied to Rue Lafayette: It's a group of people with common passions and talents working toward a singular goal: making sure you get awesome food and personal service. It's the idea that those people be accessible to the customer, instead of segregated from him: here you can look straight back into the kitchen and ask the chef what he recommends. It's the notion that you can meld concepts in uncommon mashup: the Cafe shares space with a Boutique full of random yet classy ornaments for your bohemian abode. Finally, it's the requirement that you be integrated with your community rather than superimposed on top of it: in both architecture and overall experience, Rue Lafayette pulls this off seamlessly. Do America a favor and give this place a try.

text: Took the Parents to lunch today at the Persian Grille. I hadn't been here since I was a young teen, about twenty years ago. The parents have been there since and recommended it. Since I had been there last, they really turned this into a nice restaurant. It is tastefully decorated in a contemporary-Persian décor. They have a full bar (more on that later), and the staff was very friendly and welcoming. I should note that although we were there for lunch (around 1PM) their lunch menu was not available since it was Sunday. That meant that it would be full dinner prices. This would not have changed my decision to go to lunch there, but it did catch me a little off guard, as now lunch would be about $100 for three people. Entrees are in the $18-$20 range. The place was empty when we arrived. By the time we left, it was beginning to fill up. The Parents have been there for dinner and said it gets very crowded. Upon reviewing their beer menu, I was astounded. As a lover of Belgian beer, I couldn't believe that a Persian restaurant was carrying 25 ounce bottles of La Chouffe, Delerium, Corsendonk, Chimay, Duvel, St. Bernardus, Ommegang and others! They weren't cheap, but if you think about the mark up that restaurants put on bottles of wine, $15.99 seemed reasonable to split a big bottle of La Chouffe with Father. Mother had a Stella Artois draught. Again, I don't know why the great selection of Belgians, but I will not complain. We ordered the hummus as an appetizer, which came with warm pita bread. It was mild and delicious, not overwhelming with garlic. Enough for three people to split. For entrees, Father and I both ordered Shereen Polo, which was a roasted, glazed Cornish hen served with wonderful basmati rice containing carrots, pistachio, saffron, almonds and orange. Mother ordered the Addas Polo, which was only offered with lamb or veal. She asked if she could substitute chicken and it was no problem at all. I believe that it was the owner that was serving us. Her rice contained lentils, dates, raisins and almonds. Portions are large and Mother and I both took home leftovers. For dessert we had the Baklava and the Faloodeh Shirazi. The Baklava was good. The Faloodeh is ice-cream like with noodles in the base. It was flavored with rose water. The consistency was fine, but the rose water taste was overwhelming, so much so that I felt that I was eating cheap, rose perfume. It is served with lemon juice and cherry syrup that you are to pour over it. Father really poured it on and ate quite a bit of it. He said that the syrups helped with the rose taste. It may have been the greatest Faloodeh, I think it was just not to my tastes. Overall, I loved the Persian Grille. Although I enjoy sampling different cuisines, I think the food here would appeal to a broad range of taste buds. It is foreign enough to satisfy middle eastern food lovers, yet delicious enough appease the hesitant. I would definitely dine here again. You can tell that the owner takes pride in his restaurant. I would encourage trying the Persian Grille and expanding your horizons.

text: I basically lived at this hotel for about a month when I was in town for a long term job so I got reeeally familiar with the ins and outs of the place. In short? It was awful. At most other hotels this wouldn't be too much of an issue, but since the magnetic key for my room wouldn't work at least once a day, I kept having to go back to the front desk every day to get a new card - it gets old fast. Especially when each elevator ride takes approximately 5-10 minutes with wait time. There is also a lot of false advertising. For example, they advertise wifi availability, but what they mean is that it's available, but you have to pay to use it. If you get a package delivered here, there is a fee - a big one. I think one fee I had was about 25 bucks. The business center is also very pricey. Oh! And make sure not to accidentally take something out of the mini-bar, because it will automatically show up on your bill when you check out, regardless of whether or not you consumed it. Parking is also very very expensive. You must valet - and sometimes when I would go to pick up the car, calling ahead would not be an option and I would have to wait 10-20 minutes in the valet area while the poor over-worked valets would be servicing large wedding and conference parties. All the rooms below the 42nd floor (I think) have not been redone and just look...tired. Ask for a higher floor. Also, on each floor there are two rooms that are right next to the elevators, separate from the rest of the hallway. If you find yourself to be in either of these rooms, asked to be moved IMMEDIATELY. Otherwise, you will not be able to get any sleep thanks to the constant stream of drunken revelers that come home (or depart) after midnight. I would not recommend this for business travellers (or really anyone, frankly). Maybe if you're one of the drunken revelers you won't notice how everything's overpriced.

text: Writing from the perspective of a Jew weaned on Katz's and Carnegie and Russ & Daughters who's culinary adventures down south are fulfilled in every area but my precious Jewish cuisine, I've found Stein's to be steadily disappointing. Granted, this isn't New York City or Boca Raton, but from the stature of the place among New Orleanians, I expect more. The vibe is mostly what I want (gruff employees, tightly packed, dim, and shared seating) but the bagels are dull and the corned beef and chopped liver are actually terrible. Granted, I'm looking for something specific here and not getting it, and maybe their other sandwiches and meats are stellar (the selection of specialty products is pretty ok). But the place is called Stein's, and there are certain expectations I attach to that. I want a thick, moist bagel and schmear (lox cream cheese or whitefish salad, not "salmon spread") and a piled-high, hot, juicy corned beef sandwich from a place that purports to be a Jewish deli. The corned beef is cold and bland and overpriced. Another thing to keep in mind- I rarely eat meat anymore and when I do, it's by my own strange set of rules. Yesterday I decided I needed a corned beef sandwich. So this review comes from a place of deep disappointment, All that being said, I still frequent, if only for the vibe and the dearth of bagels in this town. Grandpa would be proud of this review. And please message me if you share my plight and have found a solution.

text: I would estimate that I've honestly dropped a couple thousand dollars at Flying Pie, so I feel well qualified to submit a review. Flying Pie unquestionably serves the finest pizza in Boise and about the best I've found anywhere. First and foremost, the pizza is absolutely delicious. I've learned that different pizzas appeal to different persons, so the fact that I like it is not necessarily determinative for you. The pizza is medium but crispy crust with lots and lots of very high-quality ingredients. The crust is half-way between thin-crust New York pizzas and deep dish Chicago pizzas. The ingredients are super quality and there are lots of them. Those are the key aspects of the superiority of a Flying Pie pizza. Also, the various crusts are yummy and the pizzas are always properly cooked to crispy (crust) but gooey (cheese) perfection. The pizzas are very creative and there is a wide variety. My favorites are the zambini (sausage and jalapenos), the Denver Pie (think a Denver omelet) and the mesquite chicken. While the pizza is not inexpensive, I believe that Flying Pie is a good value. So why only four stars rather than five?, you might ask. I'll tell you. It's two things. The restaurants are dumps in very undistinguished locations. Hanging out at the Flying Pie, either location, is like hanging out in your friend's basement in 1982. The owners invested $2,450 to outfit the spaces in 1982 and haven't put a penny in since. I'm all for a funky vibe, but this crosses over from funky vibe to junky dive. The price for the pizza is at the high end but the interiors are low quality, dark shops located next to a Salvation Army depot and trailer parks (State Street) and tattoo parlors (Fairview). My second beef is that the restaurant has an almost-juvenile self-congratulation streak. In their publications, menus, sign boards, and attitude, the restaurant is always telling the customer how incredibly awesome they are. We're awesome and have the best pizza! We're incredibly awesome and everyone loves our pizza! We're the best restaurant ever and our pizza is better than everybody else's!! Ok, I get it and I'm tired of it. I don't mind when my 8 year old tells me he's awesome, but after that it's a little embarrassing. It's especially annoying in light of the dumpy physical spaces. If you're so awesome, why don't you make your interiors pleasant? If you're so awesome, why don't you put a location downtown? it seems to me that the owners should focus a little less on self-congratulation and a little more on improving the customer experience, non-eating wise. All those things being said, i think the service is excellent; the spaces are clean; and given that many of the employees have worked there for a very very long time, it must be a good place to work.

text: As I mentioned in my review of the Sheraton, I needed a place to watch the England vs. Algeria World Cup game while my lovely wife shopped with her daughter and grandkids. We timed our trip down there perfectly and I was sitting at the bar with time to spare! There were lots of TVs in this place and they had music playing that gave the bar a very cool vibe to it. I came to learn that Ernesto, the bartender, was very cool. He greeted me right away and wanted to get me set up as best as humanly possible. I picked my best vantage point and while I wasn't all that hungry, looked over the menu. Everything looked and sounded tasty, but I was in game mode and all I really wanted was a GOOD Bloody Maria. Long ago I accepted the fact that not all bars make good Bloody Marys/Marias. Would I be as lucky today as the US was against England in their first game of the World Cup or would I be victimized like we were in the Slovenian match? Ernesto was fired up to make me one and I was buoyed by his enthusiasm. It took a few minutes and when he was done, I have to say Ernesto has Fire + Spice in the plus column! My Bloody was so good I had to tell myself to slow down and savor it... I didn't want to be wasted by the time the Mrs. showed up. While England looked very uninspired during their match against Algeria, Ernesto & Co. were taking up the slack. People started to filter in for lunch, but I was the only one at the bar. Even though he started to get busy with orders for the lunch crowd he made sure to take care of me. Ernesto set out some very spicy chex mix for me. This mouth charring, endorphin pumping variant did not come out of a Chex Mix bag. It was "this is freakin' hot but I can't stop eating it" good. I meant to ask where it came from, but again I was in game mode and Ernesto could sense it. He was friendly, but not disruptive (and ended up giving me the remote so I could turn the volume up). He poured me a Dos Equis and kept tabs on me. At half time, I ordered a Sonoran Quesadilla. Not because I was super hungry, but it just looked so good: Roasted poblano's, oaxaca cheese, salsa fresca,crema ...for a buck they add beef machaca and it rolled out at $8. It came with salsa but it was so tasty, I didn't want to spoil it in any fashion. I wished I would have been starving, because I wanted to try a whole lot more on the menu. Anyway, the second half came and went uneventfully. England failed to produce, yet Ernesto & Fire + Spice came up big! I settled my tab and told Ernesto I would be back for a margarita to take back poolside. Everyone claims they have good margs...if life was only that simple. I tried two, just to make sure! They were as good as he claimed they were going to be. I wasn't completely bombed when the Mrs. returned. She tried to catch up and pitched in an order of cherry vodka & soda water. She tried two ..they tasted like cherry vodka & soda water. LOL! Our last report is on breakfast. We mosied on down there for breakfast thinking our breakfast vouchers were going to be for some prepacked bagels or honey buns and maybe a small carton of milk or Donald Duck OJ. The waitress informed us that they were good for the All- American breakfast. Mrs. asked if we could substitute it for the Breakfast Burrito..she is so good at that! They hooked us up and we both enjoyed one of the best breakfast burritos ever. It is not a humongous stomach stretching burrito, but a respectfully sized burrito. Some say that it is not the size of your burrito that matters , but what is inside. I believe it...in this case. Not only was the burrito delish....the hash browns were some of the best tasting shredded spuds we have ever had. The Mrs. couldn't finish hers and I was too full to help out. Guess it was big enough! The Sheraton is lucky to have this place on the property! I would go there even if I wasn't staying at the hotel.

text: I can't say I've been to Tokyo, but I thought the food here was good. We had salads, which were decent aside from the shameful embarrassment of my all-too-Aryan companion being unable to eat it with chopsticks, which meant we had to flag the waitress, who had that "I'm looking nice, but we're going to go in the kitchen and giggle at your expense" aura about her. After the salads, we ordered four maki rolls to share: the St. Louis, the Caterpillar, the Rainbow, and one other one I don't see on their menu (I think it was a Spider Roll). The St. Louis roll was bland, very average, but the Caterpillar, Rainbow, and whatever else we had were outstanding. The rolls were well-composed, the rice was good, and the flavors were well-conceived and balanced. As a disclaimer, I've lived my entire life in the Midwest. I've only been the west coast a few times and did not eat Japanese. I'll readily admit it's possible my palate is not fine-tuned to Pacific fish, that it's been taught to think the fish you can find in Midwestern restaurants is what good, fresh seafood tastes like when in actuality there's something better out there. But I thought the salmon and tuna were good quality here, and there was absolutely nothing wrong with the eel. Service was polite, but again gave off a discomforting vibe. I think the fact this place transparently used to be an IHOP, it would be so much more awesome if it were more of the crazy-fun Japanese (think Japanese game shows) than that stereotype of the quiet, reflective Japanese being driven by formalities and a shame and service complex. But I can't rate a place against what I would do with it or what my infantile fantasies would rather have (I'd call it "Ihos: International House of Sushi and flood it with Japanese Pop Culture stuff and have things like the "Seijun Suzuki Roll" that's cut oddly. Normally, I would absolutely, 100% abhor such a concept, but sometimes you have to swing for the fence). In any event, the place is great to me at what it is and wants to be. And after having sushi in Chicago, I think St. Louisans are being a bit ridiculous if they complain about the prices here.

text: The collective IQ in this place could barely power thread through a needle. OMG. They could not accept my PECO electricity bill as a form of ID because unlike my birth certificate, passport, social security card, and ID from my former home state, all of which I presented to PennDOT's ace eye, this particular document says Dan, not Daniel. "Dan's not your name," they concluded, to the protestations of my employers, clients, creditors, family, friends, and every cell in my being. I was instructed to see the supervisor, who flatly refused to accept my PECO bill for another reason. "It's a copy," she said. "Not an original." Really? Because I have a perfing machine at home, not to mention laser type engraving, offset printing, and other tools of the trade necessary to craft this amazing replica. Next the supervisor insisted that the only way I could get a license would be to have PECO update their records so bills start being sent to 'Daniel.' I said, OK, will do, but help me understand. Wouldn't PECO verify my name by accepting the very same forms of identification that you will not? Silence. Except maybe for the sound of Lee press-on nails clicking through a small, distracting pile of unclaimed paper clips. With hours to spare, I threw myself into oncoming traffic on Columbus Blvd., then tucked inside a taxi whose day-old curry smell was positively intoxicating and helped to offset other olfactory distractions -- not least of which was the smell of bull droppings pooting out the back of PennDOT itself. PECO was great. They had me in and out the revolving door in three minutes flat with a disarmingly unofficial looking form prepared in ballpoint with my full name splayed across the page all proper and undeniably me. The clock was ticking (as PennDOT clangs shut at the customer-friendly hour of 4:15pm) ... so rather than ghetto back down to S. Cols Blvd, I went instead to the branch closest to PECO, at 8th and Arch. Collect number, sit, forms and ID laying expectantly inside my man bag smoothed across my ladylike lap. The gentleman to my left fussed with an unruly black skank cap pressing down his precious-fed curls. A young girl with unexplained burn marks across her legs stood blank before a 99-cent store mirror, as her mother tore through her rough mane with a small pink doll's comb, one unloved strand at a time. 880, 881, 88... then my number. Speedy, considering the crowds! Now at the counter, I hand over my papers, and my gut knocks the clipboard off the counter onto a grungy piece of beige Radio Shack electronics with tiny buttons in rows and clusters like whiteheads. Which prompted the system to call the next number. So now we have a man standing behind me waiting to be served. An otherwise desirable scenario, but not here, not now, not in this way. The clerk was not amused. She also was not amused by the freshly minted documentation from PECO. "It doesn't have your Social on it," she said. I said, "Does PECO have a form with your Social? I wasn't offered the option." Silence. Next the clerk was bedazzled by my lease, which, like the PECO bill, says Dan not Daniel. "Dan is not your name," she insists, as though everyone at PennDOT is catching on to this now embarrassing fact. I'm living a lie. But she was willing to go through with the application anyway. With the warning, it could very well get rejected, so don't be surprised if your real ID never comes through. She repeated these lines in different ways and manners throughout the seemingly endless data entry process, all the while a slick-skinned baby, ostensibly fed on nothing but Mountain Dew and Hydrox, was screaming for a clean diaper and a new lease on life, so loud the souring acoustic tiles nearly rattled off their ceiling tracks. Through the tunnel, tunnel, toward the light with every keystroke. Then the magic words: "$12 please." "Cash or card?" I ask. She looked up, and all I see is her thick white eyeliner, as if from a bottle of White Out. "Are you kidding me?" she says. "It clearly says here we only accept checks or money orders. Now I'm going to have to cancel this entire order." I was dressed down because I failed to provide the correct form of payment, i.e., those favored by bail bondsmen and Ghanaian internet predators and no one else either in the US or around the globe. "And how am I supposed to explain that I'm $12 short?" she asked, as she fed my paperwork through the shredder. How indeed.

text: There's something incredibly charming about a place that drowns itself in old Western decor, serves almost all of its beverages in glass boots, and takes every opportunity available to sneak in insults towards Ralph Nader and the Green Party. The beef is seasoned just right; the bun is toasted ever so slightly; the vegetables are all fresh and crisp. Beautiful, tasty simplicity. Throw in a heaping pile of fries (they really give you a lot!), and you've just spent the best $7.00 (plus tip!) you'll probably spend in a long time. Their steaks range from $9.99 to ~$20, and they're all very good (especially the ribeye), but Wednesday nights they have a New York strip special for an incredible $9.99. That's one 12 oz strip (which is, once again, seasoned perfectly), two sides, bread, and your choice of soup or salad -- all for $9.99. How they manage to stay open with deals like this is beyond me, but it seems as though Wednesday nights are pretty popular, so it must be working. Service can be hit or miss, depending on who's serving. My friends and I discovered it during the glory days, when an exceptionally good server named Tawna was working there. At least 5x as charming as the decor and at least 10x as good as any server in Tucson, she didn't even need to ask me what I wanted. It was the first time I'd ever experienced that kind of restaurant -- the kind where a regular could simply say, "I'll have the usual," and the restaurant would know exactly what that meant. She doesn't work there anymore, and unfortunately I haven't been there since May, but the rest of the staff is also very friendly, and so I can't imagine having a bad experience here.

text: You know it has to be pretty bad for someone to write a review about a gas station... ;) As far as the cleanliness of the place, location, etc., it's all pretty average when compared with other gas stations in the area. Those big numbers up on the sign might look like a good price as you're driving by, but -- unless you're legitimately about to run out of gas -- it's worth it to just keep driving until you get to another gas station two miles or so in either direction. When you attempt to fill up your tank, you'll see that there are two prices at the pump -- cash and credit. I know gas stations want to encourage people to use cash, since there's an overhead involved with processing credit charges and stuff. Fine. I get it. But I almost wish they'd just go with whatever the higher price is, to be honest... I mean, who uses cash for stuff these days? When I see two prices like this, it doesn't encourage me to use cash -- it just ticks me off because I end up feeling like I'm being charged more than I should. But, fine, maybe you're one of those people who does pay with cash. Maybe your grandparents gave you a card for Christmas with $20 and a few "collectible" quarters... Great. Now you can take advantage of the low gas prices here, right? ...nope! Well, not unless you wanted a car wash, too. The "price" advertised on the signs here actually assumes you're paying with cash AND getting a car wash. It's pretty annoying. I still go there, though, but I only get enough to make it to a better gas station around town. Part of me just loves the idea of them paying a credit transaction fee on the few dollar's worth of gas I buy :)

As my main course I ate the jumbo Gulf shrimp and grits, and while I found the grits very enjoyable, the only flavors on the plate were spice, spice and more spice, which totally obliterated any chance that the Gulf shrimp's subtle flavors might shine. Fortunately for me, the dessert that followed was certainly a high point in my week. I ordered the Banana Cream Profiteroles, and was truly impressed by the rich flavor of the banana cream, contrasted with the concentrated flavor of the Foster's sauce, it was all very lovely. The service was mediocre, but the waitress was dingy but attentive. The concept is absolutely silly: they use dish towels for napkins, paper table cloths, random kitchen tools as plate stand-ins, and unappetizing methods and procedures for consumption of certain morsels of shelled stuffing. text: No! Not delicious and not fun! Old school done poorly! My boyfriend and I had a terrible experience here after a long great day on the beach. Ruined the evening. Have been in town for three days and had great successes wandering around with the occasional yelp update. This place was the first true spoiler. Ready for a reasonably priced steak dinner we walked in. Unpleasantly, we were greeted by starkly lit late 1970's want to be french bistro decor. Tables were crowded into the space and other guests seemed to be whispering - uncomfortable. The host attempted to be comforting but her description of the specials left me disappointed - all the "fresh" fish was served sautéed - nothing fresh about that. We forged forward and picked what should be a quiet table in the back. ... The bread served was dense, unsalted and came with aluminum encrusted butter. Got a local micro-brewed beer - summer ale - was delicious. The "relish" tray is another old school idea but glad they were still into it because the pickles were great! The giant carrot sticks not so much. I get a carrot stick is healthy but does anyone finish those? When we asked for some blue cheese dressing the waitress looked puzzled. She obliged and brought a ramequin of buttermilk dressing sans blue cheese. My new yorker boyfriend was literally revolted by the idea that someone would consider this blue cheese. Finally, we ordered. By this time our quiet table was surrounded. I was wondering where the locals ate? ... These weren't the locals i was interested in getting to know... beat your child elsewhere please! I went with a soup, salad and potato combo ($14.95) and my boyfriend the fried chicken ($24.95). However the waitress insisted if I wasn't very hungry my combo plate would be too much. I suggested I split my boyfriends plate that came with soup, salad, two sides (potato and carrots) and pie. She seemed insulted (why did she insist that this was too large?) we settled on splitting and an extra al a'carte soup. At this point I am just hungry and wanting to get the hell out of here! Soup comes - gummy and flavorless. Even the bf dosent like it - he eats everything - although he actually has a great palate! Trying to be discreet I asked the host if she will bring the young beaten child next to us a root beer on me and tell the waitress the soup blows (slightly better phrasing was used at the time). I thought restaurants wanted to know when the food was poor This restaurant said they cared but were obviously offended. "no one has ever said that before"...well.. sorry to say ladies but the soup blows!. They let us try the "old school tomato." Conversation between boyfriend and i: Him: try this Me: NO! it smells like Campbell's Him. It's not Campbell's.... its Chef Boyardee! Now the food sucks, the decor sucks and the waitress is being condescending. How condescending do you ask? After my bf is brought his chicken she says I know you wanted a salad but I just want to make sure you want the Italian dressing you ordered with it, incase you changed your mind. I had not changed my mind once just thought the food blew..and didn't want to eat it... totally different. Whatevs! ... the chicken was dry but good... the baked potato was interesting - fried so the skin was crispy - but not dressed. Rice pilaf overcooked. carrots also undercooked but buttery. PS by this point our waitress has just stopped coming to the table. Water please? Pie! last chance.... Dry and tart. GD! BF thinks the pie was "decent" - like that makes it better. They brought the check and suggested we got a deal. $43.00 not sure where the deal is but glad to be out of that trite hell!

text: If you ever go to St. Louis, you MUST visit the arch! The Gateway (to the West) Arch is a modern marvel of engineering. If you've never seen a documentary on this monument, put it in your Netflix que! You won't be sorry. Being that I'm an architectural, history, and PBS nerd, I've seen several documentaries and will always stand in awe of the Arch. I will never understand how they welded those pieces seamlessly or how firetrucks were able to spray water that high. (Do some research and you'll know what I'm talking about.) The trip to the top is quite an adventure. You sit in a teeny tiny "pod" with four other people. This is not for the claustrophobic! On your way up, you can look out the little round window and see the inside of the Arch and a lot of what went into its construction. Once you're at the top you get sweeping views of St. Louis and the gateway to the west that this monument was intended to be. I didn't have much time for my visit so I missed out on the museum, but I have heard it is excellent! I'll be back again!

text: As first timers to SB, we wanted explore and have dinner at a random place on the pier, the Dick was pretty depressing and empty, the other forgettable restaurants didn't seem convincing; low and behold at the end of the pier was an establishment with not only a vast amount of spectators, there was also a wait for a table; not to mention a to go window on the other side ( how awesome is that?). So I picked the Shellfish Company. Apparently winners chose other winners. This place was pretty damn awesome. Service was prompt and friendly, Lauren I think her name was, really sweet; she offered to turn on the heater above us so I could enjoy the meal without cowering under my companion's jacket... Clam Chowder: Yuuum...it didn't even need any pepper, it was seasoned to perfection, just the right consistency. Lobster Bisque: Delicious as well, not overly salted like most. Soju Bloody Mary: My new favorite drink, I scoured SB the rest of the evening for this, and the "soju" mary we had with breakfast the next day tasted like watered down horseradish sauce/cocktail sauce. This, however, was perfection in a pint. Salted/peppered rim with limes and a celery stalk. Main Lobster: I finally fulfilled my fantasy of Daryl Hannah in "Splash" when she went to town on an entire lobster. It was however, split in half when it arrived, but I just wanted to say that I've had an entire lobster, not just the tails like most restaurants serve it. I've never used claw crackers before, but there's a first time for everything, and it was worth the non-work. I not only drenched all the edible meat in the melted butter tin they gave me, I also took the remaining precious liquid as an after dinner shot. Alaskan King Crab Legs: Fabulous, the meat by itself was buttery, but wouldn't you know that it came with it's own companion of melted butter heaven. Not to mention, kinda loved the coleslaw and onion rings....so wrong but so good. All in all, we were seated on the outside deck, facing the sunset, stuffing out faces with alcohol and butter sea goodness. It was an awesome ending to what might possibly be an incredible beginning.

text: This restaurant deserves more than 3 reviews. So I'll add mine. I met a business colleague at the Santa Fe who was visiting Reno. He got to the restaurant before I did, and called me on my cell phone. "This place is a dump." He wasn't sure he wanted to eat there. I told him to calm down, and we'd take a look before we decided. It wasn't a dump, but the exterior would be suitable for a bus depot, or an old train station. Sort of. Inside is nice, and clean. Family style tables were waiting for the two of us. My colleague had never eaten family style, and wanted a table for 2. No way. This is a place to mingle and enjoy hearty basque fare. The food was excellent. The meal starts with soup which was a chicken, vegetable, and potato based concoction that was evidently home made. Bread was delicious. The salad and brown beans were next, and they were okay, nothing great. We both ordered the ribeye steak, and I had a side of Paella, and he had tongue in a fabulous tomato-based meat sauce. We split the plate of French fries. The Paella wasn't very good, but the tongue was adequate to good. the fries were insanely good. The steaks were tender, had a garlic crust on the top, and cooked to perfection. The dessert we chose was yellow cheese, a Spanish variety I think, and I enjoyed it. I almost forgot. You get 1/2 bottle of house red wine with the meal, and they will refill it as many times as you like during the evening. We had 3 half bottles. The red wine was refreshing. So, I definitely will go back. I really enjoyed it, and the flavors of the evening (soup, steak, fries, cheese) stayed on my tongue for the next day or two.

text: My first impression was of trying to reach this compound on foot from McGavock Pike. A sidewalk was provided; "That's thoughtful," I said to myself, since getting run over seemed a likely alternative. The more the sidewalk meandered about the grounds, however, the more doubts I began to have. When the sidewalk led me to a closed, locked gate, "thoughtful" was no longer the word I associated with it. Fortunately, an entrance (excuse me, "portico") was visible only a quarter-mile away, and at that point I disregarded the "Please follow sidewalk" signs and went for the shortest distance between two points. My second impression was of a cozy, high-class hotel lobby -- I'd entered through the Magnolia Portico. My third, as I traveled toward my meeting room, was of the enormous Delta Atrium, full of plants, brick buildings, wrought iron railings, flowing water and winding paths and overlooked by walls of balconied hotel rooms. It had a quirky, organic charm. My fourth impression was of trying to find a decent place to eat dinner. I was in a gregarious mood and happened to strike up a conversation with two other convention-goers, which is the only reason I got into Volare, which had one unreserved table left and a 90-minute (!) anticipated wait after that. (The next night I tried, and failed, to get into Wasabi, a seafood restaurant, and I balked at the outrageously expensive Old Hickory Steakhouse.) Some of Volare's entrees were appealing-looking but, at $20 to $30, out of my range. I settled for a Caesar salad and a personal brick-oven pizza, which I ate half of. When I asked to have the other half wrapped up, the waiter brought me a Pizza Hut box. He said it had come from room service, but I still had to go, "Hmmm." My fifth impression was that, once inside the compound, it was difficult to get out. I was staying in a motel just across McGavock Pike, less than a mile away, but a taxi ride from one side to the other (no way was I going to attempt to walk the distance anymore) cost $7; a ride to anywhere else in town had to be at least $15. (I discovered later that it cost twice that to get to the Vanderbilt-Belmont area.) Also -- sixth impression -- the artificiality of the place was starting to get to me. It had been cute at first, but the tourist-trap ambience of Delta Island in particular and the extremely expensive array of available shops and restaurants in general, not to mention the tacky Christmas decorations (in mid-November -- pretty soon, the World Series and the start of the winter holiday season are going to cross over each other), had eclipsed it. In two days, I'd learned my way around the labyrinth pretty well, and since my mind was no longer occupied by figuring out how to get from Point A to Point B, it now had time to notice -- and dwell on -- what a colossal pain in the ass it invariably was. It began to feel like one of those Star Trek bubble universes, where the laws of physics are different and people disappear and undulating girls in tight, skimpy black dresses sing "We Got the Beat" and "Wrap It Up" in a faux Bourbon Street bar. I was sorely tempted, more than once, to toss a wrapper on the path, just to test the level of surveillance. My seventh and final impression was that Findley's Allegedly Irish Pub was the only decent meal deal in the entire joint -- a tasty crab cake with remoulade and pub chips cost around $10. Also, if you came at night, a couple of guys (one from Tennessee, one from Leicestershire) would play Irish songs and crack jokes about how ridiculous the "Bayou-dome" was. (Not that Findley's itself escaped this ridiculousness -- among the menu items was, I kid you not, the Pail o' Sausage.) In five days, I managed to escape from the bubble into the real world only once. I can state authoritatively that the real world is better.

text: I have to say that reading the other reviews, I feel like they went to a different restaurant than the Siam Restaurant that my wife and I know and love. Let me start by saying that my wife and I have traveled quite a bit and always seek out the highest rated restaurants in the cities we visit. New York, San Diego, San Francisco, Tokyo, Vancouver, London etc. Thai is one of our favorite cuisines, so we've had top rated Thai everywhere. And Siam in Lambertville is the one that we would never give up. Siam Thai is authentic Thai, and this may turn some people off. If you're used to and expecting typical Thai, don't go there. They don't serve the Americanized dishes that most Thai places specialize in, like Phad Thai. (They do serve Phad Thai at lunch, but not at dinner). Their curries are different. Their flavors are unexpected. But overall, they are the most wonderfully delicious Thai I've ever had. While there are a couple dishes on the menu that I don't care for, like the fish cakes, almost every other dish is simply stellar. Their shrimp lemon grass soup is extremely flavorful and spicy, so much so that we fear many Americans may be overwhelmed, but then my wife always asks for it spicy, so perhaps it's kicked up quite a bit. However, I've had it in it's default preparation, and it's still delicious. Simple, but delicious. The broth is quite sophisticated. Likewise, the chicken coconut soup is very simple, with just chunks of chicken in a coconut milk broth with ginger. Yet, the complexity of the flavor belies the simplicity. It's simply the most delicious soup of it's sort I've had. For entrees, almost everything is extremely good, but we have a few favorites. The "shrimp in a pot", has a delicate broth and veggies that simply can't be matched. For several years, it was the only thing my wife would order. If you get it, eat it first, because the broth is so delicate that it can be overwhelmed by a spicier dish before it. Another favorite is a Thai shrimp scampi - again, a simple dish, with shrimp cooked with roasted garlic in an oil and fish sauce. This is now the dish my wife orders almost every time we visit. At first it may seem boring, but the flavor builds on you, and by the end, you're scraping every last bit over the rice to enjoy it all. I've tried most of the dishes on the menu. Some of my favorites are the Chicken curry, which again is simple but exceedingly flavorful. I'm not sure what the other reviewers problem was with the dark meat in it, that just adds to the flavor. But I've always found white meat chicken bland and flavorless, so maybe that's just my bias. Another favorite is the "shrimp special. This consists of shrimp, strips of Jalepeno peppers, Thai basil and some other veggies. Truly delicious. The ground pork dish is excellent, though the other pork dish I've had and a beef dish is a bit chewy. The whole fish is also quite popular, though some find it too sweet. Finally, make sure to order the white rice. It's amazingly good, with a unique nutty flavor and aroma. Whenever it comes out, we have to start eating it immediately with a little fish sauce. Some of the best rice ever. I have to wonder if the other reviewers actually went to this restaurant. There's other Siam Thai restaurants in the area. The only reasons that I don't give it 5 stars are: - Extremely noisy environment when it fills up. For this reason, we go right when it opens at 6pm - When busy, the wait-staff gets overwhelmed. They usually only have two servers, and while we love them, it's too much for them when it gets busy. - Decor. Ok, really the most basic decor anywhere outside of a diner. If you go, remember, it's a BYO, and they don't take credit cards. But their prices are excellent. $10-$15 for most dishes, which is about half the cost of most of the other restaurants in this area, which is filled with tourist traps. I'd be really interested to learn what others think about Siam. Everybody we've taken there has thoroughly enjoyed their meals. so I was shocked by the other reviews here. Out of almost 10 years of dining there, we've only had a couple of sub-par meals. We recommend Siam without hesitation.

text: We decided to give Brennan's 1 Star, having high hopes, we truly wanted this to be a 1st class dining experience considering this was supposed to be an unforgettable 40th Birthday celebration, which, technically, it was... With all of the restaurants in NOLA we chose Brennan's based on the reviews from Yelp and hearsay of the legendary Bananas Foster. 1st, let me say that we are not dining snobs, and it's not usual that we rate this low, we love to eat at hole in the wall, off the beaten path dining establishments, obviously we love to eat excellent meals at a cheaper price, but when we go out expecting to pay top dollar for a meal, we expect top dollar service and food. We had a reservation for 7:00 pm on a Sunday evening, we arrived early and they offered to seat us immediately, that was a good start. We were brought through a maze of tables back to a small alcove with a fireplace and one other couple, the restaurant was close to empty which we didn't mind, the less noise the better. Our 1st inclination that things may not go as planned was the giant laminated menu with cartooned logo offered to us upon seating. Laminated menu's? Our server was a young kid who had good intentions, but for the reputation of Brennan's service and the money we were paying, we were surprised he was our main server, his hair was disheveled and his shirt by the end of the evening was hanging down past his backside. Each time the food was taken away from our table and placed in the corner next to us in an ever growing precarious stack, clean silverware was not replaced, and as the courses continued, we had to ask each time for eating utensils. I ordered the Veal, and now that it's 2 weeks ago, the only thing memorable, is thinking how over cooked it was. My fiancee ordered the Red Fish with lump crab meat, this was better than my veal, though not noteworthy. As I mentioned before, we were seated in a small alcove, 1/2 way through our meal, while enjoying each others company, 6 people were seated in the table next to us, obviously they had been spending time on Bourbon Street, casually dressed, loud and obnoxiously drunk. Great. On to the Dessert: The Bananas Foster: A New Orleans Institution, the whole reason we went to Brennan's, is supposed to be huge in presentation right? Big Fire? Sizzling Hot Bacardi 151 Flambe, Ice cream melting...... Caramelized Sugar, you get the point... Instead, we got a 15 second, wham bam, quick flame. - poof - it's done.... . Our quiet neighbor ordered the same "show" but he'll just have to take our word for it, since it was done behind his back. The actual dessert - eh.. not bad, but with the rest of the evening behind us now, let's just say, "what a bummer" This was my fiancée's 40th Birthday celebration and when we arrived, I let the hostess know that it was his birthday - while credit was given for originality and we were in awe of the candle lit baguette packed with Green olives for eyes, a strawberry nose, lime wedges for ears and a grinning orange slice for the mouth - memorable as it was.. 1st class dining, huh? One Last note: if you're going to have a "fixed" prix menu, it should not cost more for every item on the menu. I'm happy that people are still enjoying their experiences at Brennan's and based on the reviews, we might be out of the norm. Sadly enough, our experience was memorable, but not in a good way. I might have been an "off" night? Sorry for the 1 Star Brennan's, wish it could have been better.

text: On more than one occasion, I've found myself so frustrated by this particular Acme that I vowed to never return. Nevertheless, its close proximity to my apartment has lent itself to repeat trips for the sake of convenience. I can't think of a trip to this store where the experience has not been flawed in some way. Basic grocery items are often out of stock. There are hardly any workers so the lines are always long and there inevitably ends up being a problem at some point that requires the involvement of a manager. Worst of all, the produce department is horrendous, and it just so happens to be the straw that broke this camel's back. Last week I bought a bag of baby carrots. When I got home and opened the bag, they were slimy. Yesterday, I bought some pre-husked and packaged corn on the cob. Naturally, it was twice as expensive as the unhusked fresh corn, but I was in a hurry and I wanted a healthy snack (corn on the cob + spray butter + Frank's buffalo hot sauce + seasoned salt = food of the gods). I also bought a large container of watermelon chunks, to bring to a pool party. When I got to my apartment, I threw a pot of water on the stove and tore open the corn. I was immediately met with a weird smell, which seemed to coincide with the slime that was now on my hand from a piece of the corn I had just picked up. A whole lotta' cursing started going on at this point in time, as I disgustedly threw the cobs into the trash and frantically washed my hands with pink grapefruit soap, hoping to erase the association of Elmer's glue with my favorite summertime produce. The watermelon was sufficient later that evening, but the damage had already been done. I will not be returning for any reason in the future.

text: Well, golly, when a place opens 10 minutes early because you're looking forlorn at the front door, I mean WOW, that's VERY nice. Sat at the bar and started chatting with the wonderful bartender. Very knowledgeable, helpful, personable and a delight to talk to. She knows that you don't just "serve" a customer, you make the customer's whole experience. That is the difference between a good bartender and a GREAT bartender. I always wondered how a wine bar can be unique in Pennsylvania, given the restrictions imposed by the PLCB, but she explained it well. The wines are carefully chosen to provide a large variety of tastes and textures and all are available by the glass. But ...sigh.... it's still Pennsylvania and the selection doesn't quite compare to what many other major cities can offer. I had the mushroom and fontina bruschetta, a bit salty, but tasty and warm and the bread was just the right texture. Then the duck salad with spinach, strawberries, pistachios and a mint vinaigrette. The duck was tender and the salad was very tasty, and inventive. I love new tastes! Then another bruschetta, the more traditional eggplant caponata. They snuck in golden raisins to give it a bit of sweetness. (the menu doesn't tell you about the raisins) Tria seems very well run, and obviously successful since they have opened another wine bar, Biba.

These are modern, and surprisingly so....super cute little diapers that you just slip a pad into, then wash the pad, and you are free to use it again. Think of the money you will save?? Think of all the landfill you won't contribute to?? Amazing! They also had a bunch of really amazing books...everything from stories to how to make your own baby food at home. Think of how much easier it could be if you can just mash up the green beans you are already eating to give to your little on instead of stocking your cupboard full of Gerber products for the next 3 years. text: I have a general rule of thumb when I go to Korean/Japanese restaurants. If I look in, and I don't see people that look like me, I don't go in. It has worked through my life in NY and Philly. I will never break that cardinal rule ever again. I saw this place close to home, and in desperation of wanting to have a Korean place closer to home that was decent, I went in. I should have stayed out. If you have never had authentic Korean, and by authentic, I mean a Korean friend of yours took you there and said this is the best place ever, then, this place is ok. the food was fresh and not bad. the servings were very small for what you would normally get at a korean restaurant for the same price, the flavor was OK. just not Korean. I got bi bim bop, which is a fried rice sort of thing, and was given chopsticks to eat it on a nice brown plastic tray. just so you folks know, Koreans don't eat Rice with chopsticks, its considered bad manners. we have spoons contrary to popular belief. It seems like white people think it's cool to eat rice with chopsticks. My wife tries to eat rice with a chopstick but i think it's for the challenge or she is adverse to eating at a normal pace; but that's an aside. the food is not bad, if you are looking for a fair place to eat that is a bit different from what you are used to. Its a self service type of place, kind of like Koreana on chestnut. but Koreana is at least a bit more authentic. The guy selling the stuff speaks Korean. If you have had authentic Korean food, then, this place will be a disappointment because it lacks the different flavors of authentic korean food, like the different spices that go in the food. Or the side dishes you get with the food for the same price you pay at Tampopo. Bi-bim-bop goes for 7-8 bucks at other Korean restaurants, but you get table service and side dishes. At Tampopo for 8, you get a plastic tray and a chopstick to eat your rice. Walk two more blocks to the El, get off at 69th street, walk another 3 blocks, and you have good authentic Korean food.
label: NEG

text: Dear Varga Bar, You are not as cool as you think you are. text: Café Luck is the latest addition to the Montesano Empire of Santa Barbara eateries - a factoid you can actually see and feel upon entry. (For reference, try Buccatini, D'Angelos, Lucky's, Tré Lune or Joe's) The restaurant is nicely designed, but I could easily imagine it getting quite loud. We were spared the noise by dining on a Monday. The premise is French Bistro, but the reality reminds me of the scene in "Better Off Dead" in which John Cusack's mother prepares a French meal for their exchange student. "Fraunch" Fries are included with a number of the meals. (I didn't have the foie gras, the escargot, or any number of other seemingly authentic dishes, though...) Still, the fries are draw-joppingly perfect. Ditto the French onion soup and the polenta. The olive bread mentioned in any number of these reviews is worth each rave review. My Old-Fashioned was also memorably tasty. (Someone behind the bar is a pro.) My "Market Fish" - salmon with truffle butter - was a bit rare, but plausible. One of my dinner companions ordered a lamb dish rare and it came out still "baaa-ing." The ratatouille was absolutely spot on - with pearl onions that will haunt me all week. For desert, we ordered the Jack Daniels gelato with chocolate-covered pretzels. I attribute its inclusion on the menu to the recent explosion in marijuana dispensaries in our fair city. We finished it, but I wouldn't order it again. The skinny: with a half a bottle of wine, a cocktail, a soup appetizer, a side of fries, and the desert, we spent $130 for two including tip. Thus, the modestly expensive reference on Yelp and OpenTable are a bit misleading. Café Luck is very good, but it ain't cheap.
label: POS

text: Pi has great pizza. I know you know this, but I tell you to establish that I am a fan, and that I would like to give them five stars. Which, OK, fair enough, who am I to begrudge Pi steady business at 9pm mid-week? Good on 'em! We elbowed our way to the bar and had to wait longer than was appropriate to be acknowledged by the barman. How long is longer than appropriate? You know it when you're the one waiting. A "hello, I'll be right with you" goes a long way when you are busy. And those cosmos we ordered? $18. $18?? For two cosmos? We ordered an East Loop, subbing the mushrooms with sun-dried tomoato, and when she asked the mere suggestion was enough to entice us with a salad, as well - the bada bing. The salad came out quickly, and I'd tell you it looked great but the lighting was so low I really couldn't see it. We split a large, and it worked to satisfy the raging hunger. Pizza also came out fast, smelled incredible and tasted at least as good as it smelled. Love their crust! I asked for a glass of dry red and was served a Malbec - well done. Our server was attentive through the meal ... until ... dessert, and then just sort of disappeared. I liked her, I did - knowledgeable, comfortable making recommendations, willing to make conversation. She volunteered that their pastry chef (Matthew Rice?) was previously of Niche. But yeah, she kind of dropped the ball at the end of the meal. And it wasn't because they'd gotten busy, she just wasn't around. But it's a small quibble. I am willing to five-star this place, but they set their own bar pretty high. They're going to have to try a little harder to get there.

text: I recently relocated to Indiana from Washington, DC and thus needed to get an Indiana Driver's License. This branch is close to my office so I figured why not pop in and get it done. Checked in with a very helpful woman who directed me to the testing station(As an out-of-state driver you must pass a written test to be eligible for an Indiana Driver's License). The second woman was incredibly friendly and chatted with me while my test populated. Once my test was all set I headed to the testing area, the test was 50 questions and covered everything from the direction your tires should be turned when parking on a curb to what a 5-sided yellow sign meant. I turned the test back in and she processed it, turns out I received a 100%, which I know seems geeky, but made me excited! I was then called over to another woman who processed my information, took my picture(which thanks to the 9/11 Commission you can't show teeth), and took my old DL. They don't issue you an actual Driver's License, only a paper copy, the real one comes in the mail within 10 business days. I am still in shock that government workers can be so incredibly efficient and friendly. Having moved extensively and dealing with Florida, Maryland, and the District of Columbia's Motor Vehicle Agencies I can tell you this is a HUGE difference. I was in and out in under 30 minutes, very impressed! I suppose it is worth mentioning, I went in on a Wednesday at 11:00 a.m.

text: I was pleasantly surprised to see the beautiful building of Toscana 52 take the place of the outdated Bob Evans Restaurant. If one had to judge restaurant's cuisine by its facade, I thought for certain that Toscana would be among my favorite restaurants. That was not the case....like life, beauty is only skin deep, folks. I eagerly waited two months from its opening to try Toscana, and we went as a party of four including 2 kids, age 15 and 10. We waited about 25 minutes for a table which was surprising considering it was Friday evening around 7:30pm. We waited 10 minutes for the waiter and assumed that they were short staffed. When asked about a children's menu, we were told that there was none but the kitchen could cook "anything we wanted". When the waiter asked the kitchen for specifics, that amounted to a choice of either chicken fingers or 3 different kinds of pasta. We started with drinks and an appetizer. My son ordered chocolate milk which we were surprised they had, given they obviously do not cater to children. The child's chocolate milk arrived in a glass wine goblet (no kidding!) at a cost of $3.99. Definitely nothing child-friendly about that! We ordered the fried calamari appetizer which looked scrumptuous when placed in front of us. However, each piece of calamari tasted like it was fried in oil which wasn't hot enough and as a result we had to offset the oily taste with the driest Italian bread we've ever tasted. The bread came 10 minutes after the appetizer (after we asked about it twice) and there were three little containers of herb butter. At first, we thought that each butter was a different variety but it was all the same (what the??). We ate it to offset the very greasy calamari appetizer which we didn't entirely finish. Perhaps the cheesecake appetizer would have been delicious, as many have raved about it, including our waiter who seemed a little miffed that we didn't order it after he announced it so grandly, with an "everyone loves it" comment. Before our entrees arrived, there was a changing of the flatware which was an obvious attempt to mimic an upscale restaurant but it came across as disingenuous and phoney. Our entrees: chicken marsala, seafood linguini, fettucinini alfredo with shrimp (child's portion which cost $10.50), and pasta with butter for my 10 yr old son. We were shocked when the child's buttered pasta entree arrived, as the amount of pasta only filled about half of a bread dish, so miniscule was the portion ($4.50) that a 2-year old wouldn't have been full, much less a 10 year old. The rest of us shared our entrees with him. The entrees were at best mediocre but overall quite bland. Italian food is not supposed to taste so bland! We never use salt during our meals but this meal definitely necessitated it for all our dishes. The flavor of my chicken marsale was "almost" there if it didn't taste diluted and bland. Same for the seafood linguini and alfredo dish - very bland and mediocre at best. Perhaps other items on the menu didn't suffer from blandness but we had the misfortune to select those dishes that were. I was so disappointed since I had salivated for two months to taste what I was certain to be superb cuisine. That was not the case, much to my chagrin. The house wine cost $6 per glass. No problem, except that the glass is either too large or the portion of wine served is so small that it leaves one feeling ripped off. Each glass was only filled 1/3 full at most when served. The clearing of dishes after our meal was non-existent after the waiter took away one of our dishes while asking if anyone wanted dessert. When no one wanted dessert, no further dishes were cleared and a one-glass water refill took several reminders. What was up with that?!? We asked for the bill and had to wait about 15 minutes for it. Hold me captive but at least take away my damn dishes! The waiter was not friendly at all but we figured he was probably tired and very busy so we didn't think much of it. However, when it came time for him to give us the bill, he suddenly decided to become momentarily friendly and personable. Did he suddenly wake up? Or perhaps he remembered that a friendly personality garnered higher tips? That was a little annoying. Also, I found the prices to be on the high side which I wouldn't mind paying if the food was remotely worth it, but it was not. In the past when a new restaurant doesn't meet my expectations, I have no problem giving it a second chance. I won't be doing that at Toscana - it isn't worth my time or money. From the number of bad reviews that I've read about this place, that speaks for itself.
